WAL-CLM-DDDL-000363.claim_text: Wallach treats infections with echinacea, golden seal and garlic, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, vitamin A 300,000 IU/day as beta-carotene, zinc 15 mg t.i.d., selenium 500-1,000 mcg/day, Isoprinosin, Ribavirin, and IV hydrogen peroxide, reserving antibiotics and antifungals for lifesaving situations.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000363.verbatim:
Treatment of infections should include the use of echinacea (Echinacea
angustifolia), golden seal (Hydrastis canadensis), garlic (Allium sativum),
vitamin C to bowel tolerance, vitamin A at 300,000 IU/day as beta-carotene, zinc at 15 mg t.i.d., selenium at 500-1,000 mcg/day, Isoprinosin at
100-300 mg/day, Ribavirin, H2O2 in an IV infusion over four hours;
antibiotics and antifungal medications are sometimes necessary in
lifesaving situations.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000364.claim_text: Wallach says a hiatal hernia commonly causes gas, reflux, and chest pain that mimics a heart attack, and that more than 40 percent of Americans have an undetected hiatal hernia by x-ray.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000364.verbatim:
HIATAL HERNIA is usually a congenital birth defect (not genetic) of the
diaphragm. It can also be caused by crushing the chest or abdomen as in an
auto accident. Gas, dyspepsia, reflux, and chest pain that mimics a “heart
attack” are common symptoms. It is said that more than 40 percent of the
USA population has asymptomatic hiatal hernia by actual x-ray survey!

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000365.claim_text: Wallach says gallbladder attacks are caused by the gallbladder muscles cramping after a fatty meal, or a gallstone temporarily blocking the bile duct.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000365.verbatim:
Gallbladder
“attacks” are caused by a cramping of the muscles in the gallbladder after a
fatty meal or a temporary blockage of the bile duct by a gallstone.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000366.claim_text: Wallach says the signals of a kidney or bladder stone are blood in the urine and pain or 'colic' that gets worse in the bladder or kidney area, confirmed by x-ray.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000366.verbatim:
BLADDER STONES (kidney stones, cystic calculi) are ironically caused
by a calcium and/or a magnesium deficient diet and when you
have raging osteoporosis. The minerals in the
“stones” come from your own bones!!! Diagnosis may require an x-ray (a
flat “plate” of the abdomen). Don’t forget the gonadal shield!!! The signal
to think “stones” is blood in the urine (use the urine test sticks) and pain or
“colic” that gets worse in the bladder or kidney area.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000367.claim_text: Wallach defines alopecia (baldness) as loss of hair that can be local or total, with male pattern baldness, female pattern baldness, and alopecia universalis as examples.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000367.verbatim:
ALOPECIA: (baldness): loss of hair, which can occur locally or present as
total hair loss. Male pattern baldness, female pattern baldness, and alopecia
universalis are examples.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000368.claim_text: For fingernail problems, Wallach recommends collagen/gelatin (100% Kosher beef, diabetic Jello, or Knox gelatin — especially important for former vegetarians), essential fatty acids at 5 gm t.i.d., and betaine HCl with pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 mg t.i.d. before meals.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000368.verbatim:
Treatment of fingernail problems should include collagen (Willamette
Valley which is 100 percent Kosher beef, diabetic Jello, or Knox gelatin—
this is especially important for those who have been vegetarians for any
length of time), essential fatty acids at 5 gm t.i.d., and betaine HCl and
pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 mg t.i.d. before meals.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000369.claim_text: Wallach notes that losing sodium and potassium — as in Addison's disease or heavy sweating — brings general weakness and muscle cramps with a marked "salt hunger," relieved by replacing salt (NaCl).
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000369.verbatim:
Addison’s
Disease, a loss of function of the adrenal cortex,
results in the loss of Na and K retention with clinical signs of general
weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss, and a marked “salt hunger.” The
symptoms can be relieved with the supplementation of NaCl or by
administering adrenal cortical hormones.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000370.claim_text: Wallach describes hemorrhoids (piles) as varicose veins in the rectum and anus that itch, bleed, become painful, and eventually clot (thrombose).
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000370.verbatim:
HEMORRHOIDS (piles) are varicose veins in the rectum and anus that
itch, bleed, become painful, and eventually blocked with clots
(thrombosed).

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000371.claim_text: Wallach uses the pulse test to pin down the individual food triggering irritable bowel syndrome -- commonly wheat, milk, or soy -- then has you eliminate the offending foods.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000371.verbatim:
The pulse test is an
extremely useful test for determining the individual cause of irritable bowel
syndrome.
Treatment of irritable bowel syndrome should include high fiber diets, 4-6
cups of fruit and vegetables per day, elimination of fried food, margarine,
caffeine, sugar, and offending foods based on the pulse test (i.e. wheat,
milk, soy),

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000372.claim_text: Wallach says gallstones generally come from liver problems, especially with fat and cholesterol metabolism.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000372.verbatim:
GALLBLADDER DISEASE (gall stones) is generally caused by liver
problems, especially with fat and cholesterol metabolism.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000373.claim_text: For gout, Wallach recommends avoiding organ meats, seafood, lentils, beans, and peas, along with alcohol and fructose sources, because these foods drive up uric acid.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000373.verbatim:
Treatment for gout should include an avoidance of alcohol, organ meats,
seafood, lentils, beans, peas, and fructose sources.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000374.claim_text: Wallach says lactation can be reduced and engorgement pain relieved by goldenrod, and Luperon (a posterior pituitary hormone) can stop milk production, though it may cause temporary menopausal symptoms.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000374.verbatim:
LACTATION (reduce) can be reduced and breast pain of engorgement can
be relieved by goldenrod (Solidago petradoria). Luperon, a posterior
pituitary hormone can stop milk production; however, side effects include
temporary menopausal symptoms.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000375.claim_text: Because copper builds the elastic fibers in vein walls, Wallach recommends copper at 2 mg per day for varicose veins and suggests trying a copper bracelet.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000375.verbatim:
Treatment of varicose veins should include vitamin C to bowel tolerance,
vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, zinc at 50 mg t.i.d., bioflavonoids at 600
mg t.i.d., DMSO, hydrotherapy, copper at 2 mg per day (try a copper
bracelet)

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000376.claim_text: Wallach explains that gout (gouty arthritis) is caused by deposits of uric acid crystals in the joints and surrounding tissues, classically the great toe of each foot, which become very tender and may deform in long-standing cases.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000376.verbatim:
GOUT (gouty arthritis) is caused by deposits of uric acid crystals in the
joints and surrounding tissues. These joints, classically the great toe of each
foot, are very tender and may become deformed in chronic or long-standing
cases.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000377.claim_text: Wallach argues that food allergies drive emotional problems like depression indirectly — the celiac-type gut damage they cause blocks absorption of the essential nutrients the body and nervous system need.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000377.verbatim:
FOOD ALLERGIES (sensitivities) are a concern for everyone. The reason
is that the celiac disease type changes they cause in your intestines will
prevent the absorption of essential nutrients that are required to keep your
immune system, as well as your various organs, maintained, repaired, and
in tip top working order. Many of the maladies caused by food allergies are
not a direct cause but rather an indirect cause by cutting off the flow of
essential raw materials necessary for your body to repair itself. A list of
symptoms of food allergies would perhaps fill ten pages of this book.
Suffice it to be said that if you have any chronic disease (i.e. cancer,
diabetes, arthritis, heart disease, etc.) and/or emotional problems (i.e.
hypoglycemia, depression, neurosis, schizophrenia, hyperactivity, paranoia,
etc.) you have food allergies and hypoglycemia!

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000378.claim_text: Wallach says diverticulitis treatment should include not just colonics, high fiber, water, and exercise, but also the 90 essential nutrients.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000378.verbatim:
Treatment of diverticulitis includes colonics two to three times per week,
high fiber diet, eight glasses of water per day, and regular exercise. Avoid
fried foods, margarine, and caffeine. Don’t forget the 90 essential nutrients.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000379.claim_text: Wallach explains motion sickness as the vertigo, nausea and 'green at the gills' feeling that hits when angular and linear movement happen at once; fixing your gaze on a single fixed point helps on a ship's deck but not in a car.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000379.verbatim:
CARSICKNESS (motion sickness, sea sickness, air sickness, or motion
sickness) is common in some individuals when repetitive angular and linear
movement occur at the same time. Fixing the gaze on a single geographic
point can help in seasickness when the patient is on deck but is a fruitless
exercise in other forms of motion sickness. Symptoms include “green at the
gills” feeling including vertigo, nausea, and vomiting.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000380.claim_text: Wallach states that stomach ulcers are brought on by infection with Helicobacter pylori, and that antibiotics for 4 to 6 weeks are a preferred treatment of gastric ulcers over surgery.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000380.verbatim:
ULCER (stomach) is brought on by an infection with Helicobacter pylori.
Antibiotics for 4 to 6 weeks are a preferred treatment of gastric ulcers over
surgery.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000381.claim_text: Wallach says selenium deficiency in young adults appears as anemia and chronic fatigue, together with muscular weakness, myalgia, and fibromyalgia.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000381.verbatim:
In young adults, selenium deficiency appears as anemia, chronic fatigue,
muscular weakness, myalgia, fibromyalgia, muscular tenderness,
pancreatitis, infertility, muscular dystrophy, scoliosis, and cardiomyopathy.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000382.claim_text: Wallach observed that even dolphins and whales get kidney stones, arthritis and osteoporosis, especially when they feed almost exclusively on soft-bodied squid.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000382.verbatim:
Deficiency diseases plague even the playful dolphins (and
whales), though they’re subject to arthritis, osteoporosis, and kidney stones,
especially if they feed almost exclusively on the soft bodied squid.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000383.claim_text: For muscle cramps and twitching legs, Wallach's treatment includes liquid plant-derived colloidal calcium, magnesium, and potassium, plus betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 mg three times a day before meals, and he says his Pig Arthritis Formula works like a charm.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000383.verbatim:
Treatment of muscle cramps can include liquid plant derived colloidal
calcium, magnesium, and potassium, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes
at 75-200 mg t.i.d. before meals. Dr. Wallach’s Pig Arthritis Formula works
like a charm here.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000384.claim_text: For hemorrhoids Wallach recommends a high-fiber diet, adding two heaping tablespoons of oat bran in eight ounces of juice or water before bed to encourage two bowel movements a day so stools pass without straining.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000384.verbatim:
Treatment of hemorrhoids includes high fiber diets (you may need to add
oat bran at two heaping tbsp. in eight oz. of juice or water before bed) to
encourage two bowel movements per day,

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000385.claim_text: Wallach's IBS diet emphasizes high fiber with 4-6 cups of fruit and vegetables a day and eight to ten glasses of water, and he says a macrobiotic diet can be of great benefit.
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000385.verbatim:
Treatment of irritable bowel syndrome should include high fiber diets, 4-6
cups of fruit and vegetables per day, elimination of fried food, margarine,
caffeine, sugar, and offending foods based on the pulse test (i.e. wheat,

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000389.claim_text: Wallach attributes PMS to calcium and essential-fatty-acid deficiencies and treats it with B6 at 100 mg, EFAs at 5 grams t.i.d., vitamin A during the last 14 days of the cycle, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU/day, and calcium from colloidal sources.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000390.claim_text: Wallach says an under-active thyroid frequently causes fatigue (and weight gain and edema) even without a goiter, and you can screen for it with a basal body temperature test -- take your temperature under your armpit before getting up, and a reading below 97.6 F indicates low thyroid.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000391.claim_text: Wallach says eczema is usually caused by food allergies, most often to cow's milk, wheat, and soy, and that pulse tests and elimination diets pinpoint the culprit foods.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000393.claim_text: Wallach identifies drug side effects as a cause of ringing in the ears, and includes eliminating those drug effects in the treatment.

RINGING IN THE EARS (tinnitus, Miniar’s disease, and Wallach’s

of choice.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000394.claim_text: In treating alopecia that occurs with eczema, Wallach calls betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 mg three times a day, 15-20 minutes before meals, “a must.”

mg t.i.d. is also indicated. Elimination of wheat and cow’s milk from the

at 75-200 mg t.i.d. 15-20 minutes before meals are a must.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000395.claim_text: Wallach describes ADD/ADHD as hyperactivity plus an inability to concentrate and retain information, often with disruptive, mean or cruel behavior toward other children and small animals, bedwetting, nightmares, and a fascination with fire.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000398.claim_text: Wallach warns that osteoporosis is a common result of an improperly managed menopause.

Osteoporosis is a common result of
improperly managed menopause.

by bone pain, joint pain, “dowagers” hump, and “spontaneous” fractures.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000400.claim_text: Wallach explains that the extra pressure of straining to force out a hard, constipated stool balloons the hemorrhoidal veins, so low-fiber diets and the constipation they cause are a direct mechanical driver of hemorrhoids.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000401.claim_text: Wallach says that in its most severe form sciatica is the result of advanced osteoporosis, bone spurs between the lumbar vertebrae, and vertebral arthritis.

In its most severe
form, sciatica may be the result of advanced osteoporosis, bone spurs
between the lumbar vertebrae, and vertebral arthritis.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000402.claim_text: For herpes cold sores, Wallach lists a topical herb compress made with walnut (Juglans nigra) among the treatments.

HERPES (simplex, cold sores, canker sores) is a virus that causes recurrent

Herpes.

commercial products available for topical application.

Wallach surveys how congenital birth defects ('monsters') were understood across the centuries -- from Renaissance omens and divine-punishment interpretations (the 1512 Monster of Ravenna; Ambroise Pare's 1573 catalogue of supposed causes), through the great teratological collections (Willem Vrolik's cyclops/holoprosencephaly specimens), to the modern recognition of chemical and drug teratogens exemplified by the 1961 thalidomide ('seal-limb') limb-defect epidemic. Both doctors believed that the defects were caused by the use of a sedative (phtalimido-glutarimide) by the trade name Thalidomide (the third-best selling pharmaceutical in Europe)."

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000022.claim_text: Wallach cites neuroanatomical research as evidence that homosexuality reflects a congenital difference in brain structure. He acknowledges a limitation -- some men in LeVay's study had died of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which can damage brain cells -- but notes other brain regions were unaffected. He adds that Roger Gorski's 1978 work at the University of California, Los Angeles found a prenatal testosterone surge stabilizes these cell populations in males. Wallach attributes the differences to a congenital malformation or biochemical deficiency event -- ultimately a congenital deficiency of minerals.

He cites Richard Pillard and Michael Bailey's finding that only 52 percent of the identical twins of homosexual men were themselves homosexual -- reasoning that a purely genetic trait would require 100 percent concordance -- with lower rates among fraternal and adopted brothers, and a parallel study of 147 homosexual women showing about 48 percent identical-twin concordance. He quotes geneticist Dean Hamer of the National Cancer Institute that "it is a mistake to think there is a gay gene," and concludes the consistent-but-incomplete twin concordance points to a congenital deficiency event during embryonic development rather than a genetic defect or a choice.

He argues the gradual increase in homosexuality in America and other industrialized nations parallels the gradual decrease in the mineral content of farm and range soils, and therefore of the food supply. WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000060.claim_text: Wallach describes three basic forms of minerals and their very different bioavailability. WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000064.claim_text: Wallach reports that although silver is not required by any known biological system, many researchers consider it an essential element for its role as a systemic disinfectant and immune-system support. WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000065.claim_text: Wallach identifies aluminum's known biological function as activating the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase and increasing newborn survival, and reports that Professor Gerhard Schrauzer (former chair of chemistry at the University of California, San Diego) argues it should be classed as an essential mineral for all vertebrates including humans. He stresses that aluminum is remarkably nontoxic at dietary levels -- far less toxic than heavy metals -- and that it competes with calcium absorption, so excess can reduce skeletal mineralization. He explicitly rejects the popular fear that aluminum causes Alzheimer's disease, citing the 1992 Oxford study (Frank Watt and colleagues, in Nature) that found identical brain-aluminum levels in Alzheimer's patients and controls, and the Alzheimer's Society's 2013 position that no causal link has been demonstrated.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000065.verbatim:
The known biological function of aluminum is to activate the enzyme succinic
dehydrogenase; it increases the survival rate of the newborn

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000066.claim_text: Wallach presents arsenic as an essential trace element -- known to be essential for survivability of the newborn and for neonatal growth. He notes arsenic promotes the growth rate of chicks, that the growth and metamorphosis of tadpoles is enhanced by its presence, that in combination with choline it prevents 100 percent of perosis ('slipped tendon') in poultry, and that its role in human physiology lies in methyl-group metabolism and polyamine synthesis. He distinguishes organically-bound arsenic from metallic arsenic, which carries 65 times greater toxicity potential, and recounts that low doses of arsenic trioxide are effective against acute promyelocytic leukemia, a cancer of the blood and bone marrow, with FDA approval of the compound in 2000 and 'Fowler's solution' used for psoriasis.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000066.verbatim:
Arsenic promotes the growth rate of chicks at 90 to 120 ppm. The rate of
growth and metamorphosis of tadpoles is enhanced by the presence of arsenic.

He notes the standard intramuscular schedule (10 milligrams rising to 50 milligrams weekly to a one-gram total), warns it is contraindicated in liver, kidney, and blood disease and in lupus, and lists toxic reactions including itching, dermatitis, mouth inflammation, gastrointestinal upset, blood in the urine, aplastic anemia, and hepatitis.

Barium sulfate has a very low toxicity and relatively high density and has

Robbin Warren proposed in 1983.

Cadmium can substitute for zinc in zinc deficiency states by its ability

Salt (sodium chloride) is the universal source of chloride ions. He also recounts chlorine's public-health legacy: Labarraque's chlorinated-lime solutions and Semmelweis's 1847 chlorine hand-disinfection that ended the spread of childbed fever, and the 1918 mandate to chlorinate United States drinking water.

Essential for all living organisms and electrochemical and catalytic functions,

cells to manufacture HCl for stomach acidity

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000077.claim_text: Cobalt is essential because it is the metal at the center of vitamin B12 (cobalamin): a single cobalt atom sits in B12's tetrapyrrole ring, and the vitamin acts as a cofactor for transferring methyl groups -- with folic acid, choline, and methionine -- to build RNA and DNA, and for myelin formation and red-blood-cell synthesis. He prefers 250 to 400 micrograms a day (above the 3-to-4 microgram conventional allowance), notes calcium is required for B12 to cross the intestinal wall, and warns that cobalt excess (20 to 30 milligrams a day) can drive erythropoiesis; cobalt is also a cofactor for thyroid-hormone production.

parasites (tapeworm), celiac disease, gluten intolerance, and other malabsorption
diseases. Pernicious anemia

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000082.claim_text: Wallach holds a dual stance on fluorine/fluoride. On one hand he accepts it as an essential trace mineral: prior to 1972 fluoride was thought essential only for warding off dental caries (cavities) via tooth enamel, and in 1972 the researcher Schwarz proved fluoride to be a genuine essential mineral. On the other hand he treats water fluoridation as highly controversial and links it to cancer. Following 1977 epidemiological studies by Yiamouyiannis and Burk, full-scale congressional hearings examined the charge that 10,000 excess cancer deaths were caused by fluoridating certain public water systems. The resulting U.S. National Toxicology Program animal study, reported in 1990, found increased precancerous lesions and squamous-cell carcinoma of the oral mucous membranes, a rare osteosarcoma (bone cancer) at double the rate in males as females, and a significant increase in thyroid follicular-cell tumors and liver cancer. Clinical fluoride toxicity appears as dental fluorosis at 2 to 7 parts-per-million and osteosclerosis at 8 to 20 parts-per-million, with chronic systemic toxicity at 20 to 80 milligrams per day over years; the average American already takes in about 4.4 milligrams per day from food, toothpaste, supplements and water.

In 1990 the results of the fluoride study showed an increase in rat
precancerous lesions in the oral mucus membrane cells; there was an increase
in cancers of the oral mucus membranes (squamous cell carcinoma); a rare
form of osteosarcoma appeared at double the rate in males as females;

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000083.claim_text: Iron is an essential mineral; a healthy adult carries 3 to 5 grams, most of it in hemoglobin and myoglobin, where iron carries oxygen (iron is to hemoglobin what magnesium is to chlorophyll). Wallach stresses that pica -- obsessive cravings driving children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia), dirt (geophagia), lead-paint chips and high-calorie snack foods -- is a specific sign of iron deficiency, and that the snack-food form can cause weight gain and obesity. Iron deficiency arises from unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation, chronic infection, hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid from salt-restricted diets or proton-pump inhibitors), chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding, and impaired absorption from high-fat or high-phytate diets and gluten intolerance. Its symptoms include listlessness, fatigue, heart palpitations on exertion, rapid pulse (tachycardia), reduced cognition and memory, sore tongue, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and hypochromic microcytic anemia. Stomach hydrochloric acid and vitamin C aid absorption; heme iron from meat is 10 percent absorbable versus 1 percent from plants (phytates bind it). He notes excess iron storage can be caused by deficiencies of selenium, copper or zinc and is falsely blamed for liver cirrhosis, pancreatic fibrosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes.

tongue, angular stomatitis, dysphagia (pica), hypochromic microcytic anemia,

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000084.claim_text: Wallach's stance on gallium -- a trace element claimed to be essential in 1938 and again in 1958 -- centers on the brain and brain cancer. Gallium maltolate, an orally absorbable form of the gallium ion, is used in medical treatments for brain cancer, inflammation and certain infectious diseases. Because gallium and ferric (iron) salts behave similarly in biological systems, gallium ions often mimic iron ions in medical applications.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000087.claim_text: Hydrogen is an essential structural element: it is the major constituent of water (about 70 percent of the human body is water) and of all organic molecules, and Wallach frames the body's acid-base balance as, in fact, the regulation of hydrogen-ion (H+) levels in cellular and extracellular fluids. Healthy blood pH ranges from 7.36 to 7.44; below 7.30 is acidosis and above 7.44 is alkalosis, while values below 6.8 or above 7.8 are rapidly fatal. The body controls hydrogen-ion concentration by dilution, buffering (reacting in fractions of a second), respiration (minutes) and the kidney (up to hours or days). Large amounts of hydrogen ions are generated or retained in disease states such as emphysema, diabetes, anxiety, chloride loss, cystic fibrosis and Addison's disease. He notes a practical corollary: bladder infections (cystitis) can often be controlled by acidifying the urine with unsweetened cranberry juice.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000087.verbatim:
Hydrogen functions as a major constituent of water (70% of the human body
is water) and all organic molecules. The regulation of the acid-base balance in the
human body is in fact the regulation of the hydrogen ion (H+) levels of cellular
and extracellular fluids.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000091.claim_text: Mercury occurs universally in living things and is a well-known toxic element; Wallach traces its accumulation to industry, mining, agriculture, dental amalgam fillings, and micro-organisms that convert it to methyl mercury in aquatic sediments. Methyl mercury (the form in fish) crosses the placenta easily and has a biological half-life of about 70 days; heavy fish eaters, especially of large predators such as shark, tuna and swordfish, can reach tissue levels up to 400 micrograms per kilogram. Direct mercury poisoning is primarily neurological -- tremors, vertigo, irritability, moodiness, depression, salivation, inflammation of the mouth (stomatitis) and diarrhea -- while poisoning with the more toxic alkyl mercury progresses to loss of coordination, vision and hearing. Wallach notes selenium and mercury are mutually antagonistic: selenium protects the kidney from mercury-induced tissue death (necrosis) and limits placental transfer. He cites the 1962 Minamata Bay disaster in Japan and a mass poisoning in Iran (bread from mercury-treated seed grain) as producing congenital brain defects, cerebral palsy and infant deaths, and relays the theory that dental-amalgam vapor is linked to multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, Lou Gehrig's disease) and Parkinson's disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000096.claim_text: Wallach presents lithium as an essential trace mineral for mental and behavioral health, not merely a pharmaceutical. He states that in humans, clinical depression, manic depression, 'bi-polar' disease and autism are hallmarks of lithium deficiency, and that hyperactivity, attention-deficit disorder (ADD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) belong to the same picture. WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000098.claim_text: Magnesium is essential to all living organisms, second only to potassium as an intracellular cation; the adult body holds 20 to 28 grams, about 60% of it in bone. It powers energy production and protein synthesis, muscle contractility and nerve excitability, is a cofactor for countless enzymes, and is a constituent of chlorophyll. Calcium and magnesium play antagonistic roles in muscle -- calcium the stimulator, magnesium the relaxer -- so an excess of calcium can induce magnesium-deficiency signs, and an excess of magnesium inhibits bone calcification. Wallach lists a wide range of magnesium-deficiency diseases and symptoms: asthma, anorexia, menstrual migraines, growth failure, electrocardiogram (ECG) changes, neuromuscular problems, tetany and convulsions, depression, muscular weakness, muscle tics, tremors, vertigo, and calcification of the small arteries and soft tissue. Absorption ranges from about 24% for metallic sources to 85% for plant-derived colloidal sources; fat, phytates and calcium reduce it while vitamin D has no effect. He notes there is no evidence of toxicity up to 6,000 milligrams per day when the kidneys are healthy.

early postnatal life, Wallach was summarily terminated in April of 1978 from his
Position at Yerke's without the ability to defend his observations

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000186.claim_text: Keshan disease is named for Keshan Province, China, where Wallach autopsied 1,700 children under ten and documented death by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — a thickened, failing heart muscle — traced to selenium deficiency in the local diet. He argues the collapses of seemingly healthy young athletes are the same disease: not a mysterious “silent” defect but selenium-starved heart muscle giving out under exertion. His prescription is equally direct — a complete 90-essential-nutrient program with extra selenium, and, he says, “the athlete can live.” It's the human echo of what he watched selenium do in livestock, where the identical heart-muscle disease (“mulberry heart disease”) was eliminated by simple selenium supplementation.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000186.verbatim:
In fact, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy,
sudden heart death of athletes, is KSD and is caused by a simple deficiency
of the trace element selenium. Supplement a complete 90 nutrient program
with extra selenium and the athlete can live.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000187.claim_text: The richest dietary selenium, in Wallach's telling, comes from organ meats — liver and kidneys — plus eggs and some high-selenium rice varieties (a plant's selenium depends heavily on the soil it grew in). He raises these specifically around cystic fibrosis, which he frames as a prenatal selenium deficiency: “Normal selenium levels in pregnant women will prevent CF.” But he attaches the caveat that runs through his whole framework — “you are not what you eat, you are what you absorb.” A gut damaged by gluten can't take up selenium even when it's on the plate, which is why he pairs selenium-rich food (or supplements) with a gluten-free diet rather than trusting diet alone.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000187.verbatim:
Wallach says the key to its prevention and cure is selenium, a trace
element found in liver, eggs, kidneys and some varieties of high selenium
rice.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000188.claim_text: Conventionally, cystic fibrosis strikes about 1 in every 2,500 American children, is usually fatal in infancy, and fewer than half of those affected live past 21. Wallach's position overturns the premise: he argues CF isn't an inherited genetic disease but a congenital deficiency of selenium (with zinc and vitamin B12) during pregnancy — which makes it both preventable and curable. His specific claims are that normal selenium levels in a pregnant woman will prevent CF outright, and that the disease is “100 percent curable when diagnosed within 30 days of birth,” with recovery still possible even in teenagers and young adults. It's the therapeutic flip side of his 1977 discovery: if the pancreatic, lung, and intestinal damage of CF comes from missing selenium, then supplying it early enough should reverse it.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000188.verbatim:
Normal selenium levels in pregnant women will prevent CF,” Wallach
said, and tests on thousands of monkeys (their exaggeration) have shown
the disease is 100 percent curable when diagnosed within 30 days of birth

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000189.claim_text: In Wallach's account, zinc is a true workhorse mineral: no fewer than 70 metalloenzymes require zinc as a cofactor to function properly, among them carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase, and carboxypeptidase. Zinc helps lock these enzymes onto the substances they act on by holding the right spatial arrangement. Some enzymes bind zinc so tightly that they keep working even when the body is severely depleted.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000189.verbatim:
There are no less than 70 metalloenzymes that require Zn as a cofactor to
function properly. These include carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, lactic
dehydrogenase, and carboxypeptidase. Zinc helps to bind enzymes to substrates
by maintaining special and configurational relationships. Some enzymes bind
Zn so tightly that even during severe Zn depletion they can still function.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000190.claim_text: Zinc plays a direct role in the body's genetic machinery, a central theme of Wallach's book Epigenetics. He describes zinc as an integral part of the RNA molecule — the 'zinc metallic fingers' — and says it takes part in the metabolism of nucleic acids and the synthesis of proteins. In the same passage he adds that zinc is required for cell division and the synthesis of DNA, and that the enzyme DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is itself zinc-dependent.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000191.claim_text: Wallach places zinc deficiency at the root of a striking list of congenital birth defects. Among those he associates with zinc deficiency are Down's syndrome, cleft lip and cleft palate, spina bifida, brain defects and cerebral palsy, small or absent eyes, clubbed or missing limbs, webbed fingers and toes (syndactyly), diaphragmatic and umbilical hernias, and heart, lung, and urogenital defects. In his epigenetic framework these trace to the mother's nutrition rather than to fixed genetic fate.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000191.verbatim:
Congenital Birth Defects Associated with Zinc Deficiency:

Down's syndrome

Cleft lip

Cleft palate

Brain defect (dorsal herniation, hydroencephaloceol, cerebral palsy, etc.)
Micro or anophthalmia (small or absent eyes)
Micro or agnathia jaw structure

Spina bifida

Clubbed limbs

Syndactyly (webbed fingers and toes)
Missing limbs and digits

Diaphragmatic hernia (hiatal hernia)
Umbilical hernias (gastroschisis)

Heart defects

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000192.claim_text: Zinc's status as an essential nutrient came late for humans, in Wallach's telling. He notes it was known to be essential for bread mold 125 years ago and for rats 70 years ago, but that its essentiality for humans was recognized only 40 years ago. The lateness underscores how recently zinc's importance to people was accepted.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000192.verbatim:
Zinc was known to be an essential nutrient for bread mold 125 years ago, to
be essential for rats 70 years ago, and essential for humans 40 years ago.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000193.claim_text: Much of Wallach's conviction about zinc and birth defects came from his years as a zoo and veterinary pathologist. He describes a constant stream of congenital birth defects in animals that he traced directly to nutritional deficiencies in the mother before and during pregnancy: cerebral palsy in a llama from copper and zinc deficiency, spina bifida in a monkey from folic acid and/or zinc deficiency, cleft palates in arctic foxes from vitamin A and/or zinc deficiency, and a ventricular septal heart defect in a kangaroo. Once the mothers' diets were adjusted, he says, the defects were prevented — the same logic he applies to human pregnancy.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000193.verbatim:
Wallach saw a constant stream of congenital birth defects that could be
directly attributed to nutritional deficiencies in the mother prior to and during
her pregnancy: cerebral palsy in a llama (from a copper and zinc deficiency); spina
bifida in a monkey (from a folic acid and/or zinc deficiency); cleft palates in arctic
foxes (from a vitamin A and or a zinc deficiency); a ventricular septal heart defect
in a kangaroo (from a congenital vitamin A and or a zinc deficiency).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000194.claim_text: Wallach explains that biotin, also called vitamin H, has to be converted into an active coenzyme form before the body can use it — and that this conversion depends on the presence of both magnesium and ATP (adenosine triphosphate). It is one example of how magnesium works behind the scenes as a partner to the B-vitamin system: without enough magnesium, even an adequate biotin intake cannot be fully activated.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000194.verbatim:
conversion of biotin to the active form of the coenzyme is dependent on the
presence of magnesium and adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000195.claim_text: Wallach's book presents magnesium as very safe: if the kidneys are healthy, he states there is no evidence of toxicity at intakes up to 6,000 mg per day. For reference he cites the conventional RDA at 350 mg/day for adult men, 300 mg/day for women, and 450 mg/day in pregnancy and lactation. The one caveat he flags is that an actual excess of magnesium will inhibit bone calcification — a reminder that magnesium and calcium must stay in balance rather than either one running away.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000195.verbatim:
The RDA for Mg is 350 mg/day for adult males, 300 mg/day for adult females
and 450 mg/day for pregnant and lactating females. If kidneys are healthy there
is no evidence of toxicity at up to 6,000 mg/day.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000196.claim_text: Wallach reports that osteoarthritis showed up as a universal disease across an enormous range of species he autopsied — iguanas, ducks, flamingos, pheasants, sheep, llamas, monkeys, rhinos and kangaroos among them. He attributes it to deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, sulfur and trace minerals rather than treating it as unavoidable aging or wear. In this view arthritis is a nutritional-deficiency disease, and magnesium is one of the minerals whose shortage helps drive it.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000196.verbatim:
was a universal disease found in all species, including iguanas, ducks, flamingos,
pheasants, sheep, llamas, monkeys, rhinos, and kangaroos (caused by calcium,
magnesium, sulfur, and trace-mineral deficiencies).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000197.claim_text: Wallach teaches that of all the fats, only two are classically 'essential,' meaning the body cannot manufacture them and must obtain them from the diet: alpha-linolenic acid, the omega-3 fatty acid, and linoleic acid, an omega-6. He counts three essential fatty acids among the body's 90 essential nutrients. The 'omega-3' name marks where the fat's first double bond sits, counted three carbons in from the tail or methyl end of the chain; longer-chain omega-3s such as DHA and EPA belong to the same family. In his framework these fats are structural raw materials — they build the bilipid cell membranes and the prostaglandins that help steer blood pressure, blood clotting, and brain and nervous-system function — not merely a source of fuel.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000197.verbatim:
There are two fatty acids that are classically regarded as essential: alpha
linolenic acid (omega-3 fatty acid) and linoleic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000198.claim_text: Wallach identifies DHA and EPA as the omega-3 fatty acids the body needs for the enzyme pathways that metabolize long-chain polyunsaturated fats. He notes that low plasma DHA is a marker for low levels of 5-HIAA in the cerebral spinal fluid, and that low brain 5-HIAA is directly associated with increased rates of depression and suicide.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000198.verbatim:
Omega-3 fatty acids, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid
(EPA) are essential for enzymatic pathways required to metabolize long-chain
polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). Low plasma concentrations of DHA is a
marker for low cerebral spinal fluid levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA).
Low brain concentrations of 5-HIAA is directly associated with increased rates of

depression and suicide.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000199.claim_text: Wallach points to research published in the journal Brain, Behavior and Immunity showing that supplementing omega-3 fatty acids in sedentary, obese adults lengthened their DNA telomeres and reduced their inflammation markers.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000199.verbatim:
In an article
published in the journal Brain, Behavior and Immunity, research demonstrated
that supplementation of omega-3 fatty acids to sedentary, obese adults received
a benefit of lengthening of their DNA telomeres and a reduction in inflammation
markers.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000200.claim_text: Wallach rejects the idea that cardiovascular disease is genetically inherited. He teaches it is a collection of diseases driven by free-radical damage (inflammation) to the artery lining and by specific nutritional deficiencies — pairing coronary thrombosis with omega-3 deficiency, cardiomyopathy with selenium deficiency, congestive heart failure with thiamine deficiency, and aneurysms with copper deficiency.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000200.verbatim:
cardiovascular disease is a
collection of diseases that are caused by free-radical damage to the lining of
the arteries (inflammation) and nutritional deficiencies (e.g., cardiomyopathy/
selenium deficiency; congestive heart failure/thiamine deficiency; coronary
thrombosis/omega-3 deficiency, aneurysms/copper deficiency, atrial fibrillation/
degenerative disc disease, and others).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000201.claim_text: Wallach teaches that the essential fatty acids, which include omega-3, are the raw material the body uses to manufacture prostaglandins. Those prostaglandins regulate blood pressure, heart rate, vascular dilation, blood clotting, and bronchial dilation — which he says prevents and reverses asthma — as well as the neurotransmitters of the central nervous system.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000201.verbatim:
EFA are also the raw material required by the human to manufacture
prostaglandins that regulate blood pressure, heart rate, vascular dilation,
blood clotting, bronchial dilation (prevents and reverses asthma), and
neurotransmitters of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000202.claim_text: Reviewing the common features of traditional and tribal diets, Wallach notes that they contained nearly equal amounts of omega-3 and omega-6 essential fatty acids. He observes that only four percent of those diets' calories came from polyunsaturated oils, with the remainder of the fat calories coming from saturated and monounsaturated fats.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000202.verbatim:
8. Traditional diets contained nearly equal amounts of omega-3 and
omega-6 essential fatty acids.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000203.claim_text: Wallach has been the plaintiff or co-plaintiff in eight lawsuits and claims requests against the FDA in federal courts, reaching up to the steps of the U.S. Supreme Court. His aim was to ensure that proper information about supplementing with selenium, omega-3 essential fatty acids, folic acid, and antioxidants — nutrients he says can prevent and reverse human diseases — was available to all Americans.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000203.verbatim:
Dr. Wallach has been the plaintiff and/or co-plaintiff in eight lawsuits and claims requests lodged
against the FDA in federal courts (Federal District Courts, Federal Appellate Courts, and up to the steps
of the U.S. Supreme Court) to ensure that proper information regarding supplementation with selenium,
omega-3 essential fatty acids, folic acid, and antioxidants that could prevent and reverse human diseases
was available to all Americans.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000204.claim_text: Wallach explains that the 'omega' number refers to the location of the first double bond, counted from the tail or methyl end of the fatty acid chain. In an omega-3 fatty acid that first double bond is at the third carbon; omega-6 and omega-9 are named the same way for double bonds farther along the chain.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000204.verbatim:
The location of the first double bond as counted from the “tail” or methyl end
of the fatty acid is referred to as the “omega” number (ie., omega-3, omega-6,
omega-9, etc).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000205.claim_text: Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble antioxidant. Wallach explains that many mammals can synthesize their own vitamin C internally, but humans -- like guinea pigs -- cannot, so people must obtain it from the diet. It belongs to the water-soluble vitamin class (alongside the B-complex) and serves as a required cofactor for building collagen -- the protein behind connective tissue, cartilage, bones, teeth, and blood vessels. Its classic role is preventing and curing scurvy, the deficiency disease that plagued sailors and explorers for centuries.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000205.verbatim:
Vitamin C is a water-soluble antioxidant that can be synthesized by many
mammals but not by guinea pigs or humans.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000206.claim_text: Wallach describes vitamin C as a required cofactor for producing collagen and connective tissue — the material that forms cartilage, bones, teeth, blood vessel walls and capillaries. Because so much of the body's structural framework depends on collagen, vitamin C is essential to keeping these tissues strong. It also increases the efficiency with which the body absorbs inorganic iron.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000206.verbatim:
Vitamin C required cofactor for the production of collagen, connective tissue,
cartilage, bones, teeth, blood vessel walls, capillaries, and it also increases the
efficiency of absorption of inorganic iron.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000207.claim_text: According to Wallach, vitamin C affects the function of white blood cells and macrophages — the body's immune-defense cells — and influences immune responses. It is also tied to wound healing and to how the body handles allergic reactions.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000207.verbatim:
Vitamin C also affects
the functions of white blood cells, macrophages, immune responses, wound
healing, and allergic reactions.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000208.claim_text: Wallach points out that most plants and animals can store vitamin C, with the guinea pig being the exception among animals. Humans, by contrast, are unable to store vitamin C and therefore require a fresh source of it every day. This is why a steady daily supply from food or supplements matters.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000208.verbatim:
Most plants and animals (except for the guinea pig) can store vitamin C.
However, humans are unable to store vitamin C and require a daily source of it.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000209.claim_text: Wallach warns that too much vitamin C is not harmless. Signs of overdose include tissue deposits of oxalate crystals, inflammation of the urinary tract, diarrhea, and lysis — the breaking apart of the cell walls — of red blood cells. Even a water-soluble vitamin can cause problems when taken far in excess.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000209.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: Too much vitamin C can result in tissue deposits of oxalate
crystals, urinary tract inflammation, diarrhea, lyses (breakage of cell walls) of red
blood cells,

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000210.claim_text: Wallach recounts that James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, eliminated scurvy in the British navy after studying the legend of a marooned sailor's self-cure. In 1753, as recorded in his 'A Treatise on Scurvy,' Lind divided scurvy-stricken sailors into six groups and fed each different foods; only the sailors given lemons and oranges recovered rapidly and completely. Because Lind did not prescribe a specific treatment from his results, it took another forty-two years before the British navy adopted his findings.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000210.verbatim:
James Lind, a Scottish naval surgeon, finally eliminated scurvy in the British
navy after researching the legend of Zoe and his miraculous self-cure. In 1753,
as he recorded in his A Treatise on Scurvy, Lind divided sailors with scurvy into
six separate groups. Each group was provided with different foods, and only the
sailors who consumed lemons and oranges recovered rapidly and completely.
Lind did not prescribe a specific treatment as a result of his study, so it took
another forty-two years before the British navy adopted his recommendations.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000211.claim_text: Wallach describes how Linus Pauling popularized vitamin C. Pauling's 1970 best-seller 'Vitamin C and the Common Cold' won a Phi Beta Kappa Book Award, and a later edition, 'Vitamin C, the Common Cold and the Flu,' suggested vitamin C could fend off a swine flu pandemic. Sales quadrupled, pharmacies could not keep up with demand, and roughly fifty million Americans lined up to follow Pauling's vitamin C protocol — a response vitamin manufacturers called the 'Linus Pauling effect.'
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000211.verbatim:
In 1970 Pauling's best-selling book, Vitamin C and the Common Cold, was
published. The book would be awarded the Phi Beta Kappa Book Award in
1971 as one of the most distinguished and important works published in 1970.
Paperback editions were published in 1971 and 1973, and a second edition,
Vitamin C, the Common Cold and the Flu published three years later suggested
that vitamin C could fend off a swine flu pandemic. Sales of vitamin C quadrupled
and pharmacies could not keep up with the demand. Fifty million Americans were
lining up to follow Pauling's vitamin C protocol. Vitamin manufacturers referred
to this massive response as the “Linus Pauling effect.”

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000212.claim_text: Wallach relays the naming story: Albert Szent-Gyorgyi noticed the new vitamin resembled sugar and first proposed calling it 'ignosco' — Latin for 'I do not know' combined with the sugar suffix '-ose.' When a British journal editor rejected that, he offered the tongue-in-cheek alternative 'godnose.' The substance was ultimately dubbed hexuronic acid, and the name was later changed to ascorbic acid, meaning 'without scurvy.'
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000212.verbatim:
Szent-Gyorgyi
knew that the vitamin had some similarities to sugar, and he initially proposed
that the substance be named “ignosco,” Latin for “I do not know” and “ose”
the suffix common to sugars. The editor of a British journal refused to accept
the name, prompting Szent-Gyorgyi to offer the alternative name of “godnose.”
Ultimately, when Szent-Gyorgyi’s article was published, the vitamin was dubbed
hexuronic acid and later the name was changed to ascorbic—"without scurvy"—
acid.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000214.claim_text: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin, first isolated in 1913, that exists in several active forms — retinol, retinoic acid, and retinyl esters — plus precursors. Beta-carotene is the fat-soluble precursor the body converts into vitamin A. Wallach teaches that it is required to maintain vision and night vision, healthy skin and mucous membranes, and bones and teeth, and that it has been shown to reduce the risk of epithelial cancers. Because it is fat-soluble it is stored mainly in the liver and absorbed along with dietary fats, which is why a low-fat diet or any condition that blocks fat absorption can leave you short of it.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000214.verbatim:
This vitamin, isolated in 1913, which has many active forms including, retinol,
retinoic acid and retinyl esters and precursors. Beta carotene is a fat soluble
vitamin A precursor that is required for maintenance of vision and night vision
(the Egyptians employed beef liver juice, a natural source of vitamin A, to
cure night blindness in 2000 BC), to maintain healthy skin and healthy mucus
membranes, bones, and teeth; it has been shown to reduce the risk if epithelial
cancers.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000215.claim_text: Wallach describes vitamin A as having a number of functions in the body. It plays an essential role in growth stimulation and in maintaining and running epithelial tissue, including the retina, the intestinal mucosa, and the skin. It is also involved in the synthesis of adrenocortical steroids, for example converting pregnenolone to progesterone, DHEA to androstenedione, and desoxycorticosterone to corticosterone.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000215.verbatim:
Vitamin A has a number of functions in the body. It plays an essential role in
growth stimulation, the maintenance and function of epithelial tissue including
the retina, intestinal mucosa, and skin. Vitamin A is also known to function
in the synthesis of adrenocortical steroids, particularly in the conversions of
pregneno-lone to progesterone, of dehydroepiandrosterone to androstenedione,
and desoxycorticosterone to corticosterone.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000216.claim_text: Wallach explains that fat-soluble vitamins cannot be efficiently absorbed from the intestine when people eat low-fat diets, which matters directly for getting enough vitamin A. He advises that individuals who have had their gallbladder removed should supplement with ox bile to boost the bile salts needed for efficient absorption. This applies to all of the fat-soluble vitamins, A, D, E, and K.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000216.verbatim:
Fat soluble vitamins can not be efficiently absorbed from the
intestine when humans consume low fat diets. Individuals who have their gall
bladder removed should supplement with ox bile to increase the volume of bile
salts which are required for the efficient absorption of the fat soluble vitamins A,
D, E, and K.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000217.claim_text: Wallach warns that too much vitamin A can cause overdose signs such as headaches, blurred vision, fatigue, painful menstruation, joint and bone pain, dry cracked skin, hair loss, itchiness, birth defects (for example, malformations of the cranium, face, heart, thymus, and central nervous system), and liver disease. He notes a 'pseudo-jaundice' in which the skin turns orange or yellow from high beta-carotene intake, but with no yellowing of the whites of the eyes. According to him, toxicity signs usually appear only with sustained daily intakes of 50,000 IU of retinol in adults and 20,000 IU in infants.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000217.verbatim:
Signs of overdose: too much vitamin A is indicated by headaches, blurred vision,
fatigue, dysmenorrhea, joint and bone pain, dry cracked skin, hair loss, itchiness,
birth defects (for example, malformation of the cranium, face, heart, thymus,
and central nervous system), liver disease, and pseudo-jaundice (when the skin
becomes orange or yellow as a result of high levels of beta carotene intake,
notably there is no yellowing or jaundice of the ocular sclera).

Signs of toxicity usually appear only with sustained daily intakes of 50,000 IU
of retinol for adults and 20,000 1U in infants.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000218.claim_text: Wallach explains that vitamin A was discovered through experiment rather than mere observation, in 1913. Two groups working independently, Osborne and Mendel, and McCollum and Davis, reported that animals fed artificial diets using lard as their only source of fat developed a nutritional deficiency. That deficiency could be corrected by adding foods such as butter, egg yolk, and cod liver oil to the diet, revealing the missing factor now known as vitamin A.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000218.verbatim:
Experimental, rather than observational evidence, led to the discovery of
vitamin A in 1913. Two groups (Osborne and Mendel; McCollum and Davis)
independently reported that animals fed on artificial diets with lard as a
sole source of fat developed a nutritional deficiency that could be corrected
by the addition of foods such as butter, egg yolk, and cod liver oil to the
diet.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000219.claim_text: Wallach points out that when cystic fibrosis was first described in 1933, it was originally thought to be the result of avitaminosis A, a vitamin A deficiency. This was because specific vitamin A deficiency changes were found in a subgroup of young patients who had been clinically diagnosed with celiac disease. He raises this history as part of his broader argument challenging the purely genetic theory of cystic fibrosis.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000219.verbatim:
Initially described in 1933, CF was originally thought to be the result of
avitaminosis A (a vitamin A deficiency), because of specific vitamin A deficiency
changes found in a subgroup of young patients diagnosed clinically with celiac
disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000220.claim_text: Vitamin D exists in two active forms: D2, the plant source, and D3, the animal source, which the body creates by exposing the cholesterol deposits in the skin to UV light. In Wallach's framework it is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium and phosphorus in the bones and teeth, which makes it central to skeletal health. It works hand-in-hand with parathyroid hormone to govern how the body handles calcium and phosphorus, and many consider it a hormone in its own right because it is synthesized in one place, such as the skin, and acts on a distant target, such as bone.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000220.verbatim:
This vitamin has two active forms: D2 the plant source and D3 the animal source,
which is created by exposing the skin deposits of cholesterol to UV light. Vitamin
D is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium
and phosphorus in the bones and teeth.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000221.claim_text: Wallach argues that the universal deficiency of vitamin D in the 20th and 21st centuries is a physician-caused disease. He blames the medical community's instructions to avoid sun exposure, wear sunblock, wide-brimmed hats, long sleeves and gloves, avoid dietary cholesterol such as egg yolks, chicken skin, dairy and saturated fats, and not take vitamin-mineral supplements. He calls this combination the 'perfect storm' that created a universal vitamin D deficiency.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000221.verbatim:
Deficiency: The universal deficiency of vitamin D in the 20th and 21st
centuries is a physician-caused disease. The doctor's instructions dictated by
the medical community to the American people to avoid exposure to the sun,
wear sun blocker, wear wide-brimmed hats, long-sleeved shirts and gloves, avoid
cholesterol in the diet (including egg yolks, chicken skin, dairy products, saturated
fats, etc), and not to take vitamin-mineral supplements turned out to be the

“perfect storm” to create a universal vitamin D deficiency.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000222.claim_text: Wallach observes that some consider vitamin D a hormone because it behaves like one: synthesis can take place at one site, for example the skin, while the target organ is elsewhere, such as a bone. He notes its mechanism of action is similar to that of aldosterone, estrogens, and testosterone, thought to be linked to an action on DNA-directed synthetic processes. In this sense vitamin D blurs the line between a vitamin and a hormone.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000222.verbatim:
There are some who consider vitamin D a hormone, as there are similarities
between vitamin D and hormone activity. Synthesis can take place in one site
(for example, on the skin) and the target organ found elsewhere (a bone). Its
mechanism of action, similar to that of aldosterone, estrogens, and testosterone,
is thought to be linked to an action on DNA-directed synthetic processes.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000223.claim_text: Wallach recounts that early in the 20th century two theories arose for the cause of rickets: one blamed environmental factors, especially lack of sunlight, the other revisited Trousseau's idea that diet was involved. Dr. Kurt Hulschinsky exposed rickets-deformed children from Berlin to mercury quartz lamps that duplicated the sun's ultraviolet light, and their limbs straightened out after two months. In England, Edward Mellanby confirmed the Scottish fishermen's tale that cod liver oil cured rickets, and McCollum of Johns Hopkins showed that destroying the vitamin A in cod liver oil with heat still left it able to cure and prevent rickets — pointing to a separate antirachitic factor.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000223.verbatim:
Early in the 20th century, two separate theories were developed for the
cause of rickets. One postulated that rickets was due to environmental factors,
especially lack of sunlight, the second revisited Trousseau’s theory that diet was
involved. Dr. Kurt Hulschinsky, exposed rickets-deformed children from Berlin
to mercury quartz lamps, duplicating the sun's ultraviolet light, and their limbs
straightened out after two months.

‘At the same time, in England, Edward Mellanby proved the Scottish
fishermen’s tale of curing rickets with cod liver oil to be correct. EV. McCollum
of Johns Hopkins destroyed the vitamin A in cod liver oil with heat, and it still
had antirachitic activity and cured and prevented rickets.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000224.claim_text: Wallach reports that in 2013 rickets reappeared among children in the industrialized world, with a reported 400 percent increase between 1995 and 2011. He attributes this to fears of skin cancer from sun exposure, widespread use of sunscreens, and fear of cholesterol in egg yolks, which he calls a good source of vitamin D. To Wallach, the return of rickets is a physician-caused disease.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000224.verbatim:
In 2013 rickets reappeared in children in the industrialized world with a
reported increase of 400 percent between 1995 and 2011. This is a result of
fears of increased risk of skin cancer from skin exposure to the sun as well as

widespread use of sun screens, fear of cholesterol in egg yolks (a good source
of vitamin D)

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000226.claim_text: Iron is a necessary element present in nearly all living organisms, and one of the 60 essential minerals Wallach says the body must obtain from diet or supplements. It works through iron-containing enzymes and proteins, many of them built around heme groups, that drive biological oxidation and oxygen transport, including hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochrome, and catalase. A healthy adult carries 3 to 5 grams of total iron, a newborn nearly double that per kilogram of body weight; roughly 60 to 70 percent is functional iron doing active work and 30 to 40 percent is held in storage. In Wallach's framework iron is the metal that lets blood carry oxygen, and running short of it, a deficiency he treats as common given how many everyday conditions drain it, drives fatigue, anemia, poor memory, and the strange cravings of pica.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000226.verbatim:
Iron is a necessary element found in nearly all living organisms. Iron containing
enzymes and proteins, often containing heme prosthetic groups, participate in

many biological oxidations and in transport. Examples of iron containing proteins
found in higher organisms include hemoglobin, cytochrome, and catalase.

In a healthy adult human there is an average of 3 to 5 gms of total iron.
The newborn infant has nearly double the amount of iron per kg than adults.
Sixty to 70 percent of tissue iron is classed as essential or functional iron, and
30 to 40 percent as storage iron.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000227.claim_text: Wallach traces iron deficiency to a range of causes: an unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation, chronic infections, and hypochlorhydria, which is low stomach acid that he links to salt-restricted diets or the use of proton pump inhibitors. It also results from chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding from illness such as cancer, ulcers, and parasites, and impaired absorption caused by high-fat diets, high-phytate diets, and gluten intolerance.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000227.verbatim:
Iron deficiency can result from an unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation,
chronic infections, hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid from salt-restricted diets
or use of proton pump inhibitors), chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding (from illness
from cancer, ulcers, parasites, etc.) and impaired absorption (caused by high-fat
diets, high phytate diets, gluten intolerance, etc).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000228.claim_text: Wallach's position is that excess storage of iron is itself caused by deficiencies of selenium, copper, zinc, and similar minerals, not simply by taking in too much iron. He says iron is falsely blamed for liver cirrhosis, fibrosis of the pancreas, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and diabetes. In his view these diseases are not the direct result of iron excess.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000228.verbatim:
Excess storage of iron can be caused by deficiencies of selenium, copper, zinc,
etc,, and is falsely blamed for liver cirrhosis, fibrosis of the pancreas, hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy and diabetes. These diseases are not the direct result of iron
excess.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000229.claim_text: Wallach stresses that few nutritional deficiencies occur in the pure state. If there is one obvious clinical deficiency, such as iron-deficiency anemia, the odds are that others are present as well, maybe dozens. This is why he favors supplementing the full set of essential nutrients rather than chasing a single mineral in isolation.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000229.verbatim:
The clinical realities are that few nutritional deficiencies occur in the pure
state. In other words, if there is an obvious clinical deficiency, such as iron
deficiency anemia, the odds are that there are others, maybe dozens

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000230.claim_text: Wallach cites the research to show iron reverses pica. In a 1964 study by McDonald and Marshall, twenty-five children who ate sand were split into two groups, and after three to four months eleven of the thirteen given iron were cured of the behavior, compared with only three of twelve given saline. In a 1968 report by Reynolds and colleagues, thirty-eight anemic people showed pagophagia (ice-eating) as their most common form of pica, and twenty-two of them had it disappear once their iron-depletion anemia was corrected.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000230.verbatim:
McDonald and Marshall (1964) reported on twenty-five children who ate sand.
They divided the group in half, giving one group iron and the other group saline.
After three to four months, eleven of the thirteen children given iron were cured
of their pica behavior compared to three of the twelve given saline.

Reynolds et al. (1968) reported on thirty-eight people with anemia who
exhibited “pagophagia,” or ice eating, as the most common form of pica. Twenty-two of the thirty-eight had their pica symptoms disappear after correcting an iron
depletion anemia.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000231.claim_text: Wallach recounts that the taming of fire brought the mastery of metals, and iron was the primary key of that transition, lifting human life from a brutish hunter-gatherer existence toward civilization. This early history gave iron a special, almost supernatural quality, reinforced by the fact that the first purified iron was extracted from meteors that fell from the heavens. For that reason the ancient Egyptians called iron 'the metal from the sky,' and the Aztecs called it 'the gift of heaven.'
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000231.verbatim:
The “taming” of fire by man brought the “mastery” of metals that eventually
led to human progress and civilization. Iron was the primary key of this transition,

which raised the quality of human life from a brutish animal-like hunter gatherer

existence to civilization. This early history of the ferrous metal was enough to
give iron a special supernatural quality. Additionally, the first purified iron was
extracted from meteors that fell from the heavens.

The ancient Egyptians referred to iron as “the metal from the sky,” and the
Aztecs referred to iron as “the gift of heaven.”

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000232.claim_text: Wallach states that calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body: the average man carries about 1,200 grams (roughly 3 pounds) and the average woman about 1,000 grams (roughly 2 pounds), around two percent of body weight and up to 39 percent of the body's total mineral reserve. Ninety-nine percent of that calcium is held in the bones and teeth. The remaining one percent circulates in blood, extracellular fluid, and cells, where it acts as a cofactor and activator for numerous chemical, DNA, and enzymatic reactions.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000232.verbatim:
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body. The average male
has 1,200 grams (approximately 3 pounds) and the average female has 1,000
grams (approximately 2 pounds), which makes up about two percent of the
human body weight (water makes up 65 to 75%) and up to 39 percent of the
total mineral reserves of the human body (ash). Ninety-nine percent of the total
body calcium is found in the bones and teeth, and the remaining one percent is.
found in the blood, extracellular fluid, and within cells where it is a cofactor and
activator for numerous chemical, DNA, and enzymatic reactions.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000233.claim_text: Wallach explains that in addition to being a major structural mineral, calcium releases energy from ATP (adenosine triphosphate) for muscular contraction and drives blood clotting—ionized calcium triggers thromboplastin release, converts prothrombin to thrombin, and helps form the fibrin web that traps red blood cells into a clot. Calcium also mediates transport across cell and organelle membranes, releases neurotransmitters at synaptic junctions, and governs the synthesis and secretion of hormones and enzymes. He adds that it helps regulate the heartbeat, muscle tone, and the muscle's responsiveness to nerve stimulation.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000233.verbatim:
In addition to being a major structural mineral, Ca is also required for the
release of energy from ATP for muscular contraction, blood clotting (ionized
Ca stimulates the release of thromboplastin from the platelets, converts


prothrombin to thrombin, and thrombin facilitates the conversion of fibrinogen
to fibrin. Fibrin creates the protein “web” that traps the RBCs to form blood clots);
Ca mediates the transport function of cell and organelle membranes; Ca effects
the release of neurotransmitters at synaptic junctions; Ca mediates the synthesis,
secretion and metabolic effects of hormones and enzymes; Ca helps to regulate
the heartbeat, muscle tone and muscle receptiveness to nerve stimulation and
communication.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000234.claim_text: Wallach teaches that calcium cannot do its job without vitamin D: vitamin D is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium and phosphorus in the bones and teeth. This is why he ties calcium deficiency and bone disease so closely to vitamin D status and sunlight exposure.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000234.verbatim:
Vitamin
D is required for the absorption, metabolism, and proper deposition of calcium
and phosphorus in the bones and teeth.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000235.claim_text: Wallach teaches that bone spurs, heel spurs, and calcium deposits are not a sign of too much calcium but of raging osteoporosis: they always develop at the insertions of tendons and ligaments as the body loses bone mineral. Rather than being permanent, he says they can be reversed and eliminated by supplementing with significant amounts of chelated and colloidal calcium sources.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000235.verbatim:
Bone spurs, heel spurs, and calcium deposits always develop at the sites
of insertions of tendons and ligaments during a raging osteoporosis. Bone
spurs, heel spurs, and calcium deposits can be reversed and eliminated by
supplementing with significant amounts of chelated and colloidal calcium
sources.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000236.claim_text: Working with zoo reptiles, Wallach found that tortoises and iguanas fed fruit, eggs, meat, and lettuce with no added calcium universally developed kidney stones. The calcium in those stones, he determined, came from the animals' own bones, skeletons, and shells, dissolved by raging osteoporosis when the diet lacked calcium. Because the same phenomenon was already well documented in domestic animals, he could cite refereed references showing kidney stones develop from too little dietary calcium, not too much.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000236.verbatim:
Where did the calcium come from that was in the tortoise and iguana kidney
stones? It came from the bones of the iguana and the skeleton and shell of
the tortoise when they didn’t enough calcium in their diet and they had raging
osteoporosis! The fact that kidney stones developed as the result of too little
calcium in the diet was well documented in domestic animals, so it was easy to
find appropriate refereed references for another journal article and for the book.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000237.claim_text: Vitamin B1, also called thiamine, is one of the water-soluble vitamins of the B-complex. In Wallach's framework it is essential throughout life for tissue respiration and energy production: thiamine combines with phosphorus to form the coenzyme thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), which drives the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate at the entrance to the Krebs cycle. Because carbohydrate metabolism depends on thiamine, the daily requirement rises with the amount of dietary sugar and starch. Discovered in 1897 and isolated in 1911, thiamine is also the vitamin from which the word 'vitamin' itself was coined.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000237.verbatim:
This water soluble vitamin was discovered in 1897 and isolated in 1911.
It is a cofactor required for energy production and optimal metabolism of
carbohydrates.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000238.claim_text: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a water-soluble vitamin that acts as a cofactor required for energy production and the optimal metabolism of carbohydrates. It combines with phosphorus to form the coenzyme thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), which works as a cocarboxylase enzyme. TPP is required for the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate into active acetate and acetyl coenzyme A, the critical compound of the Krebs cycle. Wallach notes the vitamin was discovered in 1897 and isolated in 1911.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000238.verbatim:
This water soluble vitamin was discovered in 1897 and isolated in 1911.
It is a cofactor required for energy production and optimal metabolism of
carbohydrates. Thiamine combines with phosphorous to form the coenzyme
thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), which functions as a cocarboxylase enzyme. TPP
is required for the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to form active acetate
and acetyl coenzyme A, the critical compound of the Krebs cycle.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000239.claim_text: Wallach treats all four forms of dementia simultaneously because doctors get the diagnosis wrong about 65% of the time. In one case, a patient diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease was actually afflicted with Korsakoff's syndrome — a disease of a single vitamin deficiency (thiamine, B1), first diagnosed and solved in the late 1700s by a Japanese naval surgeon. Because mega-doses of thiamine were included in the treatment, the patient was cured in a week; had he continued on Alzheimer's drug programs alone, Wallach says he would have died of the complications of Alzheimer's.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000239.verbatim:
he was afflicted with Korsakoff’s syndrome, a disease of a single vitamin
deficiency (thiamin B1) first diagnosed and solved in the late 1700s by a
Japanese naval surgeon. Because mega doses of thiamine were included
in the treatment, the patient was cured in a week

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000240.claim_text: Wallach recounts the naval evidence that beriberi is a dietary deficiency disease. The Japanese ship Riuyo returned from an extended voyage in 1883 with 25 dead sailors and 144 others stricken with beriberi. In 1884 naval surgeon Kanekiro Takaki joined an identical voyage and proved that a diet built primarily on polished rice was the cause; by changing the diet to include sources of thiamine (vitamin B1), the disease could be prevented and cured.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000240.verbatim:
The Riuyo, a Japanese naval ship with a complement of 276 men, returned
from an extended voyage in 1883 with 25 dead sailors and 144 other crew
members stricken with beriberi. In 1884 Takaki was able to convince the Japanese
naval command to allow him to join the crew of a second ship going on an
identical voyage.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000241.claim_text: The very word 'vitamin' traces back to thiamine (vitamin B1). Wallach explains that Funk produced a crystalline substance from rice polishings and yeast that could prevent and cure experimentally produced beriberi. Because the substance was a basic (high-pH) nitrogen compound — an amine essential to life — Funk called it a 'vit- (vital) amine.' The term was then accepted as a broad label for dietary substances deemed to be dietary essentials.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000241.verbatim:
Some years later, Funk produced a crystalline substance
from rice polishings and yeast that was effective in the prevention and cure
of experimentally produced beriberi. The substance contained a high pH (basic)
nitrogen (amine), so Funk called it a vit- (vital) amine. The term was accepted as a
broad label for dietary substances that were deemed to be dietary essentials.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000242.claim_text: In Wallach's framework, vitamin B2 — riboflavin — is a water-soluble B vitamin and a key cofactor for two flavin coenzymes, flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), that drive the oxidation-reduction reactions behind cellular energy production. Riboflavin-dependent enzymes also activate vitamin B6 and help convert tryptophan into niacin, and the vitamin is required to maintain healthy skin, mucous membranes, the cornea of the eye, and nerve sheaths. A shortage shows up early as cracks at the corners of the mouth (cheilosis), a sore burning tongue, and light-sensitive eyes.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000242.verbatim:
Vitamin B2, discovered in 1879 and isolated in 1932, is a key cofactor for
two flavin coenzymes that are required for oxidation-reduction reactions and

energy production flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide


(FAD).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000243.claim_text: Wallach describes vitamin B2 (riboflavin) as a key cofactor for two flavin coenzymes — flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) — that are required for oxidation-reduction reactions and energy production. Riboflavin-dependent enzymes also activate vitamin B6 (converting phosphorylated pyridoxine into its functional coenzyme) and help convert tryptophan into niacin. On top of that, it is needed to maintain healthy skin, mucous membranes, the cornea of the eye, and nerve sheaths.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000243.verbatim:
Vitamin B2, discovered in 1879 and isolated in 1932, is a key cofactor for
two flavin coenzymes that are required for oxidation-reduction reactions and

energy production flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide


(FAD). Among the enzymes that require riboflavin is the FMN-dependent oxidase
responsible for conversion of phosphorylated pyridoxine to functional coenzyme
and the FAD-dependent hydroxylase involved in the conversion of tryptophan to
niacin. Riboflavin is also required to maintain healthy skin, mucus membranes,
cornea of the eye, and nerve sheaths.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000244.claim_text: Niacin — vitamin B3 — is a water-soluble B vitamin that Wallach also names nicotinic acid, nicotinamide, or niacinamide. Isolated in 1900, it works in the body as part of two coenzymes, NAD and NADP (the pyridine nucleotides), which cells use to release energy from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. The body can also make its own niacin from the amino acid tryptophan. A severe niacin deficiency produces pellagra — the classic 'three Ds' of dermatitis, dementia, and diarrhea — and Wallach uses niacin at doses far above the RDA for problems ranging from high cholesterol to schizophrenia.
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000244.verbatim:
Vitamin B3, isolated in 1900, functions in humans as a part of the coenzymes
nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide
phosphate (NADP), known as the pyridine nucleotides.
