In 1901, Dr. Gerrit Grijns, a Dutch doctor, has shown that Beriberi, a disease that affects the nervous system and is characterized by 
weakness, numbness, and paralysis is caused by the deficiency of a 
nutrient (thiamine - B1) removed when white rice is polished (removal of the bran).

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000117.claim_text: Wallach notes that in America the poor are fatter than the rich because cheap, filling calories come mostly from high-carbohydrate, high-sugar foods, while wealthier, better-educated people eat more protein and take more supplements.
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000117.verbatim:
One of the unexpected observations that visitors to the United States 
report is that rich people are skinny and poor people are obese. The 
lower your income, the fatter you are! One out of every four of the 
people with below poverty incomes is obese, by contrast in households earning more than $67,000 per year show an obesity rate of 
one out of six - minorities show an obesity rate of one out of three. 
Wealthy people tend to be more educated and educated people 
tend to eat more protein and take more supplements when compared with the economically stressed. 
If one disregards all other considerations, the “bang for the buck” 
when it comes to calories out of the grocery store, is carbohydrates. 
High carbohydrate, high sugar foods are cheap, tasty, they fill you up 
and they are commonly available.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000118.claim_text: Wallach documents obesity climbing in step with modernization worldwide, noting that in China's cities obesity rose from about 4 percent in the 1970s to 28 percent by 2000 as processed foods replaced traditional diets.
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000118.verbatim:
Africa - In many parts of Africa, obesity is diagnosed in more children than classical “malnutrition.” The country of Tunisia’s urban 
population has shifted to processed flour breads. 
Asia - In Shanghai, roads are today clogged with automobiles instead of the traditional bicycles. KFC opened a drive through restaurant in Beijing in 2002. In all Chinese cities, obesity went from four 
percent in the 1970s to the twenty-eight percent level in the year 
2000.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000119.claim_text: Wallach says the medical advice to eat less fat and more grain backfired, because the refined white flour people switched to (pasta, tortillas, hamburger buns) has essentially the same food value as white sugar.
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000119.verbatim:
We humans were stampeded to eat more carbohydrates and less 
fat - we gladly followed the medical advice and we ate more servings 
of grain, however, the grains we ate were primarily processed white 
flour such as pasta, tortillas and hamburger buns which essentially 
have the same food value as white sugar - the whiter the bread, the 
sooner you're dead!

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000120.claim_text: Wallach blames childhood obesity on mineral-deficiency pica rather than on television, video games, or a lack of outdoor play, saying mineral-starved children who cannot eat dirt instead consume more soft drinks, juice, and junk food.
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000120.verbatim:
Dickens and Ford reported that twenty five percent of children 
eat dirt. We believe that mineral deficiency pica occurs in American 
children at a much higher rate than twenty five percent; we believe it 
occurs at eighty to 100 percent, however, because of the social constraints against eating dirt, kids will instead consume more soft drinks, 
more juice, more French fries, more cookies, more cake, more pasta 
and generally more calories as a result of their mineral deficiencies. 
This mineral deficiency driven pica, not playing outdoors, watching TV and playing video games, is the cause of obesity in kids.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000121.claim_text: Wallach explains that high-protein, low-carb diets help partly because animal protein supplies the iron and phosphorus that quiet pica cravings, and that adding a complete plant-derived mineral supplement makes the weight loss more dramatic and lasting.
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000121.verbatim:
The reduced pica behavior in high animal protein diets, that 
naturally contain iron and phosphorus can partially explain why 
high protein, modest fat and low carbohydrate diets work to reduce weight. We have found that by adding the complete plant 
derived mineral supplement to the weight loss and weight management programs, the weight loss will be more dramatic for all 
and will be maintained.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000122.claim_text: Wallach cites research suggesting artificially sweetened drinks may not help weight loss, because they can make it harder for the body to know when to stop eating; in studies, rats given the choice preferred the high-calorie sweet liquid.
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000122.verbatim:
“Artificially sweetened drinks might not help the (weight loss) diet, 
because they might make it harder for the body to know when to stop 
scarfing. Given a choice between (identically) flavored high and low calorie liquids, rats (preferentially) guzzle the high calorie stuff.”

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000123.claim_text: Wallach stresses that for controlling weight it is not how many minerals you consume that counts, but how many you actually absorb, so supplemental minerals only help if the body can take them up.
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000123.verbatim:
Supplemental minerals are truly the prevention and cure of 
being overweight and obese. However, all minerals are not created equal - it doesn’t matter how many minerals or how much 
of each mineral you consume - what counts is how many minerals and how much of each mineral you absorb!

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000001.claim_text: Wallach teaches that the single common cause of the cranial-nerve and spinal-cord neuropathies behind as many as 25 different diseases is osteoporosis of the skull (which he also names Paget's Disease or Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia). Nutritional deficiency drives a universal mineral loss and an over-production of bone matrix that fills the bony tunnels the nerves travel through, narrowing them and incarcerating (pinching) the nerve -- and he holds this is preventable and reversible.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000001.verbatim:
It turns out that the common cause
of these neuropathies is osteoporosis of the skull which results in a universal
mineral loss and an increase in bone matrix production. The bone matrix fills up
the tunnels that the cranial nerves and spinal cord travel through, reducing the
inside caliber of the tunnels which then produces an incarceration of the nerve.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000002.claim_text: Wallach defines 'Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia' as the replacement of normal bony architecture -- including the bone-marrow cavity -- with connective tissue, which in turn reduces the body's production of platelets, white blood cells, red blood cells, and the stem cells that make antibodies.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000002.verbatim:
The Replacement of normal boney architecture, including the bone
marrow cavity, with connective tissue. Resulting in reduced production
of platelets, white blood cells, red blood cells, and stem cells that make

antibodies.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000003.claim_text: Wallach holds that many common cranial and dental problems -- headaches, sinus trouble, tooth migration and tooth loss, receding gums, periodontal disease, jaw pain (trigeminal neuralgia), and even a change in the shape of the head (Hunter's syndrome) -- are not caused by poor flossing, brushing, or skipped dental visits, nor by autoimmune, familial, or genetic factors, but are in reality manifestations of osteoporosis of the skull.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000003.verbatim:
A wide variety of cranial (head aches, sinus, etc.) and dental issues, including

tooth migration, tooth loss, receding gums, periodontal disease, jaw pain
(trigeminal neuralgia), change in the shape of the head (Hunter's syndrome)

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000004.claim_text: Wallach's prescribed solution: osteoporosis of the skull and spine (Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia) is preventable and reversible by supplementing the full set of 90 essential nutrients -- 60 minerals, 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids, and 3 fatty acids -- dosed for bodyweight, and by protecting absorption through avoiding 'bad foods' and gluten (wheat, barley, rye, oats).
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000004.verbatim:
Osteoporosis of the skull and spine, Wallach’s Fibrous Dysplasia, are
preventable, amenable, and reversible with supplementation with the 90
essential nutrients, 60 minerals, 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids, and 3 fatty acids
appropriate for bodyweight. Absorption is essential and so avoiding the bad
foods AND gluten (wheat, barley, rye, oats) is imperative to get maximum
benefit.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000005.claim_text: Wallach explains that the olfactory (first cranial) nerve carries the sense of smell from the lining of the nose through the cribriform plate of the skull to the brain. When osteoporosis of the skull narrows that bony channel, the nerve is pinched and the sense of smell is reduced or lost entirely (anosmia).
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000005.verbatim:
The olfactory nerve originates in the nasal mucosa and travels through the
cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to the olfactory lobe of the brain to
produce the sense of smell. Osteoporosis of the skull will reduce the caliber of
the tunnels resulting in the reduction of or the total loss of the sense of smell.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000006.claim_text: Wallach teaches that the optic (second cranial) nerve carries vision from the retina through the optic canal of the skull to the brain. Skull osteoporosis narrows that canal and pinches the nerve, causing optic nerve atrophy -- a gradual vision loss that eyeglasses (lens prescriptions) cannot correct.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000006.verbatim:
Osteoporosis of the skull causes a reduction of the internal caliber of the
optic canal resulting in optic nerve atrophy (ONA) which produces a gradual
vision loss that will not benefit from lens prescriptions.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000007.claim_text: Wallach maps the oculomotor (third cranial) nerve, which controls the pupil's response to light and four of the six eye muscles -- including the elevator palpebrae that lifts the upper eyelid. When skull osteoporosis pinches this nerve (per his disease table) the result is ptosis (a drooping eyelid) and a pupil that no longer responds to light.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000007.verbatim:
This nerve travels through the eye via

the superior orbital fissure to activate the eye muscles elevator palpebrae, superior rectus, medial rectus and inferior rectus motor muscles.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000008.claim_text: Wallach describes the trochlear (fourth cranial) nerve as the motor nerve of the superior oblique muscle, which controls downward, outward and inward eye movement. When skull osteoporosis pinches it (per his disease table) the eyes no longer move together, producing double vision (diplopia), palsy, and pain above the eyebrow.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000008.verbatim:
The trochlear nerve is a motor nerve that travels through the superior
orbital fissure. This nerve enervates the somatomotor muscle and the superior
oblique muscle that controls the superior oblique muscle which controls the
downward, outward and inward eye movement.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000009.claim_text: Wallach identifies the trigeminal (fifth cranial) nerve -- the largest cranial nerve, carrying sensation from the face and motor control of the jaw -- as the source of classic trigeminal neuralgia when osteoporosis of the skull strangles (pinches) it. This reframes trigeminal neuralgia as a nutritional/structural problem rather than an idiopathic one.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000009.verbatim:
Strangulation of the trigeminal nerve is secondary to osteoporosis of the
skull which produces the classic trigeminal neuralgia.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000010.claim_text: Wallach explains the abducens (sixth cranial) nerve controls the lateral rectus muscle that turns the eye outward. When it is squeezed in the superior orbital fissure it produces an 'eye palsy' in which the eyes cross inward toward the nose -- strabismus.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000010.verbatim:
This nerve originates in the
pons region of the brain stem then enters the eye socket where it controls the
lateral rectus muscle. When squeezed as it travels through the superior orbital

fissure it produces an “eye palsy” where the eyes cross inward toward the nose.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000011.claim_text: Wallach attributes Bell's palsy (facial paralysis) to strangulation of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve as it passes through bony tunnels narrowed by skull osteoporosis (Paget's Disease / Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia), which he says produces many forms of neuralgia including the classic Bell's palsy.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000011.verbatim:
Strangulation of the facial nerves as it passes through the obstructed
tunnels (Paget's Disease / Wallach’s Fibrous Dysplasia) produces many forms
of neuralgia including the classic Bell’s palsy.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000012.claim_text: Wallach maps the vestibulocochlear (eighth cranial) nerve, which carries hearing and balance. When its cochlear branch is incarcerated by skull osteoporosis a tinnitus (ringing tone) is produced and gradual deafness can follow; when its vestibular branch is incarcerated it produces vertigo. Wallach renames this vertigo 'Wallach's Vertigo' and (in his disease table) equates it with Meniere's disease -- recasting Meniere's as a treatable nerve-incarceration rather than an unexplained inner-ear disorder.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000012.verbatim:
When the cochlear branch is incarcerated a “tinnitus” or tone is produced
(gradual deafness can occur); when the vestibular nerve is incarcerated it
produces a vertigo (Wallach’s Vertigo).

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000013.claim_text: Wallach describes the glossopharyngeal (ninth cranial) nerve, which carries taste from the rear of the tongue and sensation from the throat, and drives the stylopharyngeal swallowing muscle. When skull osteoporosis pinches it (per his disease table) the result is loss of the gag reflex, loss of taste, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), and voice change.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000013.verbatim: This nerve sends sensory information from the sinuses, back of the throat, inner ear, and posterior region of the tongue; it records the sense of taste from the rear of the tongue. Through its motor branches it provides voluntary movement of the stylopharyngeal throat muscle

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000014.claim_text: Wallach ties several major conditions to incarceration of the vagus (tenth cranial) nerve -- the longest cranial nerve, which carries signals to the heart, lungs, and digestive tract. When skull osteoporosis pinches it, he says it produces throat and esophageal problems, gastroparesis (a sluggish, bloated stomach with reflux and diarrhea), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), atrial fibrillation (A-fib, an abnormal heart rhythm), and hiccups when the recurrent branch is involved.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000014.verbatim:
When the vagus nerve is incarcerated it will produce throat and esophageal
issues, gastroparesis (bloating, reflux, diarrhea, etc.) COPD, A-fib, and hiccups
if the recurrent branch is also involved.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000015.claim_text: Wallach describes the accessory (eleventh cranial) nerve as the motor nerve that rotates, flexes, and extends the neck and shoulders by driving the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. When skull osteoporosis pinches it as it passes through the foramen magnum and jugular foramen (per his disease table) the result is loss of function of those neck and shoulder muscles.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000015.verbatim:
The accessory nerve travels through the foramen magnum into the skull
and then exits quickly through the jugular foramen to innervate the motor
functions of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000016.claim_text: Wallach describes the hypoglossal (twelfth cranial) nerve as the motor nerve of the tongue, supplying all the tongue muscles except the palatoglossus. When skull osteoporosis pinches it in the hypoglossal canal (per his disease table) the tongue wastes away (atrophy) and speech malfunctions.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000016.verbatim:
The hypoglossal nerve is involved with the motor function of the tongue, it originates in the medulla oblongata then travels into the jaw and tongue. The
hypoglossal nerve travels through the hypoglossal canal and provides motor

innervation for all of the tongue muscles except for the palate glossus.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000017.claim_text: Wallach extends the same mechanism to the spinal cord: impingement where it exits the skull through the foramen magnum (which he names Erb's Palsy / Wallach's Fibrous Dysplasia) produces numerous diseases. He says it is often misdiagnosed as carpal tunnel syndrome (numbness and tingling in the arms, wrist, and hands), behaves like a sciatica of the shoulder girdle, and that fibromyalgia, atrial fibrillation (A-fib), lupus, and sciatica are among its other manifestations.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000017.verbatim:
Fibromyalgia, A-fib, Lupus, and Sciatica are some of the other symptoms of
Erb's Palsy / Wallach’s Fibrous Dysplasia.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000018.claim_text: Wallach explains why the 90 essential nutrients matter at the cellular level: vitamins and minerals act as cofactors that enzymes and coenzymes require to do their work, and if an essential cofactor is missing the enzyme cannot perform properly, if at all. He notes that most people never reach optimal levels of all 90 nutrients — a state he calls subclinical (marginal) deficiency — which typically shows up as chronic fatigue, lethargy, depression, and lack of concentration.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000018.verbatim:
The general role of vitamins and minerals is their requirement as cofactors to
implement the activity of enzymes and coenzymes.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000019.claim_text: Wallach argues you cannot eat your way to full nutrition because the food supply itself is depleted: vitamin levels in food fell more than 37% (1950 to 1999) and trace minerals 77% (1940 to 1991). He attributes this not to fertilizers or seed types but to two facts — minerals occur in veins rather than spread evenly through the soil and plants cannot manufacture them, and the traditional renewal of farm-soil minerals through wood ashes ended once the Industrialized World switched from wood fuel to electricity, natural gas, and propane after Thomas Edison's first commercial power plant opened in 1882. Even organic and vegetarian diets fall short, so he calls a complete 90-nutrient supplementation program a cornerstone of optimal health.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000019.verbatim:
Vitamin levels in food
have decreased by more than 37% between 1950 and 1999, and trace mineral
levels have decreased by 77% between 1940 and 1991.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000020.claim_text: Wallach's About-the-Author biography records the recognition his trace-mineral research has received: the 1988 Wooster Beach Gold Medal for a breakthrough in understanding the cause of cystic fibrosis, a 1991 Nobel Prize in Medicine nomination for linking selenium deficiency to cystic fibrosis, and the 2011 Klaus Schwarz Commemorative Medal for discovering the animal model of cystic fibrosis and elucidating its cause in humans. He is also credited as a co-author of the Dietary Supplement and Health Education Act — the law that keeps nutritional supplements legally categorized as food rather than pharmaceuticals. Accepting the Klaus Schwarz Medal, the awards committee wrote: "From a Historical perspective, Wallach is to be regarded as one of the first practitioners, if not founders, of epigenetics, the new research discipline that investigates heritable alterations in gene expression caused by mechanisms other than changes in DNA sequence."
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000020.verbatim:
From a
Historical perspective, Wallach is to be regarded as one of the first practitioners, if not
founders, of epigenetics, the new research discipline that investigates heritable alterations
in gene expression caused by mechanisms other than changes in DNA sequence.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000021.claim_text: Wallach's central thesis on the cranial nerves: neuropathies of one or more of them (and the spinal cord) can produce as many as 25 different diseases. He argues the common cause is osteoporosis of the skull — a universal mineral loss that increases bone matrix, filling the bony tunnels the nerves travel through, narrowing them and pinching (incarcerating) the nerve.
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000021.verbatim:
Peripheral neuropathies of one or more of the cranial nerves and spinal cord
can produce as many as 25 different diseases. It turns out that the common cause
of these neuropathies is osteoporosis of the skull which results in a universal
mineral loss and an increase in bone matrix production. The bone matrix fills up
the tunnels that the cranial nerves and spinal cord travel through, reducing the
inside caliber of the tunnels which then produces an incarceration of the nerve.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000001.claim_text: Wallach frames goiter (an enlarged, or 'colloid,' thyroid) as a straightforward nutritional-deficiency disease rather than a mysterious gland disorder. It is caused by a simple deficiency of the nutrients the thyroid needs — chiefly iodine, but also copper, molybdenum, and the amino acid tyrosine. Goiter can also be driven by 'goitrogens' — substances such as the nitrates in luncheon meats, hot dogs, and fertilizer-contaminated well water, plus vegetables like cabbage, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts — which depress thyroid activity and can produce a goiter even when iodine is present in the diet. Starved of its nutrients, the thyroid gland swells 50 to 100 times its normal size, creating the visible lump at the front of the neck.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000001.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000002.claim_text: Wallach's health framework is built on an unusually large base of comparative pathology. As a pathologist for a multi-institution research program - The Center for the Biology of Natural Systems, funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) along with several zoos and universities - he performed autopsies on a scale almost no one else has: more than 20,000 of them, spanning over 17,500 captive wild, laboratory, and domestic animals across more than 454 species, plus 3,000 humans for comparison. That vast cross-species record is what led him to his central claim - that creatures dying of so-called "natural causes" were really dying of nutritional deficiency diseases.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000002.verbatim:
As a comparative pathologist, I (Wallach) performed
more than 20,000 autopsies of over 17,500 captive wild
animals, laboratory species and domestic animals, of over 454
species and 3,000 humans for a comparison.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000003.claim_text: Wallach's stance on carbohydrates and sugars: they are not essential nutrients. His reasoning is that the body can make all the carbohydrate and sugar it needs - for energy, upkeep, and structural repair - by breaking down and rebuilding fats and proteins inside the cell, so none has to come from the diet. This runs counter to the popular view of carbohydrates as a required food group.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000003.verbatim:
Contrary to popular belief, carbohydrates and sugars
are not essential nutrients by anybody’s standards, as we
can make all of the carbohydrates and sugars we need for
energy and maintenance and repair of structural components
by breaking down and reconfiguring fats and proteins at the
cellular level.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000004.claim_text: Wallach counts 12 essential amino acids - the protein building blocks the body cannot make for itself and so must obtain from the diet: valine, tyrosine, tryptophan, lysine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, histidine, phenylalanine, arginine, taurine, and leucine. He warns that if any essential amino acid is missing from the diet for any length of time, a specific - sometimes reversible - disease results. A footnote adds that selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer considered selenomethionine (the selenium analog of methionine) a 13th essential amino acid.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000004.verbatim:
There are 12 amino acids that are required by the body
as protein building blocks, and because the body is unable to
manufacture them, they are termed “essential amino acids.”

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000005.claim_text: For more than 65 years it was known that omega-3 essential fatty acids were needed to prevent disease - but because the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had ruled the evidence "inconclusive," it was actually illegal to tell people that omega-3 supplements could lower their risk of stroke and sudden cardiac death. Wallach fought this: his company (Wellness Lifestyles, Inc.) petitioned the FDA for a qualified health claim, and after a hard-fought battle, won - on September 8, 2004 the FDA allowed the claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk (Docket No. 03Q-0401).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000005.verbatim:
To make a long story short, Wellness Lifestyles,
Inc (Wallach) filed a petition for an Amended Health
Claim: Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Coronary Heart Disease
(Co-Petitioner); Docket No. 03Q-0401; filed on 6/23/2003;
qualified claim allowed by FDA on 9/8/2004.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000006.claim_text: Is cholesterol bad for you? Wallach's answer is no - he calls it an essential nutrient. He points out that cholesterol is a necessary building block of the structural membranes of every cell, of all steroid hormones, and of the brain's myelin (the fatty insulating sheath around nerves) and nerve cells themselves. This counters the popular view of cholesterol as merely something to avoid.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000006.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential nutrient and an essential
component of the structural membranes of all cells, all steroid
hormones and is a major component of brain (myelin) and
nerve cells.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000007.claim_text: Wallach warns that vitamin deficiencies during pregnancy can cause catastrophic birth defects - he lists neural tube defects, mental retardation, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft lip, cleft palate, and heart defects among the possible outcomes.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000007.verbatim:
Deficiencies of many vitamins during pregnancy
can result in catastrophic birth defects (neural tube defects,
mental retardation, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft
lip, cleft palate, heart defects, etc.).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000008.claim_text: Wallach attributes the "morning sickness" of early pregnancy to a deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): he notes it is commonly seen in the first trimester and is thought to be caused by too little B6. This complements his morning-sickness protocol elsewhere, which treats it with B6 plus a B-complex.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000008.verbatim:
“Morning sickness” commonly observed in the first
trimester of pregnancy is thought to be due to pyridoxine
deficiency.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000009.claim_text: Does the birth-control pill deplete a nutrient? Per Wallach, yes: 15 to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives show symptoms of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency - including malaise, depression, and glucose intolerance (trouble regulating blood sugar).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000009.verbatim:
Fifteen to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives
show the symptoms of pyridoxine deficiency manifested by
malaise, depression and glucose intolerance.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000010.claim_text: Wallach corrects even Linus Pauling - the two-time Nobel laureate - on minerals. Pauling (author of The Nature of the Chemical Bond) treated minerals as secondary to vitamins, recommending only eight to eleven of them at minimal doses. His selenium advice is Wallach's example of how wrong this was: Pauling insisted selenium's safe upper limit was just 15 mcg, whereas today the recommended safe limit is 200 to 1,000 mcg for an adult.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000010.verbatim:
Linus Pauling, two time Nobel laureate, and author of the
great work, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, relegated minerals
to secondary importance to vitamins, recommending only eight
to eleven minerals (calcium, magnesium, phosphorous, iron,
zinc, copper, manganese, chromium, molybdenum, iodine and
selenium) and then only at minimal doses - an example was
selenium for which he insisted the upper safe limit was 15 mcg
(today the recommended safe limit for selenium is 200 to 1,000
mcg for an adult).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000011.claim_text: Wallach links selenium deficiency to prostate cancer - and uses Pauling himself as the example: Pauling, who downplayed minerals, died of prostate cancer at age 94, which Wallach attributes to a selenium deficiency (selenium is strongly prostate-protective in his framework).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000011.verbatim:
Pauling died of prostate cancer at age 94 - a
common result of a selenium deficiency.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000012.claim_text: Wallach reframes obesity as a mineral-deficiency disease - "not a disease of excess." His evidence: a study in the Journal of the American Medical Association (December 15, 2004) found that the longer immigrants live in the US, the more likely they are to be obese, averaging about a 10-pound weight gain after 15 years. He calls this the "Feedlot Syndrome" - people placed on the mineral-depleted American "four food group" diet, having lost their traditional mineral-rich "culinary" and garden ashes, gain weight unless they consciously supplement with plant minerals.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000012.verbatim:
“The longer you live in America,
the more likely you are to be obese.” (Remember - obesity is a
mineral deficiency disease - not a disease of excess)

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000013.claim_text: A central Wallach teaching: our food has been massively depleted of vitamins and minerals as farm soils were stripped. A USDA database comparing common foods between 1975 and 2004 shows dramatic losses - for example, broccoli lost 54% of its calcium and 74% of its vitamin A, onions lost 95% of their vitamin A, apples lost 60% of their iron, and kale lost 46% of its calcium. His conclusion: we can no longer get adequate minerals from food alone and must supplement, especially with plant-derived minerals (the "culinary ashes" of traditional diets).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000013.verbatim:
Only when one looks at a USDA data base that
compares the level of vitamins and minerals in certain common
foods between 1975 and 2004, do we truly understand how
depleted our foods have become since we gave up the back
yard gardens and wood ashes (plant minerals).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000015.claim_text: Wallach's rule of thumb for how much a single missing mineral can cost you: on average about ten different deficiency diseases can arise from the absence of any one essential mineral - and calcium is his extreme case, capable of producing as many as 147 different diseases when the body is short of it.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000015.verbatim:
On the average there are ten deficiency diseases that
can occur in the absence of each essential mineral, others, like
calcium can produce as many as 147 different diseases when
the body is deficient.

Pica, or the “munchies” appear in a mild form
in this early stage of deficiency. This phase of trace mineral

Initial depletion of trace elements in animals and

The decompensated phase of trace element deficiency is

gain, obesity), cognitive (i.e. - learning disabilities, ADD,
ADHD, autism, etc.), emotional (i.e. - DR. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde,
“Bad Seeds,” depression, manic depression, bipolar

The clinical phase of trace mineral deficiency is

He notes the form was a 1940s livestock-industry invention (the original chelating agent, calcium EDTA, was a German pre-WWI antidote for arsenic and lead exposure, still used today for intravenous chelation of clogged arteries), and that you can spot chelated forms on a label as selenomethionine, chromium picolinate, or 'amino acid chelate.'

Chelated minerals are approximately 40 to 65%

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000024.claim_text: What is a colloidal mineral - and what does 'nano-technology' have to do with it? Wallach describes a colloid as a substance existing as ultra-fine particles suspended in a medium of different matter - so small (about one billion would fit into 0.01 cubic inch) that they cannot be seen with the naked eye. In the colloidal state, he says, the particles remain grouped together instead of separating into individual atoms the way salt does in a true solution. The interesting
thing about colloids is that they remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble at different concentrations as long as a
larger number if not all of the particles are within a range of

In the presence of amino acids, a small
percentage of the inorganic colloids form chelated minerals
and organic colloids which are able to be dialyzed through the

Crystalloids or organic colloids readily pass

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000026.claim_text: Wallach classifies colloidal minerals into four forms that differ wildly in usability: (1) unprotected 'rock flour' - bare inorganic colloids from sea beds, clays and 'glacial milk,' which are really just metallic minerals and only feed plants (and only in healthy, microbe-rich soil); (2) organic mineral colloids from living systems (bacteria, fungi, green food crops, animals, humans) coated in a water-loving substance like gelatin, albumin or collagen - a 'crystalloid' with bioavailability up to 98%; (3) a carbon-coated form (a 10-12 carbon chain), thought to be the most stable natural type; and (4) an industrial form not found in nature, made by coating metallic colloids with sulfated castor oil. The second type of mineral colloid is found in living
systems of bacteria, fungi, green plants (food crops), animals

Humans can consume 400 mcg of silver per day. A

Silver is an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-metabolite that disables specific enzymes that microorganisms
use for respiration. Silver is such an efficient bactericide that

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000029.claim_text: Beyond killing germs, Wallach says silver actively drives tissue repair: it stimulates fibroblast (stem) cells to multiply faster, generating primitive, embryonic-like cells in wounds that can then differentiate into whatever cell types are needed to heal the wound or rebuild lost tissue.

Human fibroblast (stem) cells were able to multiply at a

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000030.claim_text: Is silver dangerous? Wallach's answer: at standard intake it is absolutely non-toxic - but chronic overdosing carries one distinctive risk, argyria: a permanent, whole-body dusky blue-gray discoloration of the skin (a 'tattoo' that does not fade).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000030.verbatim:
Silver is absolutely non-toxic to humans at standard rates of consumption. CAUTION:

colloidal silver is free from the drawbacks of

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000032.claim_text: Surprisingly, Wallach classifies aluminum as an essential nutrient - specifically the organically-bound colloidal aluminum found in all soil-grown plants, which he considers nontoxic. Aluminum’s known biological function is to activate
the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase. Deficiencies of aluminum

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000033.claim_text: Aluminum is everywhere in the food supply, and Wallach frames that as normal, not alarming: it is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust (12%) and is taken up by every plant grown in soil - so you cannot eat any grain, vegetable, fruit or nut, or drink any natural water, without ingesting it. He notes it is especially high in plankton and red algae and concentrates in mammals' hair and lungs.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000033.verbatim:
Aluminum represents 12%
of the earth’s crust and is the third most abundant element in the
earth’s crust and the most abundant metal in the earth’s crust.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000035.claim_text: Actinium is a naturally occurring (and radioactive) element that Wallach includes among those detected in living tissue. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000035.verbatim:
Actinium accumulates in and presumably has metabolic
functions in the bones and liver.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000036.claim_text: Arsenic is an essential nutrient in Wallach's framework, determined to be one in 1947 - though he notes some soil regions in Argentina and New Zealand carry toxic levels of it. Arsenic was determined to be an essential nutrient

Arsenic

According to the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer

Gold compounds (gold sodium thiomalate, gold

Boron is required for the maintenance of bone density

As the barium

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000046.claim_text: Bismuth is not one of Wallach's essential nutrients, but he gives it a memorable entry. His larger point is a myth-buster: stress has historically been blamed as the cause of gastric, peptic and duodenal ulcers, but the true cause turned out to be infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori - a link Australians Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed in 1983 (and one already known in pigs back in 1952). Stress has historically been blamed as the boogy-man
as the cause of gastric, peptic, and duodenal ulcers. Animal
and human studies have in fact demonstrated that the true
cause of ulcers is an infection with a bacterium known as
Helicobacter pylori.

Australian gastroenterologist Barry Marshall, M.D.
and pathologist J. Robin Warren proposed their theory for the

(H. pylori) for gastric ulcers was known in pigs in 1952.

Sodium bromide, a salt of bromine, is a mild sedative

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000049.claim_text: Carbon is the element most essential for life on Earth - Wallach calls it the center of the 'organic' world. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000049.verbatim:
Carbon functions as an essential structural element for
all living organisms and organic molecules (i.e.- carbohydrates,
fats, amino acids, vitamins, enzymes, etc.).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000050.claim_text: Outside of nutrition, Wallach shares his personal view on climate. He is skeptical of blaming human activity for global warming - he calls humanity's share of the planet's biomass 'pitifully small' and argues that Ice Ages and warm periods have cycled naturally throughout Earth's history, so today's warming is part of that long-running cycle. His proposed remedy is simply to plant more trees, which pull carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen and water.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000050.verbatim:
While many individuals and organizations, want to
blame man’s activities and pitifully small biomass for “global
warming,” we must look to the past for the cycles of Ice Ages and
“global warming” that have taken place over and over through
the millennia to understand the cyclic nature of these events.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000051.claim_text: What are carbohydrates? Wallach explains that carbs and sugars are the body's convenient everyday fuel, but - importantly - they are NOT essential nutrients: the body can make all the carbohydrate it needs by reconfiguring proteins and fats. Plants build carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight (photosynthesis, which runs on chlorophyll, a magnesium/carbon ring). Carbohydrates are classified by size: single sugars (monosaccharides like glucose and fructose), double sugars (disaccharides like sucrose, maltose and lactose), and large chains (polysaccharides like starch, cellulose, fiber and glycogen).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000051.verbatim:
While
carbohydrates and sugars are convenient sources of fuel for
energy, they are not essential nutrients as all living organisms
can make them by reconfiguring proteins and fats.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000052.claim_text: A primer on fats: like carbohydrates, fats (lipids) are built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but they don't dissolve in water and pack more energy - about 9 calories per gram versus 4.5 for carbohydrate or protein. The main form of fat is the triglyceride: a molecule of glycerol joined to fatty acids. Fatty acids are described three ways - chain length (short, medium or long, by the number of carbons), how 'saturated' they are with hydrogen (no double bonds = saturated; one = monounsaturated; several = polyunsaturated), and where the first double bond sits counting from the tail (the 'omega' number, e.g. omega-3, omega-6).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000052.verbatim:
Triglycerides (the primary component of fats and oils)
are composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Structurally,
they are esters of a trihydric alcohol (glycerol) and fatty acids.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000053.claim_text: Essential fatty acids (EFA) are the fats the body cannot make for itself and so must get from the diet. Wallach names three polyunsaturated ones - linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic acid - and notes only two (linoleic and linolenic) are strictly essential, since the body can build arachidonic acid from linolenic; 3% of daily calories must come from EFAs. They do vitamin-like jobs: carrying and processing fat, keeping cell membranes intact, lowering blood cholesterol, and serving as the raw material for prostaglandins that help regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood-vessel and airway width, blood clotting, and brain and spinal-cord function. A shortage is especially damaging in infants.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000053.verbatim:
EFA deficiency in human infants results in a poor growth rate,
lowered IQ, seizures, learning disabilities, eczema, asthma,
and a lowered resistance to infectious diseases.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000054.claim_text: Is cholesterol bad for you? Wallach's answer is emphatically no - it is essential. It is a structural part of every cell membrane and of the myelin that insulates the brain and spinal cord, and it is the raw material the body uses to make vitamin D, bile acids (which digest fat), the adrenal stress hormones, and the sex hormones estrogen, progesterone and testosterone. Because of that hormone role, he warns that a cholesterol deficiency can make menopause miserable for women and can flatten a man's sex drive.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000054.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential part of the structure of cell walls,
brain and spinal cord (myelin), the raw material for the
production of vitamin D in the human body, bile acids, adrenal
cortical hormones, estrogens (a cholesterol deficiency makes
menopause a living hell), progesterone, and testosterone (a
cholesterol deficiency will turn hubby into a TV watching
steer who is totally disinterested in sex).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000055.claim_text: What are proteins? Like carbohydrates and fats they contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but proteins add nitrogen (about 16%, the 'amine' group), sometimes with phosphorus, iron, sulfur or cobalt. Their basic building block is the amino acid; amino acids link by 'peptide bonds' into long chains, and digestion breaks those bonds to free the individual amino acids again. Proteins are the most abundant carbon-based compound in the body - the main stuff of muscle and every cell - and enzymes (the workers that speed up the body's chemical reactions) are themselves proteins.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000055.verbatim:
Proteins are the fundamental structural components
of the living cell (cytoplasm). They are essential parts of the
cell nucleus and protoplasm. Proteins are the most abundant
of all carbon containing organic compounds in the human
body.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000056.claim_text: Can you eat too much protein? Wallach's view: a healthy person can consume even 300 grams of protein a day - nearly three-quarters of a pound of meat - with no ill effects, as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and they supplement properly with vitamins and minerals.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000056.verbatim:
An individual consuming protein at even 300 gm per
day (almost 3/4 of a pound of meat a day) will have no adverse
effects as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and
supplement properly with vitamins and minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000057.claim_text: Wallach's essential amino acids and what each does. Classically there are nine that must come from the diet because the body cannot make them, and Wallach would add three more - arginine, taurine and tyrosine. Their roles: valine, lysine, threonine, leucine and isoleucine build protein; tryptophan is the precursor of niacin (vitamin B3) and serotonin; phenylalanine makes thyroxine (a thyroid hormone) and epinephrine (adrenaline); methionine makes choline and creatine phosphate; histidine makes histamine; and the added three help prevent specific diseases (arginine, taurine, tyrosine - see the related claim).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000057.verbatim:
Classically there are nine essential amino acids that are
required in the daily diet as they cannot be manufactured by
the human body.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000058.claim_text: Beyond the classic list, Wallach singles out three amino acids that, over the long haul, help prevent specific diseases: arginine guards against cancer and PAD (peripheral arterial disease, clogged arteries in the limbs), taurine against macular degeneration (an eye disease that erodes central vision), and tyrosine against goiter (a swollen thyroid).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000058.verbatim:
To the classic list of essential amino acids, we would
add arginine, taurine, and tyrosine. Over the long haul, these
three amino acids help prevent certain specific diseases,
respectively, these diseases are cancer and PAD, macular
degeneration and goiter.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000059.claim_text: What are vitamins? Wallach defines them as a group of unrelated, carbon-based organic compounds the body needs in tiny daily amounts for specific chemical reactions - essential for normal growth, development, maintenance, health, longevity and life itself. They work mainly as coenzymes (helper molecules that switch enzymes on) and cannot be manufactured by the human body, yet they supply no calories and add no body mass. Getting optimal vitamins, he says, goes a long way toward preventing birth defects and many debilitating degenerative diseases.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000059.verbatim:
Vitamins are essential nutrients in that, they can not
be manufactured by humans; they do not supply calories or
contribute to body mass.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000061.claim_text: Calcium is essential for all living organisms — it forms the cell walls of plants, all calcareous tissues, and mammalian bones and teeth. Beyond that structural role, it also helps regulate the electrochemical functions inside cells and is a required cofactor that activates several enzymes. It is the fifth most abundant mineral element in the earth's crust and biosphere.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000061.verbatim:

found in the cell walls of plants, in all calcareous tissues, and

necessary to activate several enzymes.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000062.claim_text: Wallach argues humans are biologically designed to eat high-calcium diets. In the late Paleolithic (35,000–10,000 years ago), wild plant foods and game supplied about 1,600 mg of calcium a day at rest and 2,000–3,000 mg at the activity levels of hunting and labor. The agricultural revolution ~10,000 years ago narrowed the variety of foods and permanently lowered mineral intake — by the 20th century American adults took in only one-fifth to one-third as much, a median of 300–508 mg/day for women and 680 mg/day for men (National Health & Nutrition Examination Survey II).

The
uncultivated food plants and wild game commonly available
to Stone Age humans would supply 1600 mg of calcium at
basal energy intakes and between 2,000 and 3,000 mg of
calcium at the energy levels required to support hunting and
work.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000065.claim_text: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body. The average man holds 1,200 grams and the average woman 1,000 grams — 2% of adult body weight, and up to 39% of the body's total mineral reserves (the ash left after cremation). Ninety-nine percent of it sits in the bones and teeth; the remaining 1% circulates in blood, extracellular fluid and inside cells, where it acts as a cofactor and activator for numerous enzyme systems.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000065.verbatim:
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human
body. The average male has 1,200 grams and the average
female has 1,000 grams. Calcium makes up two percent of the
adult body weight (water makes up 65 to 75%). Calcium also
composes up to 39% of the total mineral reserves (ash after
cremation). Ninety-nine percent of body calcium is found in
bones and teeth. The other one percent is found in the blood,
extracellular fluids, and within cells where it is a cofactor and
activator for numerous enzyme systems.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000066.claim_text: In bone, calcium is stored as hydroxyapatite salts (calcium phosphate plus calcium carbonate) laid down in a crystal lattice bound to a protein scaffold called the "bone matrix." Wallach offers a simple demonstration of that matrix: put a chicken "drumstick" bone in a quart of vinegar for two weeks and the calcium is leached out of the bone, leaving the protein matrix behind.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000066.verbatim:
in a classic crystal structure bound to a protein framework
called “bone matrix.”

To extract the calcium from a bone and reveal the

vinegar for two weeks and the calcium will be leached out of
the bone leaving the protein matrix.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000067.claim_text: Beyond its structural role, calcium is a working cofactor throughout the body. It is required to release energy from ATP (adenosine triphosphate) for muscle contraction, and it is a required cofactor in blood clotting: ionized calcium stimulates platelets to release thromboplastin and converts prothrombin to thrombin, which helps convert fibrinogen into fibrin — the protein web that traps red blood cells to form a clot. Calcium also mediates transport across cell and organelle membranes, affects the release of neurotransmitters at synapses, mediates the synthesis, secretion and metabolic effects of hormones and enzymes, and helps regulate the rate and strength of the heartbeat, muscle tone and how receptive muscle is to nerve stimulation.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000067.verbatim:
In addition to being a major structural mineral, Ca is also
required as a cofactor for the release of energy from ATP for
muscular contraction, and blood clotting. In the blood clotting
process, ionized Ca stimulates the release of thromboplastin
from platelets and converts prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin
helps to convert fibrinogen to fibrin, and fibrin is the protein
web that traps red blood cells to create blood clots.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000068.claim_text: How well calcium is absorbed depends heavily on its form and the gut environment. It is taken up mainly in the duodenum while the contents are still acidic; once the intestine turns alkaline, absorption falls off. Plain metallic calcium may be only 1-3% absorbed, whereas an organically bound, plant-derived colloidal or water-soluble chelated form can reach up to 98%. Wallach lists the causes of a calcium deficiency as: too little vitamin D; low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, which can follow a salt-restricted diet); lactose intolerance; celiac disease; a high-fat or low-protein diet; and heavy fiber and phytate intake. Phytic acid (in grain bran, oatmeal, whole wheat) and oxalic acid (in rhubarb, spinach, chard, mustard greens) each bind calcium into insoluble, unabsorbable salts, and excess sugar, carbonation and caffeine leach stored calcium from the bones.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000068.verbatim:
Causes of a calcium deficiency can include, a
deficiency or lack of vitamin D; the lack of stomach acid
or hypochlorhydria can result from a restricted NaCl (salt)
intake; lactose intolerance; celiac disease; high fat diet; low
protein diet; and a high fiber and phytate consumption.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000069.claim_text: The body holds blood calcium within a tight range using two hormones. Parathormone (from the parathyroid glands) and calcitonin (from the thyroid) keep serum calcium at 8.5-10.5 mg/dL, largely by drawing on the calcium reserves in bone. Parathormone raises blood calcium — pulling it from bone, making the kidney retain more, and making the gut absorb more efficiently; when blood calcium climbs above 10.5 mg/dL from too much parathyroid activity, calcitonin reduces how much calcium is released from the bones.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000069.verbatim:
Under optimal conditions, parathormone secreted by
the parathyroid gland and calcitonin secreted by the thyroid
gland, maintain a serum calcium of 8.5 to 10.5 mg% by drawing
on calcium reserves from the bones.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000070.claim_text: Several common features of the modern diet quietly raise the body's calcium requirement — an increased calcium "cost." Overloading on fiber, salt and phosphates (soft drinks) all force more calcium out: urinary calcium loss rose from 96 mg to 148 mg per day when food was heavily salted, and doubling phosphate intake raised urinary calcium output by 50%. Wallach argues the industrialized diet is chronically calcium-poor and phosphorus-rich, so the ideal calcium-to-phosphorus (Ca:P) ratio of 2:1 is impossible to hit by eating alone (you would have to eat 25 pounds of broccoli for every 16 oz T-bone steak); the only practical route is to avoid high-phosphorus foods and supplement with plant-derived colloidal and chelated calcium.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000070.verbatim:
Other nutrients that are commonly found in the

phosphates (soft drinks) result in an increased calcium “cost.”
In effect, these foods increase the dietary requirements for
calcium. Urinary calcium loss increased from 96 mg per day
to 148 mg per day when food was excessively salted. As


 

phosphate intake is doubled, the output of urinary calcium
increases by 50%.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000071.claim_text: Wallach ties chronic calcium deficiency to high blood pressure. In 1980 McCarron and colleagues theorized that chronic calcium deficiency leads to hypertension, and more than 30 later studies supported it; serum ionized calcium runs consistently lower in people with untreated hypertension. The link is clearest in people taking in less than 500 mg of calcium a day. In salt-sensitive hypertension, a rise in blood pressure tracks with urinary calcium loss from excess salt on top of an existing calcium deficiency — and among Black and elderly white people with essential hypertension, low calcium and potassium (rather than high salt) drive the "salt sensitivity." In a four-year study of 58,218 nurses, hypertension was more likely in women taking in less than 800 mg of calcium per day.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000071.verbatim:
In 1980, McCarron et al theorized that chronic calcium
deficiency probably led to hypertension. More than 30
subsequent studies supported the original theory of calcium
deficiency as the cause of hypertension. In addition, recent
studies have shown that serum ionized calcium is consistently
lower in humans with untreated hypertension.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000073.claim_text: Wallach warns that nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism — driven by a raging calcium deficiency — raises blood calcium and makes the parathyroid glands enlarge as they strain to pull more calcium from the gut. Surgeons almost always mistake the enlarged (hypertrophied) glands for a "tumor" and recommend surgery; Wallach says supplementing with the right amounts of usable calcium resolves the problem rapidly and completely, and bluntly advises: DO NOT GET SURGERY.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000073.verbatim:
Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, resulting

elevation in blood calcium levels. The parathyroid glands

almost always result in the surgeon calling the enlarged or

recommend surgery. Supplementation with the appropriate

resolution of the problem - DO NOT GET SURGERY!

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000080.claim_text: Vitamin B12 (and its cobalt) does some of the body's most fundamental work. Together with folic acid, choline and the amino acid methionine, it transfers single-carbon (methyl) groups used to build RNA and to make DNA from RNA — so it sits at the heart of gene function, which is why Wallach ties preconception nutrition to preventing birth defects. Growth, the formation of myelin (the insulating sheath — made by converting cholesterol — around nerves in the brain, spinal cord and large nerve trunks), and red-blood-cell production all depend on B12. Cobalt is also a required cofactor for making the thyroid hormone thyroxine.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000081.claim_text: How well cobalt/B12 is absorbed depends on stomach acid and intrinsic factor. Metallic cobalt is absorbed at 20–26.2% only if intrinsic factor (Castle's factor, a mucoprotein in normal stomach secretions) is present and the stomach pH is 2.0 or lower. If a person has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid — usually from a salt/NaCl deficiency), intrinsic factor fails and B12/cobalt isn't absorbed — which is why doctors often give B12 shots to older people on salt-restricted diets (sublingual and oral-spray B12 are alternatives). Plant-derived cobalt is highly bioavailable, but because of low-salt diets and cobalt-depleted soils, vegetarians frequently run B12 deficiencies.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000084.claim_text: Wallach gives the quantitative picture for cobalt/B12. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000085.claim_text: Some biochemistry of vitamin B12: its cobalt sits chelated in a large tetrapyrrole ring — the same ring family as the porphyrin ring that holds iron in hemoglobin and magnesium in chlorophyll. B12 is a red, water-soluble crystalline substance (the red comes from the cobalt atom), slowly destroyed by acid, alkali, light and oxidizing/reducing agents — and about 30% of its activity is lost in cooking. It was isolated from liver extracts in 1948 and shown to have anti-pernicious-anemia activity.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000085.verbatim:

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000086.claim_text: Wallach explains how animals actually get their B12 from elemental cobalt — a job done by microbes, not the animal itself. Ruminants (cows, sheep, goats, deer, antelope, buffalo, giraffe) rely on the microbes fermenting plant material in their first stomach (the rumen) to convert elemental cobalt into vitamin B12, which the animal then absorbs. Carnivores get their B12 secondhand by eating the stomach contents, liver, bone and muscle of their ruminant prey. And poultry, lagomorphs (rabbits and hares) and rodents eat feces at night (coprophagy) to recover the B12 their own gut microbes manufactured.

Ruminants (i.e. cows, sheep, goats, deer, antelope,
buffalo, giraffe, etc.) can use elemental cobalt because the
microbes fermenting and digesting plant material in their first
stomach (rumen) convert elemental cobalt into vitamin B12,
which the animal then uses.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000093.claim_text: The element's backstory — and why it colors gemstones. Chromium was discovered by the French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek chroma, 'color,' because all its compounds display a color (the pure metal itself, though, is a hard, brittle, silver-white). Added to steel at 18% it makes stainless steel, and its almost-invisible oxide layer makes it extremely resistant to corrosion — the decorative, protective plating on bathroom fixtures, jewelry and car bumpers. Trace chromium is what tints many gems: it makes rubies red (in corundum), emeralds green (in beryl), and gives alexandrite (in chrysoberyl) its color-shift — red in firelight, blue in daylight.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000093.verbatim:
Chromium was discovered by French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek word
chroma, which translates to “color.”

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000094.claim_text: Cesium is an alkali (alkaline) metal, so chemically it behaves much like sodium, potassium and rubidium. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000097.claim_text: The element's name and history. Copper makes up only 0.007% of the earth's crust. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000101.claim_text: One of the earliest proofs that copper deficiency causes neurological disease. In 1937, 'enzootic ataxia' in newborn lambs — also called sway back or lamkruis, a loss of muscle coordination — was recognized as a copper deficiency in pregnant sheep. Giving the ewes copper supplements prevented it. The disease was marked by demyelination (loss of the protective myelin sheath around nerves) in the cerebellum (the brain's coordination center) and the spinal cord.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000101.verbatim:
Neonatal “enzootic ataxia” (sway back, lamkruis) was
recognized as a clinical and disease entity in 1937 as a copper
deficiency in pregnant sheep. Copper supplements prevented
the syndrome, which was characterized by demyelination of
the cerebellum and spinal cord.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000102.claim_text: Wallach classifies Mad Cow Disease — technically Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) — and its human counterpart, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, as copper-deficiency diseases. His evidence is the brain damage itself: the lesions of BSE closely resemble those of enzootic ataxia in sheep, a long-established copper-deficiency disease.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000102.verbatim:
The brain lesions of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy
(BSE) appear to be similar to those of Enzootic Ataxia in sheep
- a copper deficiency.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000103.claim_text: Wallach extends the copper-deficiency argument to cerebral palsy. In sheep, copper deficiency produces a set of brain lesions — cavities or jelly-like damage in the cerebral white matter, chromatolysis (breakdown of nerve-cell structures), nerve-cell death, and myelin aplasia (myelin failing to form during fetal development). He says these congenital lesions are identical to the classic brain changes of human cerebral palsy.

congenital lesions are identical to those of the classical changes
of human cerebral palsy.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000104.claim_text: To dramatize how common copper deficiency is, Wallach names famous people he says show its signs — mostly fatal aneurysms (weak arterial walls that balloon and burst, an elastin failure copper is meant to prevent): Albert Einstein (ruptured aortic aneurysm), Franklin D. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000105.claim_text: Wallach gives the body's copper content and daily needs. A well-nourished adult holds about 80–120 mg of copper total, concentrated in the brain, liver, heart and kidneys; bone and muscle hold lower percentages but, by sheer mass, store about half the body's copper. Newborns carry the highest concentrations. The daily copper requirement is highest per unit of body weight in the newborn — 0.08 mg per kilogram (mg/kg) — dropping to 0.04 mg/kg for toddlers and just 0.03 mg/kg for adults.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000105.verbatim:

mg/kg; toddlers require 0.04 mg/kg; and adults only 0.03
mg/kg.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000106.claim_text: Typical copper levels in the blood. Wallach gives average plasma copper as 87–153 mg/dl (women) and 89–137 mg/dl (men). About 90% of the copper in plasma travels bound to a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000107.claim_text: The mechanism behind copper's cardiovascular effects. Copper activates numerous 'cupro-enzymes' (copper-dependent enzymes) that build and maintain the heart and blood vessels. In a copper-deficient pregnancy this causes congenital defects of the heart and vessels (Kawasaki disease) and of the brain (cerebral palsy, plus atresia — failure to form — and hypoplasia, or underdevelopment, of the cerebellum). Copper deficiency also lowers the activity of lysyl oxidase, the enzyme that converts proelastin into elastin; with less elastin, the walls of veins and arteries lose tensile strength — producing spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids and aneurysms.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000107.verbatim:
Copper functions as a cofactor and activator of numerous
cupro-enzymes that are involved with the development and
maintenance of the cardiovascular system. Deficiency of
copper in the pregnant female results in congenital defects of
the heart and vascular system (Kawasaki disease) and brain
(cerebral palsy, atresia and hypoplasia of the cerebellum).
Deficiency of copper also results in reduced lysyl oxidase
activity causing a reduction in conversion of proelastin to
elastin causing a decrease in the tensile strength of venous
and arterial walls (spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids
and aneurysms).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000108.claim_text: Copper deficiency also weakens the body's structural framework — bone, connective tissue and muscle. connective tissue and muscular integrity which can produce
a specific type of arthritis in children that forms bone spurs in
the bone growth plates.

Infants whose diets are primarily cow's milk frequently develop copper-deficiency anemia and/or iron storage disease.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000109.verbatim:

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000110.claim_text: Menkes' Kinky Hair Syndrome is the genetic disorder Wallach ties most directly to copper. Because of the copper absorption problem, Wallach says injections of copper and liver extracts plus a diet program designed for celiac patients will be useful for these children.

It occurs in the ores monazite and bastnäsite — monazite (found in the river sands of India and Brazil and in Florida beach sand) carries all the rare earths plus thorium and calcium, and large bastnäsite deposits sit in Southern California.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000116.claim_text: Fluorine is a halogen — the family Wallach calls the 'salt formers,' which also includes chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. These elements react by grabbing electrons from other atoms and readily combine with metals to make salts. The name comes from the Latin fluere, 'to flow.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000118.claim_text: Wallach's stance on fluoride's essentiality. Before 1972 fluoride was only 'considered' essential in animals, based on its apparent benefit to tooth enamel in warding off cavities. Then in 1972, Schwarz proved that fluoride was in fact an essential mineral for both animals and humans. (Note: despite this, fluoride is not carried in this system's operational list of Wallach/Youngevity supplement essentials — see the full fluoride stance for why the picture is two-sided.)

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000119.claim_text: How fluoride protects teeth — the mechanism behind fluoride toothpaste. Tooth enamel is made of a hard mineral, hydroxyapatite. Acids that mouth bacteria produce from sugary food and drink slowly dissolve it, and that loss of enamel starts tooth decay ('caries'). The body constantly fights back by rebuilding enamel (remineralization). When sodium fluoride is present, the rebuilt enamel forms as fluorapatite — a version considerably more resistant to acid damage than natural enamel. That acid-resistance is exactly why manufacturers add sodium fluoride to toothpaste.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000119.verbatim:
The resulting loss of the hydroxyapatite enamel


promotes the initiation of tooth decay or “caries.” One of the
body’s defenses against the breakdown of hydroxyapatite is
to generate new enamel continuously (remineralization).

In the presence of sodium fluoride, the remineralization
process manufactures a form of enamel referred to as
fluorapatite. Fluorapatite is considerably more resistant to
damage from acid than the natural enamel.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000120.claim_text: How much fluoride is in and around us. The skeleton of an adult man can hold up to 2.6 grams (2,600 mg) of fluoride in reserve, and the average American takes in 4.4 mg per day from the combination of food, water, toothpaste and nutritional supplements.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000120.verbatim:

and nutritional supplements.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000121.claim_text: Fluoride's toxicity thresholds — the other side of the mineral. Wallach lays out where fluoride becomes harmful by concentration: dental fluorosis (mottled, discolored teeth) appears at fluoride concentrations of 2 to 7 ppm; osteosclerosis (an abnormal hardening/thickening of bone) at 8 to 20 ppm; and chronic whole-body (systemic) toxicity when daily fluoride intake stays above 20 to 80 ppm for several years.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000121.verbatim:
Clinical toxicity
is observed as dental fluorosis at fluoride concentrations of 2
to 7 ppm and osteosclerosis at 8 to 20 ppm. Chronic systemic
toxicity appears when the daily fluoride intake levels are
above 20 to 80 ppm over several years.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000122.claim_text: The scale of U.S. water fluoridation and its trade-off. About 10,000 American towns and cities — serving 100 million people — add fluoride to municipal drinking water at 1 mg/L (one part per million), which has reportedly cut dental cavities by 60 to 70%. But in certain western U.S. states there is an excess of fluoride — 10 to 45 ppm — with the visible result of mottled (fluorosis-stained) teeth in children.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000122.verbatim:
Approximately 10,000 American towns and cities

reaching levels of 10 to 45 ppm with a resultant mottling of
