WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000242.claim_text: Wallach gives four ways to judge a chocolate: the percentage of chocolate in the product, the country of origin, the ORAC value, and taste. He treats dark chocolate as a genuine antioxidant food on two lines of evidence. The Kuna studies found high cocoa consumption tracked with better cardiovascular health, that urban Kuna eating less cocoa lost the advantage, and that risk factors fell again when consumption rose. And in the Engler trial, 21 people ate either high- or low-flavanoid dark chocolate daily for two weeks, with the high-flavanoid group showing significantly better function in the endothelial lining of their blood vessels.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000243.claim_text: Free radicals are molecules carrying an extra unpaired electron, and Wallach quotes Dr. Roy Walford calling them the great white sharks in the biochemical sea. The damage runs in steps: they attack polyunsaturated fats and cholesterol in cell membranes, producing lipid peroxides, which decompose into aldehydes that cross-link proteins, lipids and DNA. The result is membranes that stiffen, so nutrients and oxygen cannot get in and wastes cannot get out. They reach us through skin, breath, food and drink, and are also produced internally during normal metabolism.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000243.verbatim:
quench or neutralize free radicals that attack our cells, cell walls, mitochondria and
physiological processes and increase our risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer,
Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, cataracts, diabetes and aggressively speed up
the process and damage of aging itself.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000244.claim_text: Age spots and liver spots are ceroid lipofuscin, the pigment left behind by free-radical damage - and Wallach's point is that the ones you can see are the readable surface of an accumulation happening throughout the body. It is the end byproduct of malondialdehyde attacking oxidised cell-wall and mitochondrial fats, and it builds up inside the cell's cytoplasm over a lifetime. He cites measurements of how much of a human brain cell's interior it occupies with age: roughly 35 percent at 30 to 40 years, 41 percent at 50 to 60, 55 percent at 70 to 80, and 78 percent at 90 to 100.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000244.verbatim:
Ceroid lipofuscin shows up in humans as “age spots”
or “liver spots” on the skin of the hands or face. If you have
one liver spot or age spot on the outside you have millions of
them on the inside!

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000245.claim_text: Wallach treats age spots as a readable gauge of internal damage: how many you have and how dark they are tracks your level of free-radical damage directly. He calls them a predictive barometer for cataracts, macular degeneration, coronary artery disease, diabetes, senile dementia, Alzheimer's disease and cancer. The reasoning follows from what the pigment is - the same ceroid lipofuscin is accumulating in the brain, heart, liver, lungs, bone marrow and eyes, where it cannot be seen.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000245.verbatim:
The number and intensity of pigment levels in age
spots are directly related to the level of free radical damage
and can be a predictive barometer of sinister things to come -
i.e. - cataracts, macular degeneration, coronary artery disease,
diabetes, senile dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, cancer, etc.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000246.claim_text: On the aging pigment specifically, Wallach says reversal is possible, and he calls the opposite view a medical dogma that is simply wrong. His charge is that doctors and most gerontologists falsely believe accumulated ceroid lipofuscin is not preventable, removable or reversible, and he points to cell-culture, animal and human studies showing otherwise. He draws a real limit in the same chapter, though: raising antioxidant intake alone increases a population's mean lifespan, not its maximum. Clearing the pigment is not the same as extending the human ceiling.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000246.verbatim:
Fortunately, the accumulation of ceroid lipofuscin
in the brain, heart, liver, lungs, bone marrow, eyes, etc. can
easily be prevented and quickly reversed.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000247.claim_text: Wallach's method for reversing the aging pigment has three parts: cut free-radical foods hard, take every known essential nutrient, and push antioxidants to 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points a day. The foods he names to cut are fried foods, trans fats, burnt fats, heterocyclic amines, super-heated carbohydrates, acrylamides, nitrites, alcohol and sugar. He frames the whole thing inside Clive McKay's equation - a calorie-restricted diet without malnutrition yielding a 30 to 100 percent longevity increase - where without malnutrition means every known essential nutrient at optimal levels well above the RDI, with a special focus on minerals.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000247.verbatim:
Preventing and reversing the accumulation of ceroid
lipofuscin pigments is well documented in many animal
species and humans - to accomplish this “antiaging” feat
requires a significant reduction of the intake of free radicals
(fried foods, trans fats, burnt fats, heterocyclic amines, super-heated carbohydrates, acrylamides, nitrites, alcohol, sugar,
etc.) and a significant increase in the intake of all known
essential nutrients and an extraordinary increased intake of
antioxidants (20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points/ day).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000248.claim_text: Wallach is more careful here than he is often given credit for. He says antioxidant intake alone raises a population's mean lifespan but not its maximum. What moves the 50 percent survival rate is combinations - vitamins A, C and E, selenium, the sulphur-bearing amino acids methionine, cysteine and cystine, plus catechins, resveratrol, proanthocyanins, leutines, lycopenes, flavonols and polyphenols. His clearest evidence is a fruit-fly study: engineering the flies to overexpress SOD alone, or catalase alone, changed longevity little or not at all, while doing both together raised mean and maximum lifespan by as much as 40 percent.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000248.verbatim:
Daily consumption of antioxidant rich food and drink is a universal feature of those
living in Blue Zones and in particular centenarians.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000249.claim_text: The world's longest-lived people eat dark fruits and berries, yellow and red vegetables, cocoa, red wine, green tea and coffee - every day rather than occasionally. Wallach maps compound to source: lycopenes from tomatoes, leutines from green leafy vegetables, proanthocyanins from red grape skins and seeds, resveratrol from red wine, red grape juice and giant Japanese knotweed, and flavonols and polyphenols from dark chocolate, red wine and green tea. What he stresses is the constancy - seasonal variety changes with the growing season, but daily consumption of multiple antioxidant sources does not.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000249.verbatim:
In the "Blue Zones" of the world, large quantities of vitamin C, Beta carotene,
flavanols, lycopenes, leutenes, proanthocyanins, resveratrols, catechins (EGCGs) and
polyphenols are found in dark fruits and berries, yellow and red vegetables, cocoa, red
wine, green tea or coffee - these are the antioxidants that have universally been found
to be consumed daily in the Blue Zones and are known to protect the centenarians.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000250.claim_text: Wallach's anti-aging framework has exactly four parts, and he is blunt that leaving any one out causes total failure. The four longevity pieces are the section headings of his own chapter: ANTIOXIDANTS (20,000-25,000 ORAC points a day), CALORIE RESTRICTED DIETS (1,250 to 1,800 calories, without malnutrition), MINERAL-RICH DIETS (an absolute requirement, and the piece he says a low-vitamin diet can survive but a low-mineral diet cannot), and avoiding the LAND MINES (smoking, excess alcohol, street or prescription drugs, fried foods, burnt meat, sugar). ORAC is one quarter of the answer, not the whole of it.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000250.verbatim:
The omission of any one or any part of the four longevity pieces will result in
catastrophic failure:

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000251.claim_text: Wallach's position is that living past 100 is standard human equipment, not a lottery win. Every human, he says, has the genetic potential, the genetic equipment and the genetic capacity to live well beyond 100 - and the only reasons people do not get there are that they leave pieces of the anti-aging circuitry out of their daily lives, or they knowingly step on the land mines. He accepts there is a genetic upper limit; his argument is that almost nobody is anywhere near it.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000251.verbatim:
While there are genetic upper limits to human longevity, all humans certainly and
predictably have the genetic potential, the genetic equipment and the genetic capacity
to live well beyond 100!

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000252.claim_text: The goal Wallach states is not extra years in decline - it is reaching beyond 100 in a beautiful, healthful and functional way. That phrasing is the whole answer to the objection that a longer life just means a longer old age: the same accumulated knowledge that adds the years is what prevents the deterioration people are picturing when they say they would not want them. He frames aging as something that starts at conception and runs at a rate you influence daily, not a switch that flips at 70.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000252.verbatim:
There is an accumulated knowledge, however, that will allow each of us to prevent and
slow the aging process so that we can successfully reach beyond 100 years of age in a
beautiful, healthful and functional way.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000253.claim_text: Wallach dismisses both halves of the genetics excuse. Good genes will not carry you to 100 if you ignore the physiological requirements - and bad family history will not stop you if you meet them. His example is deliberately extreme: even if everyone in your family died at 35, fulfilling the requirements and avoiding the land mines can still get you healthfully to 100. He calls these physiological laws as unforgiving and predictable as gravity, and compares ignoring them to stepping off a third-storey roof without a ladder.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000253.verbatim:
On the other hand, if everyone in your family died at 35 years of age and you accurately
fulfill your physiological requirements for longevity and you avoid the land mines, you
can easily make it healthfully to 100.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000254.claim_text: Wallach's measure of the gap is stark: the industrialized world should be averaging 95 to 100 years, and instead averages about 75 - some 20 to 25 years short of our genetic potential. He tracks the American slide with CDC and WHO rankings: 17th in the world for longevity in 1990, down to 24th by 2000, down to a pitiful 46th by 2005, and 48th by 2008.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000254.verbatim:
the
average age of peoples in the industrialized world should
be somewhere between 95 and 100 years of age. However,
the average age of those living in the industrialized world
is somewhere around 75 years of age (give or take five
years), in fact 20 to 25 years short of our genetic potential for
longevity.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000255.claim_text: The second longevity piece is a calorie-restricted diet WITHOUT malnutrition - a distinction Wallach says most practitioners of calorie restriction miss entirely. It is universally known to extend the life span of laboratory, pet and farm animals, and it is a common thread among centenarians both historically and in every Blue Zone today. The levels he cites are 1,250 to 1,800 calories a day, with those doing heavier physical labour at the upper end. The 'without malnutrition' half means every known essential nutrient at optimal levels, well above the RDI, in fewer calories - which is why the mineral piece and the calorie piece are inseparable.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000255.verbatim:
In most cases the caloric levels fall between 1,250 and
1,800 calories per day, with those performing more physical
labor consuming the higher calorie levels.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000256.claim_text: This is Wallach's sharpest line on why minerals outrank vitamins, and it is the third longevity piece. Mineral-rich diets are found universally across every Blue Zone and he calls them an absolute requirement to reach the centenarian club - in every case those populations have multiple sources rich in a wide spectrum of minerals. His rule of thumb: a high protein, low carbohydrate diet is relatively forgiving of a low vitamin intake, but unforgiving of a low mineral diet. Antioxidants raise your average; this is the piece that gets you to the ceiling.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000256.verbatim:
A high protein, low carbohydrate diet is relatively
forgiving of a low vitamin intake, but unforgiving of a low
mineral diet.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000257.claim_text: Where the world's longest-lived populations actually got their minerals, in Wallach's list: glacial milk, river silt, rock dust, wood ashes (which he marks as universal across all Blue Zones), kelp ashes, seaweed ashes, rice straw ashes, peat moss ashes and manure ashes. None of it is a supplement aisle - it is dust, ash and silt entering the food and water supply. It is the same argument behind plant-derived minerals: the minerals reached people because the ground they ate from still had them.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000257.verbatim:
Mineral rich diets, found universally in all Blue Zones,
are an absolute requirement to reach the centenarian club. In
all cases, the Blue Zones have multiple sources rich in a wide
spectrum of minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000258.claim_text: The fourth longevity piece is subtractive - the things that will stop you reaching 100 no matter what else you do right. Wallach's land mines are smoking, drinking excess alcohol, using street or prescription drugs, not getting second medical opinions, eating fried foods (trans fatty acids), eating burnt or well-done meats (heterocyclic amines), consuming sugar and large quantities of super-heated carbohydrates (acrylamides), and indulging in high-risk behaviour. He notes an unintended advantage of the Blue Zones: they are remote enough to have little or no access to doctors, pharmaceuticals, commercial fried food, high fructose corn syrup, soft drinks or white flour.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000258.verbatim:
Land mines that will certainly prevent you from reaching
100 years of age include smoking, drinking excess alcohol,
using street or prescription drugs, not getting second medical
opinions, eating fried foods (trans fatty acids), eating burnt or
well-done meats (heterocyclic amines), consuming sugar and
large quantities of super-heated carbohydrates (acrylamides),

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000259.claim_text: Wallach puts a number on the payoff and ties it straight to cost. He calculates that a 150 to 175 pound person can add 25 to 50 additional HEALTHFUL years to their life - not years of decline - by practicing a calorie-restricted diet and faithfully following a supplement program. And it saves money rather than costing it: the reduced cost of food more than compensates for the cost of the supplements. It is the same prevent-don't-cure logic that runs through his work, and the direct rebuttal to 'I don't want to live to 150' - the years he is offering are healthful ones, and the bill is lower, not higher.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000259.verbatim:
We calculate that a 150 - 175 pound person can add
25 to 50 additional healthful years to their life with a net
savings in their cost of living by practicing a CR diet and by
faithfully employing a modified supplement program

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000260.claim_text: This is Wallach's boldest statement of the ceiling. He lines up a history of things the experts swore were impossible - that our hearts would explode if we drove cars at 50 mph, that no one could break the four-minute mile (then 300 runners did within a year), that the sound barrier could not be broken, that a man would never reach the moon and return - and then asks: who is to say we can't live to be 150, 175 or 200? We believe we can. It is the direct answer to the ceiling question: antioxidants raise your average, the full program raises the maximum, and Wallach puts that maximum far past 100.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000260.verbatim:
it was believed that we would never
get a man to land on the moon and return to earth and so on - who is to say we can’t live
to be 150, 175 or 200 - we believe we can!

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000261.claim_text: Wallach cites Adelman's data on how the aging pigment ceroid lipofuscin accumulates in human brain cells with age: it fills about 35% of a cell at 30-40 years, 41% by 50-60, 55% by 70-80, and 78% by 90-100.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000262.claim_text: Wallach tracks the US decline in world longevity rankings from CDC and WHO surveys: Americans ranked 17th in 1990, fell to 24th by 2000, 46th by 2005, and 48th by 2008.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000262.verbatim:
In a CDC (Atlanta, GA) and WHO survey in 1990,
Americans ranked 17th in the world in longevity; in the year
2000 Americans dropped in ranking to 24th in longevity; and
in 2005, Americans dropped in ranking again to a pitiful 46th,
and in 2008 Americans again dropped to 48th in the world
when it comes to health and longevity.
