WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000265.claim_text: Wallach singles out selenium as an antagonist of mercury: the two compete in the body, so keeping selenium up blunts mercury's toxicity. He names dental amalgams and industrial pollution as the common chronic-exposure routes, and gives a practical rule — anyone at risk should supplement selenium before, during, and after a detox, so mercury freed during the process does not do damage on its way out. It sits inside his broader case for selenium as a cornerstone mineral; he links its deficiency to conditions ranging from cardiomyopathy and muscle weakness to a raised risk of cancer.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000265.verbatim:
Selenium acts as an antagonist of mercury. Those at
risk for chronic mercury toxicity (dental amalgams, industrial
pollution, preservatives, etc.) should supplement with
selenium prior to, during and after detoxification activities.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000266.claim_text: EDTA has a striking origin: calcium EDTA was a man-made amino acid the Germans engineered just before World War I to antidote the arsenic and lead of chemical-warfare exposure — it was born as a heavy-metal antidote. That same claw-like binding ('chelate' is Latin for claw) is why it is used today for intravenous chelation therapy to open obstructed arteries, and Wallach folds IV EDTA chelation into his programs for cardiovascular problems — poor circulation, arteriosclerosis, stroke. Do not confuse it with the 'chelated minerals' on a supplement label (a livestock-industry invention for better absorption) or with plant-derived colloidal minerals — EDTA is the therapeutic chelator that grabs metals and pulls them out.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000266.verbatim:
The original chelating agent use was calcium EDTA, a
man-made amino acid that was created by the Germans just
prior to WWII to antidote arsenic and lead exposure in chemical
warfare attacks (calcium EDTA is used today for intravenous
chelation therapy to open up obstructed arteries).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000267.claim_text: The gerontologist Roy Walford — cited throughout Wallach's longevity work — called free radicals 'the great white sharks in the biochemical sea': short-lived but voracious molecules that oxidize and damage tissue, hitting cell membranes and mitochondrial membranes hardest. Most free radicals the body meets are oxidants — a loose electron whirling around a super-activated oxygen atom — and their 'shark attacks' on the polyunsaturated fats in those membranes produce lipid peroxides that go on to cross-link proteins, lipids and DNA. It is the vivid image behind why Wallach treats antioxidants, and the ORAC score that measures them, as essential defense.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000267.verbatim:
Dr. Roy Walford referred to free radicals as the “Great
white sharks in the biochemical sea” - these short-lived but
voracious chemicals oxidize and damage tissue, particularly
cell membranes and mitochondrial membranes.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000268.claim_text: Antioxidants are the body's defense against free radicals — the reactive molecules that oxidize and damage your cells, cell walls and mitochondria. Wallach's signature point is that they don't work alone: the antioxidant enzyme systems present in every healthy cell need raw materials and mineral cofactors to run at full capacity — glutathione, for example, requires selenium. So in his framework, getting the benefit of antioxidants is inseparable from getting the minerals that power them, and he measures the antioxidant strength of foods by their ORAC score.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000268.verbatim:
Antioxidant enzyme systems are normally present in all
healthy aerobic cells - remember, antioxidants also need raw
materials and mineral cofactors to operate at their optimum
capacity (glutathione requires selenium, etc.).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000269.claim_text: Wallach explains a mutual “metabolic antagonism” between mercury and selenium — each blunts the other's toxicity. In practice that means selenium supplements protect against mercury poisoning two specific ways: they guard the human kidney against the tissue death (necrosis) mercury causes, and they block mercury from crossing the placenta into the fetus — a real concern in his view, since mercury vapor off-gasses continuously from “silver” dental amalgam fillings. The antagonism runs both directions (mercury, in turn, protects against selenium overdose), but the practical upshot is that he treats adequate selenium as a frontline defense for anyone carrying mercury fillings or exposed to environmental mercury.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000269.verbatim:
Because a mutual antagonism between
Hg and Se exists, Se protects the human kidney from necrosis
(tissue death) by mercury poisoning and the placental transfer
of mercury.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000270.claim_text: Wallach explains pica and 'cribbing' — the compulsion to eat non-food items — as a sign of zinc deficiency. The behaviors he lists include geophagia (dirt eating), pagophagia (ice eating), and the eating of wool, hair, and paint. Rather than treating these cravings as purely psychological, he reads them as the body signaling a mineral shortfall, one that also shows up in unsupplemented athletes who lose heavy zinc in sweat.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000270.verbatim:
Pica/Cribbing (geophagia, pagophagia, wool eating,
hair eating, dirt eating, paint eating, etc.)

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000271.claim_text: In Wallach's account magnesium is a white, silvery, very lightweight metal that is essential to all living organisms. It works as a cofactor with electro-chemical, catalytic and structural roles, activating numerous enzymes throughout the body, and it is a constituent of every chlorophyll molecule -- which is why Wallach calls it the ultimate source of all biological energy. An adult body holds 20 to 28 grams of magnesium, most of it locked in bone and skeletal muscle. Wallach treats magnesium as the calcium 'relaxer' and blames a shortage for problems ranging from muscle cramps, migraines and heart palpitations to the arterial 'malignant calcification' he pins on magnesium deficiency rather than on cholesterol.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000271.verbatim:
Magnesium, as a mineral is essential to all living
organisms and has cofactor, electro-chemical, catalytic, and
structural functions. It activates numerous enzymes and is a
constituent of all chlorophylls.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000272.claim_text: Wallach states that an adult human carries 20 to 28 grams of magnesium in total, with roughly 60% stored in bone and about 26% in skeletal muscle; the rest is spread across organs and body fluids. In the blood, magnesium runs 1.5 to 2.1 mEq/L and is second only to potassium as an intracellular cation. About half of the body's magnesium — most of it bound in bone — is not exchangeable, meaning it can't be readily called on when you run short.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000272.verbatim:
The adult human contains 20 to 28 grams of total body
Mg. Approximately 60% is found in bone. Twenty-six percent
is associated with skeletal muscle and the balance is distributed
between various organs and body fluids. Serum levels of Mg
range from 1.5 to 2.1 mEq/L (a measure of electrolytes) and is
second to potassium as an intracellular cation. Half of the Mg,
including most that is bound in bone, is not exchangeable.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000273.claim_text: Unlike some deficiencies, a magnesium shortfall doesn't produce a specific pica craving for magnesium itself, Wallach notes — magnesium-deficient animals instead crave and eat common salt. In fact magnesium tastes bad enough that animals will die of magnesium-deficiency-initiated seizures rather than consume a pure magnesium supplement. He adds that recovery from the deficiency can be so unpleasant that the bad taste of the needed supplement outweighs the misery of the deficiency itself.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000273.verbatim:
There is no evidence of a specific pica behavior unique
to a magnesium deficiency. Magnesium deficient animals will
crave and eat common salt. Magnesium tastes bad enough that
animals will die of magnesium deficiency initiated seizures
rather than consume a pure magnesium supplement.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000274.claim_text: Wallach points to two familiar over-the-counter products built on magnesium. Milk of magnesia is a suspension of magnesium hydroxide in water, used as an everyday laxative. Epsom salts are a hydrated form of magnesium sulfate — first found in the well water of Epsom, England in the mid-1600s — and are still used today as a wound disinfectant and to reduce the swelling and inflammation of bruises, strains and sprains.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000274.verbatim:
Milk of magnesia is a suspension of magnesium
hydroxide, Mg(OH),, in water, it is used as an everyday OTC
laxative. Another OTC remedy containing magnesium is
Epsom salts. These salts are a hydrated form of magnesium
sulfate; it was first discovered in well water from Epsom,
England in the mid 17th century. Epsom salts are still used
today as a wound disinfectant and for reducing the swelling
and inflammation of bruises, strains and sprains.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000275.claim_text: Wallach notes that water itself can be a real source of magnesium. He points to the Nicoyan water supply in Costa Rica, which percolates up through limestone bedrock and carries high levels of calcium, magnesium and other minerals. It was reportedly so hard — so loaded with calcium and magnesium — that it had to be diluted 50% with distilled water before it could even be tested.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000275.verbatim:
The Nicoyan water supply percolated up through the
Nicoya limestone bedrock and contains high levels of calcium,
magnesium and other minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000276.claim_text: Wallach explains that magnesium — a white, silvery, very lightweight metal — takes its name from its ore, magnesite (dolomite), which is primarily magnesium carbonate. That ore is believed to have first been mined in Magnesia, a district in ancient Greece. The element itself was later identified as a separate element by the British chemist Sir Humphry Davy in 1808, who used electrolysis to extract it from magnesium oxide.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000276.verbatim:
Magnesium is a white silvery metal that is very light
weight, its name is derived from the ore magnesite (dolomite)
which is primarily magnesium carbonate. Magnesite is
believed to have been originally mined in Magnesia, a district
in ancient Greece.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000277.claim_text: Wallach puts the daily requirement for essential fatty acids, which include omega-3, at two to three percent of total calories consumed. He works the example that a 1,500-calorie daily diet would call for 45 calories, or about five grams, of EFA.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000277.verbatim:
The daily requirement for the essential fatty acids is
two to three percent of the total calories consumed. A daily
diet containing 1,500 calories would dictate an essential fatty
acid requirement of 45 calories or five grams of EFA.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000278.claim_text: Wallach explains that bile salts are required to absorb essential fatty acids, good fats such as triglycerides and cholesterol, and the fat-soluble vitamins. He advises that people who have had their gallbladders removed should supplement with ox bile to restore the bile salts needed for efficient absorption of these fats.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000278.verbatim:
People who have
their gall bladders removed should supplement with ox bile
to increase the availability of bile salts which are required
for the efficient absorption of essential fatty acids, good fats
(triglycerides, cholesterol, etc.) and fat soluble vitamins.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000279.claim_text: Wallach recounts that for years the FDA ruled the evidence 'inconclusive' and made it illegal to tell people they could reduce their risk of stroke and coronary-thrombosis sudden death by supplementing with omega-3 essential fatty acids. He holds that omega-3 supplementation does lower those cardiovascular risks, and fought to win the right to say so.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000279.verbatim:
because the FDA ruled that the information was “inconclusive”
it was deemed illegal to inform people that they could reduce
their risk of stroke and coronary thrombosis sudden death by
supplementing with omega-3 essential fatty acids.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000280.claim_text: Wallach reports that, after much fanfare, vitamin C supplementation has been shown to reduce the rate, severity and duration of a cold on the average by 20%. So while it is not a cure, taking vitamin C can meaningfully cut how often, how badly and how long a cold hits you.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000280.verbatim:
After much fanfare, vitamin C supplementation has
been shown to reduce the rate, severity and duration of a cold
on the average by 20%.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000281.claim_text: Wallach states that cigarette smoking increases the need for ascorbic acid (vitamin C) to about twice the normal requirement. Smokers therefore need to take in roughly double the vitamin C of a non-smoker to meet their body's demand.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000281.verbatim:
Cigarette smoking increases the need for ascorbic acid
to about twice the normal requirement.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000282.claim_text: Wallach recounts that pure ascorbic acid was first isolated in 1928 by Albert Szent-Gyorgyi, who found it in adrenal tissue, orange and cabbage and called it hexuronic acid. It was not until 1932 that C. Glenn King, at the University of Pittsburgh, reisolated ascorbic acid from lemons and identified it as vitamin C, showing it had the properties of preventing and curing scurvy in guinea pigs.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000282.verbatim:
Pure ascorbic acid was isolated in 1928 by Albert
Szent-Gyorgyi, who discovered it in adrenal tissue, orange
and cabbage and identified it as hexuronic acid. It was not
until 1932 that C. Glenn King at the University of Pittsburgh
reisolated ascorbic acid from lemons that it was identified as
vitamin C and had the properties of preventing and curing
scurvy in guinea pigs.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000283.claim_text: According to Wallach, British sailors were often called 'limeys' because they carried lemons - not limes - on their ships to prevent and cure scurvy, the vitamin C deficiency disease. The vitamin C in the citrus kept crews from developing scurvy on long voyages.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000283.verbatim:
British sailors
were oftentimes referred to as “limeys” because they carried
lemons (not limes) on their ships to prevent and cure scurvy.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000284.claim_text: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin, absorbed along with the ordinary dietary fats in a meal and stored mainly in the body's fat. Because of this, any health problem or habit that interferes with fat absorption also interferes with vitamin A absorption and function — Wallach names antibiotic use, gallbladder disease, celiac disease, dietary fat deficiencies, high-fiber diets, and taking mineral oil with meals.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000284.verbatim:
The fat soluble vitamins are absorbed along with other
common and essential dietary lipids and any health challenge
or health practice that interferes with the absorption of fats
(antibiotic use, gall bladder disease, celiac disease, dietary
fat deficiencies, extremely high fiber diets, mineral oil
consumption during meals and overt deficiencies) interferes
with fat soluble vitamin absorption and function.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000285.claim_text: Vitamin A comes both preformed in animal foods and as carotenoids in plants. The book's food table lists beef liver highest by far (about 43,900 units per 100 g), then raw carrots (11,000), baked sweet potato (8,100), cooked spinach (7,300), and dried apricots (5,500). Wallach notes vegetables carry vitamin A activity in proportion to their carotenoid content — carotene, cryptoxanthin, and other yellow, red, or orange pigments that are often hidden by the green pigment of chlorophyll.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000285.verbatim:
Vegetables were later found to contain vitamin A
activity in relation to their carotenoid content - carotene,
cryptoxanthin and other yellow, red or orange pigments that
were oftentimes hidden by the green pigment of chlorophyll.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000286.claim_text: Investigators noticed that animals kept longer on fat-free diets developed inflammation and infections of the eyes — problems that were quickly reversed when fats from butter or cod liver oil were added to the diet. In 1924 the Danish investigator Bloch showed that xerophthalmia (dry, damaged eyes) in children was the same disease described in laboratory rats in 1913, and that it could be prevented or cured by adding liver, butter, or cod liver oil to the diet.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000286.verbatim:
Investigators also noted that those animals that lived
longer on fat free diets developed inflammation and infections
of the eyes - these conditions were quickly rever sed when fats
from butter or cod liver oil were added to the diet.

In 1924, Bloch, a Danish investigator, showed that
xerophthalmia in children was the same disease described in
1913 in laboratory rats, and that the disease could be prevented
or cured by adding liver, butter or cod liver oil to their diet.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000287.claim_text: Wallach lists vitamin D's core functions as stimulating the active, energy-requiring intestinal absorption of calcium and the active phosphate-transport system in the intestine. Working with parathyroid hormone, it mobilizes calcium from bone to maintain normal blood calcium levels, and it mobilizes phosphate from bone to maintain proper serum phosphate levels. It also supports the kidney's reabsorption of calcium from urine. In short, vitamin D governs how the body handles calcium and phosphorus.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000287.verbatim:
Vitamin D Functions:

Stimulates the active, energy requiring intestinal

absorption of calcium.

Stimulates the active phosphate-transport system in
the intestine.

With the parathyroid hormone, it mobilizes calcium
from bone to maintain normal blood levels of calcium.

It mobilizes phosphate from the bone to maintain
proper serum phosphate levels.

It supports reabsorption of calcium from urine by the
kidney.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000288.claim_text: Wallach explains that cholesterol is converted by the intestinal mucosa into 7-dehydrocholesterol, the provitamin of vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol), and that the skin and other tissues also carry out this process when exposed to ultraviolet light and sunlight. Separately, ergosterol, a yeast sterol, is converted into vitamin D2 on exposure to sunlight or UV light. This is why sun exposure is a primary source of vitamin D and why cholesterol is its raw material.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000288.verbatim:
Ergosterol, a yeast
sterol, is converted to vitamin D2 when exposed to ultraviolet
light. Cholesterol is converted by the intestinal mucosa
to 7-dehydrocholesterol, the provitamin of vitamin D3,
cholecalciferol. This process is also carried out by the skin and
other tissues, when exposed to ultraviolet light and sunlight.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000289.claim_text: Wallach cites Dr. Michael Holick of Boston University, who said the bottom line is that vitamin D is important for the health of both children and adults and may help prevent many serious chronic diseases. He reports Holick's finding that vitamin D deficiency in adults increases the risk of heart attacks, increases mortality in breast and colon cancer victims, raises mortality in dialysis patients, and increases the risk of type II diabetes in children. This positions vitamin D as protective against major chronic diseases, not just rickets.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000289.verbatim:
In 2006 Dr. Michael Holick, a professor of medicine,
physiology and biophysics at Boston University said, “The
bottom line is, we now recognize that vitamin D3 is important
for health for both children and adults and may help prevent
many serious chronic diseases.”
Holick’s studies have shown that deficiencies of
vitamin D3 in adults results in an increase in risk of heart

attacks, increased mortality in breast and colon cancer


 

victims, increased risk of mortality in dialysis patients and an
increased risk of developing type II diabetes in children.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000290.claim_text: Not all dietary iron is equal, Wallach explains: heme iron from meat is about 10% absorbable, while iron from fresh plant sources is only about 1% available, because the plants' own phytates lock it up. Absorption happens mainly in the duodenum — the first stretch of the small intestine, where the contents are still acidic — which is one reason low stomach acid worsens iron status. It underlies his caution that vegetarians are especially prone to iron deficiency.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000290.verbatim:
Iron is stored in bone marrow and liver (i.e. hemosiderin
and ferritin). Heme iron from meat is 10% available for
absorption, while iron from fresh plant sources are only one
percent available because of the endogenous phytates in the
plant. Iron absorption takes place primarily in the duodenum
where the intestinal environment is still acid.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000291.claim_text: Wallach explains that calcium is primarily absorbed in the duodenum while the environment is still acid, and the absorption rate falls once the intestinal contents turn alkaline. It is taken up by active cellular transport and simple diffusion, but metallic calcium absorption may be limited to one to three percent or less and is easily disrupted by other substances in the gut. Under ideal conditions calcium is highly absorbable — up to 98% in the organically bound, plant-derived colloidal and water-soluble chelated forms.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000291.verbatim:
Calcium is primarily absorbed in the duodenum, where
the environment is still acid. Once the food in the intestine
converts to an alkaline pH, the absorption rate of calcium will
decline. Calcium is absorbed from the small intestine by active
cellular transport and by simple diffusion. Metallic calcium
absorption may be limited to one to three percent or less and
can be affected by many substances in the gut. Under ideal
circumstances calcium is highly absorbable, up to 98% in the
organically bound plant derived colloidal mineral and water
soluble chelated form.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000292.claim_text: Wallach explains that a 1,000 mg calcium carbonate tablet only contains 400 mg of metallic (elemental) calcium, and metallic minerals are only about 8 to 12% absorbable in the young and as little as 3 to 5% after age 35 to 40. So two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules do not deliver 2,000 mg of calcium — they supply 800 mg of elemental calcium, of which roughly 80 mg is actually absorbed. To get 2,000 mg of usable calcium from calcium carbonate, he calculates you would have to take 25 capsules a day, meaning a 100-capsule bottle would last only four days.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000292.verbatim:
A typical metallic mineral supplement, either alone or
part of a multiple is calcium carbonate. Calcium carbonate can
be purchased in 1,000 mg tablets or capsules, which breaks
down to 400 mg of metallic calcium and 600 mg of carbonate.
Two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules or tablets do not
give you 2,000 mg of calcium - they only supply 800 mg of
elemental calcium and at a 10% availability rate you will net
only 80 mg of available calcium. Therefore, to get 2,000 mg of
usable calcium from a 1,000 mg capsule or tablet of calcium
carbonate, you would have to take 25 capsules each day! A
100 capsule bottle of calcium carbonate will therefore only
last 4 days.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000293.claim_text: Wallach notes that in the 1st century the Romans used a calcium compound they called calx, the Latin word for lime -- the root of the modern name. The pure metal itself was first isolated in 1808 by Sir Humphry Davy. Calcium is an extremely reactive element that is never found in pure form in nature.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000293.verbatim:
In the 1st century, the Romans used a compound of
calcium they called calx (lime) in Latin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000294.claim_text: According to Wallach, mild vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency produces mental confusion, muscular weakness, peripheral paralysis, calf muscle tenderness, muscle fatigue, emotional instability, loss of appetite, loss of interest in daily tasks and general lethargy. Chronic deficiency advances to a polyneuritis and congestive heart failure with edema and life-threatening pulmonary edema. The signs therefore span both the nervous system and the cardiovascular system.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000294.verbatim:
Mild deficiencies produce mental confusion, muscular
weakness, peripheral paralysis, calf muscle tenderness,
muscle fatigue, emotional instability, loss of appetite, loss of
interest in daily tasks and general lethargy.

Chronic deficiencies of thiamine result in a polyneuritis
and congestive heart failure with edema and life-threatening
pulmonary edema.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000295.claim_text: Wallach explains that fats spare thiamine because they can be metabolized for energy without the need for it, whereas the metabolism of carbohydrate requires thiamine. In practical terms, a diet high in sugar and refined carbohydrate increases the body's demand for vitamin B1. Fats also aid in the transport and absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000295.verbatim:
Fats aid in the transport and absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Fats spare thiamin since they
can be metabolized for energy without the need for thiamin,
whereas, the metabolism of carbohydrate requires thiamine.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000296.claim_text: Where to get riboflavin (vitamin B2): Wallach lists milk, cheddar and cottage cheese, organ meats such as liver, heart, and kidney, eggs, and green leafy vegetables — but only in small amounts, so variety matters. He adds that B2 was first spotted in 1879 as the yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey, and that a shortage shows up first as soreness and burning of the lips, mouth, and tongue, along with light-sensitive, itchy eyes.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000296.verbatim:
Riboflavin is present in small amounts in milk, cheddar
and cottage cheese, organ meats (liver, heart, kidney, etc.),
eggs and green leafy vegetables.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000297.claim_text: Wallach recounts that riboflavin (vitamin B2) was recognized in 1879 as a yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey, but its biological significance was not understood until 1932, when a team of German investigators isolated 'Warburg's yellow enzyme' from yeast and demonstrated that the substance was necessary for an intracellular enzyme to function. The substance was synthesized in 1935 by Kuhn, who gave it the name riboflavin.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000297.verbatim:
Riboflavin or vitamin B2 was recognized in 1879 as a
yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey. The biological
significance of this yellow pigment was not understood
until 1932 when a team of German investigators isolated
“Warburg’s yellow enzyme” from yeast and demonstrated
that the substance was necessary for the functioning of an
intracellular enzyme. The substance was synthesized in 1935
by Kuhn and named riboflavin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000298.claim_text: The early stages of niacin deficiency show up as muscular weakness, anorexia (loss of appetite), indigestion, and skin eruptions. Severe niacin deficiency produces classic pellagra, characterized by the '3 D's' — dermatitis, dementia, and diarrhea — along with tremors and a sore tongue ('beef tongue').
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000298.verbatim:
The early stages of niacin deficiency show up as
muscular weakness, anorexia, indigestion and skin eruptions.
Severe deficiency of niacin produces classic pellagra which is
characterized by the “3 D’s” of pellagra (dermatitis, dementia
and diarrhea), tremors and sore tongue or “beef tongue.”

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000299.claim_text: Vitamin B5, also called pantothenic acid, is one of the essential B-complex vitamins. In Wallach's framework it is indispensable because it forms part of coenzyme A, the molecule that runs two-carbon unit metabolism. Through coenzyme A the body requires B5 to metabolize all three major food groups - carbohydrates, lipids (fats), and proteins - which places it at the center of energy production and the manufacture of fatty acids, steroid hormones, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Because it is water-soluble and continuously used up, it must be supplied through diet and daily supplementation; a shortfall shows up as burning feet, dermatitis, fatigue, depression, and a racing heartbeat.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000299.verbatim:
Pantothenic acid or vitamin B5 is part of coenzyme A,
which functions in two-carbon unit metabolism. Pantothenic
acid is required for the metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids
and proteins.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000300.claim_text: Wallach describes a pyridoxine deficiency syndrome in mentally retarded children who also have convulsions caused by an inborn error of B6 metabolism. These children are thought to be unable to synthesize GABA, and correcting the syndrome requires daily ingestion of large amounts of B6 to prevent permanent retardation. He adds that children with cryptogenic epilepsy appearing at several years of age likewise need large oral doses of B6 to improve the EEG and control seizures.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000300.verbatim:
A deficiency syndrome for pyridoxine has been
identified in mentally retarded children that also have
convulsions due to an inborn error of B6 metabolism. It is
thought that these children are unable to synthesize GABA;
correction of this syndrome requires daily ingestion of large
amounts of B6 to prevent permanent retardation.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000301.claim_text: Wallach recounts that pyridoxine, or vitamin B6, was identified in 1938 as a separate entity within the vitamin 'B-complex.' Rather than a single molecule, B6 is a functional complex of three closely related chemical compounds: pyridoxine, pyridoxamine, and pyridoxal. Together these forms carry out the vitamin's roles in the body.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000301.verbatim:
Pyridoxine or vitamin B6 was identified in 1938 as a
fraction or separate entity of the vitamin “B-complex.” Vitamin
B6 is a functional complex of three closely related chemical
compounds - pyridoxine, pyridoxamine and pyridoxal.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000302.claim_text: In pernicious anemia, which is caused by a vitamin B12 deficiency, folic acid will produce a marked improvement in the anemia. However, the gastrointestinal symptoms and the neurologic lesions continue to progress unchecked. Wallach calls this the 'masking effect' of folic acid, because the corrected blood picture hides the ongoing B12-related nerve and gut damage.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000302.verbatim:
In pernicious anemia (B12 deficiency), folic acid will
produce a marked improvement in the anemia, however,
the gastrointestinal symptoms and neurologic lesions will
continue to progress - this is referred to as the “masking
effect” of folic acid.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000303.claim_text: Folacin, or folic acid, was first identified as one of many growth factors in bacteria and laboratory animals and in the prevention and treatment of anemia; it was synthesized in 1946 and quickly established as an essential nutrient for humans. Wallach states that folic acid deficiencies may be the most common vitamin deficiency in humans. The deficiency produces poor growth, megaloblastic anemia, multiple blood disorders, glossitis, and gastrointestinal tract disturbances.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000303.verbatim:
Folacin or folic acid was identified as one of many
growth factors in bacteria and laboratory animals and in
the prevention and treatment of anemia. It was synthesized
in 1946 and quickly established as an essential nutrient for
humans.

Folic acid deficiencies may be the most common

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000305.claim_text: In Wallach's framework, vitamin B12 -- also called cobalamin -- is a red, water-soluble vitamin, and both its color and its function trace to a single cobalt atom held at the center of the molecule, which makes B12 the body's main way of using the essential mineral cobalt. It is a fragile compound, slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances, and about 30% of its activity is destroyed during cooking. B12 works together with folic acid to build DNA and RNA, supports the bone marrow in making red blood cells, and is needed to form the myelin that insulates nerves -- so a deficiency shows up as pernicious anemia and progressive nerve damage. Because only bacteria, fungi, and algae can actually manufacture it, B12 reaches people mainly through animal foods and supplements, and absorbing it depends on adequate stomach acid plus an acid-dependent 'intrinsic factor.'
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000305.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water
soluble. The red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule.
Vitamin B12 is slowly deactivated by exposure to acid, alkali,
light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. About 30% of
B12 activity is lost during cooking (electric, gas, microwave,
wood, charcoal, etc.).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000306.claim_text: For vitamin B12 to be absorbed, the intrinsic factor must be present and the stomach must be acidic, at a pH of 2.0 or less. Intrinsic factor is a mucoprotein enzyme (Castle's intrinsic factor) that is part of normal stomach secretions. When a person has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid, usually from a salt/NaCl deficiency), the intrinsic factor stops working and B12 cannot be absorbed, which is why doctors frequently give B12 shots to older people on salt-restricted diets.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000306.verbatim:
Metallic cobalt itself is absorbed at the rate of 20 to
26.2% by mice and in humans if intrinsic factor is present
in the stomach and the stomach pH is 2.0 or less. Intrinsic
factor is a mucoprotein enzyme known as Castle’s intrinsic
factor and is part of normal stomach secretions. If a person
has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid- usually a NaCl
deficiency) the intrinsic factor will not work and B12 cobalt is
not absorbed - this is why doctors frequently give B12 shots
to older people on salt restricted diets.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000307.claim_text: In pernicious anemia, which is a B12 deficiency, taking folic acid will produce a marked improvement in the anemia itself. However, the gastrointestinal symptoms and the neurologic lesions continue to progress unchecked. Wallach calls this the 'masking effect' of folic acid, because the visible improvement in the blood hides the ongoing nerve and gastrointestinal damage of untreated B12 deficiency.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000307.verbatim:
In pernicious anemia (B12 deficiency), folic acid will
produce a marked improvement in the anemia, however,
the gastrointestinal symptoms and neurologic lesions will
continue to progress - this is referred to as the “masking
effect” of folic acid.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000308.claim_text: The very first vitamin B12 molecule isolated in the laboratory happened to contain a cyanide group, and that is how it got the name cyanocobalamine. Several different cobalamine compounds carry vitamin B12 activity, but cyanocobalamine and hydroxycobalamine are the most active.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000308.verbatim:
The original B12 molecule isolated
in the laboratory contained a cyanide group, thus the name
cyanocobalamine. There are several different cobalamine
compounds that have B12 activity, with cyanocobalamine and
hydroxycobalamine being the most active.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000310.claim_text: Wallach groups copper oxide with the metallic minerals such as calcium carbonate, oyster shell and iron oxide. He says metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary, are only 8 to 12 percent biologically available to younger people and drop to just 3 to 5 percent after age 35 to 40, so he treats copper oxide as a poor form of copper compared with plant-derived colloidal minerals.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000310.verbatim:
Metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary
are only 8 to 12% biologically available to younger animals
and humans; after attaining the age of 35 to 40 years, the
availability of metallic minerals for humans plummets to 3 to
5%.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000311.claim_text: According to Wallach, the radiant colors of many precious gems come from trace amounts of chromium. Small amounts of chromium in the form of corundum give rubies their red color, while the chromium-bearing mineral beryl produces the characteristic green of emeralds.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000311.verbatim:
The beautiful and radiant colors, of many precious gems,
are also due to the presence of trace amounts of chromium.
The red color of rubies is produced by small amounts of
chromium in the form of corundum. The characteristic green
color of emeralds is produced by the presence of the chromium
bearing mineral beryl.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000312.claim_text: Wallach describes where chromium occurs in nature, from about 100 ppm in igneous rocks and 90 ppm in shale down to trace levels in fresh and sea water, with soils ranging from 5 to 3,000 ppm (highest in soils derived from basalt and serpentine). In living tissue, he notes, chromium accumulates in RNA and insulin.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000312.verbatim:
Cr-Chromium is found in igneous rocks at 100 ppm,
shale at 90 ppm, sandstone at 35 ppm, limestone at 11 ppm,
fresh water at 0.00018 ppm, sea water at 0.00005 ppm, soils
at 5 to 3,000 ppm (highest in soils derived from basalt and
serpentine), marine plants at 1 ppm, terrestrial plants at 0.23
ppm, marine animals at 0.2 to 1.0 ppmand in terrestrial animals
at 0.075 ppm, where it accumulates in RNA and insulin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000313.claim_text: Wallach highlights a steady decline in the average American serum chromium since 1948. His figures fall from 28 (city) and 1000 (rural) in 1948 to roughly 13 in 1971, down through the 1970s, and to just 0.13 by 1985 — a dramatic collapse in the population's chromium status over a few decades.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000313.verbatim:
Of greater concern has been the steady decline in the
average American serum chromium since 1948.

Mean Chromium Blood Levels (ug/l) Year
28 (city) 1000 (rural) 1948
13 1971
10 1972
4.7-5.1 1973
0.73 - 1.6 1974
0.16 1978
0.43 1980
0.13 1985

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000314.claim_text: Wallach explains that the balance of sodium, potassium and chloride is regulated by hormones from the adrenal cortex together with the anterior pituitary gland. In Addison's disease — a loss of adrenal-cortex function — the body can no longer retain sodium and potassium properly, producing general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss and a marked 'salt hunger.' He notes these symptoms can be relieved by supplementing salt (NaCl) or by giving adrenal cortical hormones.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000314.verbatim:
Hormonal control of Na, K and Cl balance is regulated
by the adrenal cortex hormones as well as by the anterior
pituitary gland. Addison’s Disease, a loss of function of the
adrenal cortex, results in the loss of Na and K retention with
clinical signs of general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss,
and a marked “salt hunger.” The symptoms can be relieved
with the supplementation of NaCl or by administering adrenal
cortical hormones (steroids).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000315.claim_text: Potassium was first isolated in 1807 by the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy, Wallach records, who pried the highly reactive metal from its compounds using electrolysis — passing an electric current through them. He adds context that makes the element feel less abstract: the human body holds roughly 140 grams of potassium, and because a small fraction is the naturally radioactive isotope potassium-40, each of us carries a lifelong trace of internal background radiation.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000315.verbatim:
Potassium was first isolated by Sir Humphry Davy
in 1807 using electrolysis as a means of separating elemental
potassium from its compounds.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000316.claim_text: Iodine is a violet-black solid element, the heaviest and one of the most reactive members of the halogen family, found in seaweed, brine wells, and the sea. In Wallach's framework it is an essential nutrient for all vertebrates: the body combines it with the amino acid (protein building block) tyrosine to manufacture thyroxin, the main thyroid hormone that regulates metabolism, heart rate, and body temperature. When iodine runs short -- which Wallach says is common, especially since many Americans cut back on salt on their doctors' advice -- the thyroid gland enlarges into a goiter and the body slows into hypothyroidism.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000316.verbatim:
Iodine is a violet-black solid that vaporizes to give a
violet gas. It is found in sea weed and brine wells, in the sea,
in the form of inorganic salts and organic iodides. It is the
heaviest element in the halogen family and is highly reactive.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000317.claim_text: Trace minerals differ widely in how well the gut absorbs them, and iodine is among the best. Wallach states that the metallic form of iodine is absorbed at a ratio of almost 1:1, compared with about 1:10 for iron and just 1:100 for chromium. He uses this to argue for taking the most efficient, absorbable form of trace-mineral supplement.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000317.verbatim:
For the metallic form of iodine the ratio of absorption
is almost 1:1; for iron its 1:10 and for chromium its 1:100.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000318.claim_text: Iodine takes its name from the Greek word iodes, meaning "violet-colored," a reference to the striking violet gas it gives off. It was discovered in 1811 by Bernard Courtois, who noticed a purple vapor rising from a sample of kelp to which he had added sulfuric acid. A drop of iodine will also turn starch, as in potato or flour, a deep blue.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000318.verbatim:
The color of the gas
determined its name, translated from the Greek word iodes,
meaning “violet-colored.” A drop of iodine will turn starch a
deep blue (potato, flour, etc.).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000319.claim_text: Wallach reports that vitamin E deficiency can directly harm reproduction. Its effects include miscarriage, fetal reabsorption, testicular atrophy and birth defects. Deficiency can also produce muscular dystrophy, hemolytic anemia, degeneration of the heart muscle (myocardial degeneration), softening of the brain (encephalomalacia) and liver necrosis. This reproductive link echoes vitamin E's discovery, which came from reversing infertility in rats.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000319.verbatim:
Additional symptoms of vitamin E deficiency include
miscarriage, fetal reabsorption, testicular atrophy, birth
defects, muscular dystrophy, hemolytic anemia, myocardial
degeneration, encephalomalacia and liver necrosis.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000320.claim_text: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant that shields the lipids in cell membranes from peroxidation, a form of free-radical damage. Wallach explains that this ability to protect membrane fats from oxidation is directly related to vitamin E's anti-aging properties. In the same role it prevents oxidation damage to polyunsaturated fatty acids and protects cellular and mitochondrial membranes, helping keep cells from breaking down over time.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000320.verbatim:
The ability of vitamin E to protect membrane lipids from
peroxidation has been related to its anti-aging properties.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000321.claim_text: Wallach describes a clearly demonstrated relationship between vitamin E, selenium, glutathione peroxidase, the amino acid cystine and the polyunsaturated fats in the cell membrane. Selenium activates glutathione peroxidase, which destroys peroxides after they form but before they can cause cell membrane damage. Vitamin E and selenium therefore act as partners in protecting cells from oxidative damage.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000321.verbatim:
A relationship between vitamin E, selenium,
glutathione peroxidase, cystine and polyunsaturated fats in
the cell membrane has been clearly demonstrated.

Selenium, which activates glutathione peroxidase, destroys
peroxides after they are produced but before they can cause
cell membrane damage.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000322.claim_text: Vitamin E, also called tocopherol, was first identified by Evans and Bishop in 1922. They observed that infertility in rats could be reversed when the animals were fed a substance isolated from vegetable oils. The vitamin was later chemically identified in 1938. Its origin in fertility research is reflected in its very name.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000322.verbatim:
Tocopherol or vitamin E was first identified by Evans
and Bishop in 1922, when they observed infertility in rats
could be reversed when they were fed a substance isolated
from vegetable oils.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000323.claim_text: Vitamin E was chemically identified in 1938 and given the name tocopherol. The word is built from the Greek 'tokos,' which translates to 'offspring.' The name reflects vitamin E's early association with fertility and successful reproduction. This ties back to its discovery through experiments on infertility in rats.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000323.verbatim:
Vitamin E was chemically identified in
1938 and named tocopherol after tokos from the Greek which
translates to “offspring.”

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000324.claim_text: Wallach highlights osteocalcin, a vitamin K-dependent protein now known to modulate the deposition of calcium into the bone matrix. Because of this role, he states that vitamin K is as essential to healthy bone maintenance as vitamin D. In other words, calcium needs vitamin K — not just vitamin D — to be laid down properly in bone.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000324.verbatim:
The vitamin K-dependent Gla-containing protein called
“osteocalcin” is now known to modulate calcium deposition
into bone matrix - vitamin K is as essential to healthy bone
maintenance as vitamin D.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000325.claim_text: According to Wallach, the coumarin anticoagulant drugs warfarin and dicumarol prevent the blood from coagulating specifically by antagonizing the action of vitamin K. Since vitamin K is required to make the clotting proteins, blocking it thins the blood. This is why these drugs and vitamin K work in direct opposition to each other.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000325.verbatim:
The coumarin anticoagulant drugs (warfarin and
dicumarol) act to prevent coagulation by antagonizing the
action of vitamin K.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000326.claim_text: Wallach considers vitamin K deficiency uncommon. It tends to occur only when the diet is low in green leafy vegetables, when the growth of intestinal flora has been inhibited by antibiotics, or when there is a fat-absorption problem. Because gut bacteria make much of our vitamin K and the vitamin is fat-soluble, both antibiotics and poor fat absorption can quietly cause a shortage.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000326.verbatim:
The deficiency of vitamin K is uncommon except when
an individuals diet is low in green leafy vegetables

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000327.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in 1935, Dam in Copenhagen observed a fatal hemorrhagic (bleeding) disease in newly hatched chickens fed a laboratory diet that contained all of the then-known essential nutrients. When hog liver fat extract or alfalfa was added to the diet, normal clotting time was restored. This revealed a previously unrecognized fat-soluble nutrient — vitamin K — that blood needs in order to clot.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000327.verbatim:
In 1935, Dam in Copenhagen observed a fatal hemorrhagic
disease in newly hatched chickens fed a laboratory diet that
contained all of the known essential nutrients. When hog liver
fat extract or alfalfa was added to the diet normal clotting time
was restored.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000328.claim_text: In Wallach's framework a biotin deficiency in humans produces a progressive loss of both hair and hair color. Alongside the hair changes he describes skin lesions over the nose and mouth, depression, hyperesthesia and paresthesia (especially in the extremities), muscle pain, conjunctivitis, and blepharitis.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000328.verbatim:
Symptoms of biotin deficiency in humans include skin
lesions over the nose and mouth, depression, hyperesthesia
and paresthesia particularly over the extremities, muscle
pain, conjunctivitis, blepharitis and a progressive loss of hair

and hair color.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000329.claim_text: Biotin, also known as vitamin H or coenzyme R, was first isolated in 1936 and synthesized in 1943. Its deficiency was originally observed in chicks and rats fed raw egg whites, which were later found to contain an egg-white-injury factor.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000329.verbatim:
Biotin or vitamin H (coenzyme R) was first isolated in
1936 and synthesized in 1943.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000330.claim_text: Choline is an essential nutrient with a vitamin-like coenzyme function that Wallach groups among the water-soluble vitamins. It has been recognized as essential for more than a hundred years. Choline serves as a structural building block of all cell membranes, plasma lipoproteins and lung surfactant, and in the nervous system it forms sphingomyelin and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. It also carries fat out of the liver, so a shortage leads to a fatty liver. The body can make some choline from the amino acids methionine or serine with vitamin B12 and folate, but not enough to meet daily needs, which is why it must be supplied through diet or supplements.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000330.verbatim:
Choline has been known for more than 100 years as
being essential and it has a vitamin-like coenzyme function.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000332.claim_text: Wallach classifies choline as a water-soluble vitamin, placing it in the same group as the B-complex vitamins, biotin and vitamin C. He describes water-soluble vitamins as essential nutrients that function in the metabolic processes of all living cells.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000332.verbatim:
2) Water soluble - B-complex, biotin, choline and
vitamin C - Water soluble vitamins consists of 10 separate
water soluble B vitamins and vitamin C.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000333.claim_text: Choline is a component of the phospholipid sphingomyelin, an important part of the brain and peripheral nerves. Because it is a precursor for the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, choline is directly involved in the transmission of nerve impulses.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000333.verbatim:
Choline is also a component of another phospholipid,
sphingomyelin, which is an important component of the
brain and peripheral nerves. As a precursor for acetylcholine,
choline is involved in the transmission of nerve impulses.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000334.claim_text: Choline is part of fat metabolism and the transport of fat out of the liver, so a deficiency can result in a fatty liver. Working through phospholipids, it carries triglycerides and forms lecithin in the liver, a process that removes fatty acids from the liver's glycerides and lowers the triglyceride level. Wallach warns that in a severe form, choline-deficient fatty liver can land a person on a liver transplant list.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000334.verbatim:
The function of choline in humans is part of the
metabolism of and in the transport of fat from the liver. A
deficiency of choline can result in a fatty liver. As a component
of phospholipids, choline functions in triglyceride transport
and in cell membrane structure. In the liver, choline forms
lecithin (phosphatidyl choline). During this process, fatty
acids are removed from the glycerides of the liver, thus
reducing the triglyceride level.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000335.claim_text: The body can synthesize choline from the amino acids methionine or serine, a process that requires vitamin B12 and folacin (folate). However, the rate of that internal synthesis is too slow to meet daily requirements, which is exactly why Wallach counts choline as an essential nutrient that must be supplied.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000335.verbatim:
Man can synthesize choline from the amino acids methionine
or serine in the presence of vitamin B12 and folacin. The rate at
which choline can be synthesized is insufficient to meet daily
requirements and for this reason it is considered an essential
nutrient.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000336.claim_text: Because choline is a raw material for acetylcholine — a key nerve-signaling chemical — and a building block of the brain's and nerves' insulating sphingomyelin, Wallach reports it has real value in movement disorders. Large doses of choline, he says, have proven beneficial for managing and easing the symptoms of tardive dyskinesia (the involuntary movements that can follow long-term drug use) and of Huntington's disease in people. He notes, too, that a choline shortage produces a 'fatty liver.'
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000336.verbatim:
Large
doses of choline have proved to be beneficial for managing
and alleviating the symptoms of tardive dyskinesia and
Huntington’s disease in humans.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000337.claim_text: Wallach explains that myoinositol — nicknamed "muscle sugar" — has a chemical structure resembling glucose and is concentrated in the brain, cerebrospinal fluid, skeletal muscle, heart muscle and other tissues. Free inositol reaches especially high levels in the organs of the male reproductive tract, particularly in semen.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000337.verbatim:
Myoinositol, “muscle sugar,” has a chemical structure
that resembles glucose and is concentrated in the brain,
cerebrospinal fluid, skeletal muscle, heart muscle and other
tissues. Free inositol is found in especially high levels in the
organs of the male reproductive tract, particularly in semen.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000338.claim_text: Inositol — recognized as a vitamin in 1940 — is plentiful in whole grains and raw vegetables, Wallach notes, where it occurs both as inositol phospholipids and as phytic acid (inositol hexaphosphate, the 'phytates'). He flags the double edge: the very phytic acid that carries inositol also binds calcium, iron, and zinc in the gut and blocks their absorption, so what is a nutrient in one sense is an anti-nutrient in another.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000338.verbatim:
Inositol was identified as a vitamin in 1940. It
occurs abundantly in diets containing whole grains and
raw vegetables as inositol phospholipids and as phytic acid
(inositol hexaphosphate or “phytates”).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000339.claim_text: Wallach states that inositol has been shown to have a therapeutic role in diabetic neuropathy — the nerve damage that develops in diabetics. He also notes that a deficiency of inositol will produce pathological fatty liver disease.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000339.verbatim:
Inositol has been shown to have a therapeutic role in
diabetic neuropathy.

Deficiencies of inositol will produce pathological fatty
liver disease.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000340.claim_text: Wallach explains that flavanols found in dark chocolate help maintain the strength of capillaries, lower blood pressure, and improve blood flow by increasing production of nitric oxide — a molecule the vascular endothelium uses to signal the surrounding muscle to relax. He adds that these flavanols also carry vitamin C-like functions in the body.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000340.verbatim:
Flavanols found in dark chocolate, participate in
maintaining the strength of capillaries, lower blood pressure,
improve blood flow via increased production of nitric oxide
(a molecule used by the vascular endothelium to signal
the surrounding muscle to relax) and have vitamin C-like
functions.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000341.claim_text: Flavonoids, also known as vitamin P and commonly found in cocoa, tea, and wine, are now considered a third category of vitamins, according to Wallach. He states they have been officially added to the water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamin groups by Harvard Medical School. This places flavonoids alongside the traditional vitamins as a distinct class the body requires.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000341.verbatim:
Flavonoids or vitamin P commonly found in cocoa,
tea and wine are now considered to be the third category of
vitamins and are officially added to the water soluble and fat
soluble groups by Harvard Medical School.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000342.claim_text: Wallach cites Norman Hollenberg of Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women's Hospital, who reported that the island-dwelling Kuna people, who drink flavanol-rich cocoa, have a 10% lower risk of four of the five most common killer diseases: stroke, heart failure, cancer, and diabetes. Hollenberg regarded the finding as so striking that, if these observations predict the future, they may be among the most important observations in the history of medicine.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000342.verbatim:
Norman Hollenberg from Harvard Medical School
and Brigham and Women’s Hospital reports, “that the island-dwelling Kuna people who drink the flavanol-rich cocoa,
have a 10% lower risk of four of the five most common killer
diseases: stroke, heart failure, cancer and diabetes.”

“If these observations predict the future, then we can
say without blushing that they are among the most important
observations in the history of medicine,” said Hollenberg.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000343.claim_text: Wallach recounts that flavonoids were first used clinically in 1936 by Szent-Gyorgyi, who treated patients whose diseases were marked by increased permeability and fragility of the capillary wall that resulted in hemorrhages.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000343.verbatim:
Flavonoids were first used clinically in 1936 by Szent-Gyorgyi to treat patients with diseases characterized by
increased permeability and fragility of the capillary wall that
resulted in hemorrhages.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000344.claim_text: According to Wallach, chromium and vanadium deficiencies show up as an intense thirst for liquids, with sugary soft drinks usually the first choice and water the last, plus a hunger for carbohydrates like soft drinks, sweetened coffee and tea, alcohol, pasta, desserts, and bread. The 'munchies,' cravings for alcohol, and candy cravings, especially for chocolate, are sure signs of a chromium and vanadium deficiency.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000344.verbatim:
Chromium and vanadium deficiencies are manifested
by an intense thirst for liquid (high fructose corn syrup laden
soft drinks being the usual first choice and water the last for
minerally deficient humans) and hunger for carbohydrates
(i.e. - soft drinks, coffee and tea with added sugar, alcohol,
pasta, deserts, bread, etc.).

The “munchies,” cravings for alcohol and “candy
cravings” (especially chocolate) are sure signs of chromium
and vanadium deficiencies.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000345.claim_text: Wallach recounts that vanadium was discovered in 1801 by a Mexican professor of mineralogy, Andres Manuel del Rio. It was later named for the Scandinavian goddess Vanadis because of its many beautifully colored compounds. Vanadium makes up 0.02% of the earth's crust and is present in trace amounts in more than 60 different ores, with vanadinite as its predominant source.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000345.verbatim:
Vanadium makes up 0.02% of the earth’s crust, and is
present in trace amounts in more than 60 different ores. The
predominant source of vanadium is vanadinite. A Mexican
professor of mineralogy, Andres Manuel del Rio, discovered
vanadium in 1801. It was later named for the Scandinavian
goddess Vanadis because of its many beautifully colored
compounds.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000346.claim_text: Germanium is a poor conductor of electricity, which places it in semiconductor status. Adding tiny amounts of other elements such as arsenic, gallium, or antimony -- a process called 'doping' -- greatly increases its ability to conduct electricity. Doped germanium is used to manufacture transistors, which essentially become micro-computers.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000346.verbatim:
Germanium is a poor conductor of electricity
and therefore is relegated to a semi-conductor status.

The addition of small amounts of other elements such
as arsenic, gallium, or antimony is called “doping” - this
process greatly increases its ability to conduct electricity.
Doped germanium is used to manufacture transistors, which
essentially become micro-computers.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000347.claim_text: Even though the total body content of manganese in humans is only 10 to 20 mg, it is essential to all living organisms. It activates numerous enzyme systems, including those involved in glucose metabolism, energy production, and the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase (SOD). Manganese is also a major constituent of several metalloenzymes, hormones, and proteins essential to all vertebrates and humans.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000347.verbatim:
The total body content of manganese in humans
is only 10 to 20 mg. Manganese is known to be essential
for all living organisms. Manganese activates numerous
enzyme systems including those involved with glucose
metabolism, energy production and antioxidant properties
of superoxide dismutase (SOD). It is a major constituent of
several metalloenzymes, hormones, and proteins essential to
all vertebrates and humans.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000348.claim_text: Manganese is an essential part of the developmental process and the physical structure of the three fragile ear bones and joint cartilage. Because of this role, a shortage of manganese shows up as defects in cartilage and in the ear's bony structure. This is why Wallach links manganese deficiency to both joint problems and hearing loss.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000348.verbatim:
Manganese is an essential part of the developmental
process and the physical structure of the three fragile ear
bones and joint cartilage.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000349.claim_text: Among the deficiency diseases of manganese, Wallach lists infertility, meaning failure to ovulate in women and testicular atrophy in men, as well as still births and spontaneous abortions (miscarriages). He also names loss of libido in both males and females. In his framework, reproductive failure and low sex drive can be signs that the body is short of manganese.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000349.verbatim:
Infertility (failure to ovulate, testicular atrophy)
Still births/ spontaneous abortions (miscarriages)
Loss of libido in both males and females

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000350.claim_text: Manganese was identified in 1774 by the chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele. He named it from the Latin word magnes, meaning 'magnet,' a nod to the magnetic properties of pyrolusite, the manganese ore. The nutrient's name thus ties it directly to the magnetic mineral it was first drawn from.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000350.verbatim:
Manganese was identified in 1774 by Carl Wilhelm
Scheele who named it from the Latin word magnes, which
translates to “magnet,” referring to the magnetic properties
of pyrolusite.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000352.claim_text: Boron is far more concentrated in plants than in animals. Marine plants carry 120 ppm (highest in brown algae) and land plants 150 ppm, while marine animals hold 20 to 50 ppm and land animals only 0.5 ppm. Wallach notes that the plant families Chenopodiaceae and Plumbaginaceae are indicator plant families for boron. The pattern shows that plants take up and hold far more boron than animals do.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000352.verbatim:
marine plants 120 ppm (highest levels found in brown
algae), terrestrial plants at 150 ppm (chenopodiaceae and
plumboginaceae are indicator plant families), marine animals
at 20 to 50 ppm, and terrestrial animals at 0.5 ppm.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000353.claim_text: Prior to 1981, boron was not considered an essential nutrient at all. It was first shown to be an essential mineral for growing chicks, and it was not until 1990 that boron was accepted as an essential nutrient for humans. Boron's recognized status as a human essential is therefore a relatively recent development.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000353.verbatim:
Prior to 1981, boron was not considered an essential
nutrient. Boron was first shown to be an essential mineral for
growing chicks. It was not until 1990 that boron was accepted
as an essential nutrient for humans.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000354.claim_text: Boron was first isolated in 1808 by the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy, working alongside two French chemists, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis-Jacques Thenard. Before this, boron existed only in its combined mineral forms, since it is never found pure in nature.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000354.verbatim:
English chemist Sir Humphry Davy and two French chemists,
Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis-Jacques Thenard.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000355.claim_text: In Wallach's framework, cobalt is an essential trace mineral required by every form of life, from blue-green algae, bacteria and fungi to plants, insects and all the vertebrates including humans. It works as a cofactor and activator for enzymes and helps "fix" nitrogen during amino-acid production, but its defining role is nutritional: a single cobalt atom sits at the very center of vitamin B12 (the cobamide coenzymes). Because of that, the body's cobalt requirement is really a requirement for the finished B12 molecule — cobalt/B12 is needed to build DNA and RNA, form red blood cells, make the myelin that insulates nerves, and produce the thyroid hormone thyroxine. Cobalt is a rare element, making up only about 0.003% of the earth's crust, and where soils are cobalt-depleted the crops, animals and people that depend on them fall deficient.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000355.verbatim:
Cobalt is essential for all forms of life including blue-green algae, some bacteria and fungi, some plants, insects,
birds, reptiles, amphibians and mammals including man.
Cobalt functions as a cofactor and an activator for enzymes,
“fixes” nitrogen during amino acid production, and a single
cobalt atom is the central metal component of vitamin B12,
which itself is a cofactor and activator (cobamide coenzymes)
for several essential enzymes.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000356.claim_text: Wallach explains that vitamin B12 is a water-soluble red crystalline substance, and its red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule. B12 is slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. About 30% of B12 activity is lost during cooking, whether by electric, gas, microwave, wood, or charcoal.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000356.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water
soluble. The red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule.
Vitamin B12 is slowly deactivated by exposure to acid, alkali,
light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. About 30% of
B12 activity is lost during cooking (electric, gas, microwave,
wood, charcoal, etc.).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000357.claim_text: Wallach explains why megadosing vitamin B12 has limits: the body can store at most about 2 mg of B12, which it releases slowly to the bone marrow as needed, and any intake beyond that storage ceiling is simply flushed out in the urine — what he memorably calls 'expensive urine.' He adds the body recycles B12 through the liver and bile so efficiently that a vegan's deficiency may not surface for five to ten years after giving up meat.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000357.verbatim:
The maximum storage level of B12 is 2 mg which is slowly
released to the bone marrow as needed. Excess intake of B12
above the body’s storage capacity is shed in the urine (expensive
urine).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000359.claim_text: Too much cobalt has a specific effect Wallach flags: in humans, an excess of about 20 to 30 mg a day can drive accelerated erythropoiesis — an over-production of red blood cells — by stimulating the kidney to release more erythropoietin, the hormone that signals the marrow to make red cells. He stresses that the body's real cobalt need is tiny, since it is required mainly as the cobalt atom at the center of vitamin B12 (an RDA of just 3 to 4 mcg a day).
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000359.verbatim:
Cobalt excess in man (20 to 30 mg/day) may create an
accelerated erythropoiesis (RBC -red blood cell- production)
by stimulating an increased production of the kidney hormone
erythropoietin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000360.claim_text: Cobalt puts Wallach's soil-to-people thesis in sharp numbers: when farmland holds less than 0.07 ppm of cobalt, the animals — and the people — that live on crops grown there develop cobalt deficiency, while just 0.11 ppm in the soil is enough to prevent and cure it. Because the body needs cobalt mainly as the core of vitamin B12, he links this shortfall to pernicious anemia and to demyelination of the spinal cord and major nerves — serious, sometimes permanent nerve damage.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000360.verbatim:
Less than 0.07 ppm Co in the soil results in cobalt
deficiency in animals and people who eat crops grown from
those soils; 0.11 ppm Co in the soil prevents and cures Co
deficiency.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000361.claim_text: Wallach notes that cobalt is a rare element, making up only 0.003 percent of the earth's crust, with cobalite - a compound of cobalt, arsenic and sulfur - as one of its common ores. The pure metal has a characteristic bright bluish-white color and is obtained by roasting the ore in air. Cobalt metal was first isolated by the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt in 1739.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000361.verbatim:
Cobalt is a rare element, making up only 0.003 percent
of the earth’s crust. Cobaltite is one of its common ores, a
compound made up of cobalt, arsenic and sulfur. The pure
metal, which has a characteristic bright bluish-white color,
is obtained by roasting this ore in air. Cobalt metal was first
isolated by the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt in 1739.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000362.claim_text: Wallach describes cobalt as well known for its ability to be magnetized - it is easily magnetized and retains its magnetism at temperatures far higher than those that demagnetize iron. Twenty-five percent of all the cobalt produced in the world is used to make a super-magnetic substance called 'alnico,' an alloy of aluminum, nickel and cobalt used for making industrial magnets.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000362.verbatim:
Cobalt is well known for its ability to be magnetized. It
is easily magnetized and retains its magnetism at temperatures
far higher than those that demagnetize iron. Twenty five
percent of all of the cobalt produced in the world is used to
make a super magnetic substance called “alnico.” Alnico is an
alloy of aluminum, nickel and cobalt and is used for making
industrial magnets.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000363.claim_text: Lithium is an alkali metal so light it can actually float on water, and in Wallach's framework it is one of the essential trace minerals the body must have — not merely a psychiatric drug. He treats it as a nutrient central to mental and emotional health: he holds that depression, manic-depression (bipolar disorder), hyperactivity, ADD/ADHD, certain forms of autism, and even rage and violent behavior are, at root, hallmarks of a lithium deficiency aggravated by high sugar and alcohol intake. He points to conventional medicine's own use of lithium for bipolar disorder, and to research linking higher lithium in drinking water to lower rates of crime and suicide, as evidence of how essential this mineral is — and calls for lithium, not fluoride, to be added to public water.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000363.verbatim:
Lithium’s density is so low
that a small piece can actually float on water.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000364.claim_text: Wallach describes lithium as an extremely reactive metal whose density is so low that a small piece can actually float on water. It reacts vigorously with water to produce hydrogen gas and with oxygen to form lithium oxide, so free lithium is usually stored in oil or kerosene to keep these reactions from occurring.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000364.verbatim:
Lithium is an extremely reactive metal. It reacts vigorously
with water, to produce hydrogen gas, and with oxygen to form
lithium oxide (Li2O). To prevent these reactions from occurring,
free lithium is usually stored in oil or kerosene.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000365.claim_text: Wallach points out that mainstream medicine already treats severe bipolar disorder with a trace mineral: lithium, given as lithium carbonate, with more than 3 million prescriptions filled a year. Its exact mechanism, he notes, is thought to involve how brain cells respond to certain hormones and neurotransmitters. He turns this into a larger argument — that if a mineral can steady the most severe mood disorder, everyday depression and irritability may likewise reflect a simple lithium shortage.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000365.verbatim:
Lithium carbonate is regularly used to treat patients
with the severe form of bipolar disorder. More than 3 million
prescriptions for this trace mineral are filled yearly. The role of
lithium is thought to be related to the role the brain cells play
and respond to certain hormones and neurotransmitters.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000366.claim_text: While psychiatrists attribute depression and manic depression to feelings of being out of control, negative thinking and self-recrimination, Wallach points out that they nonetheless treat it successfully with the trace mineral lithium. In his framework, depression and manic depression with all that the diagnosis implies are simply a lithium deficiency aggravated by a high consumption of sugar.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000366.verbatim:
While the professional psychiatrist says that depression
and manic depression are due to feelings that “we are out of
control of our lives,” negative thinking, and self recrimination
(‘I'm a loser”), they treat depression successfully with the
trace mineral lithium. Depression and manic depression with
all that implies, are simply a lithium deficiency aggravated by
a high consumption of sugar.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000367.claim_text: Lithium was discovered in 1817 by the Swedish chemist Johan August Arfvedson while assaying ore from a Swedish mine, Wallach recounts, and was named from the Greek word 'lithos,' meaning 'stone.' He adds a memorable quirk of the metal: it is so light that a small piece will actually float on water, and so reactive that pure lithium must be stored under oil or kerosene to keep it from reacting with air and moisture.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000367.verbatim:
Lithium was discovered in 1817 by the Swedish chemist
Johan August Arfvedson during a routine chemical assay of
ore from a mine in Sweden. It was named for the Greek word
lithos, which translates to “stone.”

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000368.claim_text: Wallach classes molybdenum as one of the essential trace minerals every living organism requires, even though it is technically a hard, silvery metal. It is extracted from an ore called molybdenite, with large deposits in Colorado, and was identified as a distinct element in 1778. In the body it works as a constituent of numerous metalloenzymes — Wallach names it an integral part of at least three: xanthine oxidase, aldehyde oxidase, and sulfite oxidase. He cites an RDA of 250 mcg per day but recommends far more as a supplement, and warns that a molybdenum deficiency is among the causes of goiter.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000368.verbatim:
Molybdenum is a hard, silvery metal that is extracted
from an ore called molybdenite (MoS,). There are large
deposits of “Moly” molybdenite in Colorado.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000370.claim_text: Wallach notes that molybdenum in soil is strongly concentrated by humus, especially in alkaline soils, and that a few soils worldwide hold enough of it to cause molybdenum poisoning in animals that consume the local plants. At the same time, he says numerous soils are known to be molybdenum-deficient. He gives a typical soil concentration of about 2 ppm.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000370.verbatim:
soil at 2.0
ppm (strongly concentrated by humus, especially in alkaline
soils; a few soils worldwide are rich enough in molybdenum

In 1778, molybdenum was originally extracted from

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000372.claim_text: In Wallach's mineral encyclopedia, sodium is a highly reactive, bright, silvery metal — light enough to float on water and soft enough to cut with a knife — and the sixth most abundant element in the earth's crust. Sodium is a highly reactive, bright, silvery metal, light
enough to float on water and soft enough to cut witha knife. It
is the sixth most abundant element in the crust of the earth.

Anything less than 85% sodium chloride in a salt block will be ignored by the animals — even when they have major mineral deficiencies.

Farmers and husbandrymen use the salt hunger of
animals to ensure the consumption of trace minerals by
incorporating trace minerals into salt blocks containing 85%
salt - anything less than 85% sodium chloride in a salt block
will be ignored by the animals even if they have major mineral
deficiencies!

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000375.claim_text: Sodium chloride — the chemical name for ordinary table salt — is mined in vast quantities from ancient salt mines on every continent, Wallach notes, and can also be drawn from the sea, where every gallon of seawater holds about a quarter-pound of salt. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000375.verbatim:
Sodium chloride, the chemical name for common table
salt, is mined in large quantities from ancient salt mines on
every continent on earth. Sea water is another common source
of salt, every gallon of sea water contains a quarter pound of
salt.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000376.claim_text: Wallach says that historically, eating salt to satisfy a pica craving had real value because unprocessed salt often contained trace minerals and rare earths. He argues salt consumption today is not, in and of itself, harmful — but processed salt creates the problem of letting the body think it is getting minerals, the equivalent of an "empty calorie" diet of processed-food calories without vitamins.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000376.verbatim:
Historically, the consumption of salt to satisfy a pica
behavior was of value because salt was not processed and did

Today, salt consumption, although contrary to popular

calories without vitamins).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000377.claim_text: Sodium was first isolated in 1807 by the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy, Wallach recounts, who separated the reactive, silvery metal from molten sodium hydroxide. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000377.verbatim:
The English chemist, Sir Humphry Davy first isolated and
