English word soda, which itself is derived from the Latin word
sodanum, a common headache remedy of ancient Rome.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000378.claim_text: Phosphorus is a nonmetal element discovered by the German physician Hennig Brand in 1669. Working in the tradition of the ancient alchemists, Brand distilled the residue from boiled-down urine and obtained a new element that glowed in the dark and burst into flames when exposed to warm air. He had discovered white phosphorus, a waxy white solid that melts at 44 degrees C.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000378.verbatim:
Phosphorus is a nonmetal element that was discovered
by the German physician Hennig Brand in 1669. Brand carried
out experiments in the fashion of the ancient alchemists. He
distilled the residue from boiled-down urine and obtained a
new element that glowed in the dark and burst into flames
when exposed to warm air.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000379.claim_text: In Dr. Wallach's framework, sulfur (which he usually spells 'sulphur') is one of the 60 essential elements, metals and minerals the body must obtain. He describes it as an important structural atom in most proteins, carried in through the sulfur-bearing amino acids cystine, cysteine, and methionine, and into small organic molecules. The -SH and -S-S- bonds sulfur forms are what hold many structural proteins in shape and let enzymes do their work, and it is essential to glutathione. Sulfur concentrates in cartilage, tendons, keratin, skin, hair, and nails — the connective tissue and structural proteins that depend on it — and its loss shows up as degenerative arthritis and other collagen diseases.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000379.verbatim:
Sulfur is an important structural atom in most proteins as
sulfur amino acids (cystine, cysteine and methionine) and small
organic molecules.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000380.claim_text: Wallach describes sulfur as an important structural atom in most proteins, built in through the sulfur-bearing amino acids cystine, cysteine, and methionine. Glutathione, a cysteine-containing tripeptide, depends on these sulfur amino acids for the cellular reactions it drives. Sulfur exists in a reduced form (-SH) in cysteine and in an oxidized form (-S-S-) as the double molecule cystine, and these bonds are what give many proteins their working structure.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000380.verbatim:
Sulfur is an important structural atom in most proteins as
sulfur amino acids (cystine, cysteine and methionine) and small
organic molecules. Glutathione, a tripeptide containing cysteine,
is essential to normal cellular reactions involving sulfur amino
acids in proteins. Sulfur is found in a reduced form (-SH) in
cysteine and in an oxidized form (-S-S-) as the double molecule
cystine.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000381.claim_text: Wallach reports that in land animals sulfur runs 5,000 ppm, with the highest levels in cartilage, tendons, keratin, skin, intervertebral discs, hair, and nails, and its lowest concentrations in the bones.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000381.verbatim:
S-Sulfur is found in igneous rocks at 260 ppm, shale
at 2,400 ppm, sandstone at 240 ppm, limestone at 1,200
ppm, freshwater at 3.7 ppm, sea water at 885 ppm, soils at
700 ppm, marine animals at 5,000 to 19,000 ppm (highest
in coelenterates and molluscs) and in terrestrial animals at
5,000 ppm (highest levels in cartilage, tendons, keratin, skin,
intervertebral discs, hair and nails). Its lowest concentrations
are in bones.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000382.claim_text: In Immortality, Wallach cites considerable evidence that a population's 50 percent survival rate can be extended significantly by consuming combinations of antioxidants, including vitamins A, C, and E, selenium, the sulfur-bearing amino acids methionine, cysteine, and cystine, and plant phytochemicals. There is very little niacin in corn

soaked in lye and wood ashes overnight before it is consumed
- the alkali in the lye and wood ashes allows the tryptophan
to be absorbed and pellagra is rare

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000385.claim_text: Cobalt's name carries an old superstition. He adds the metal was first isolated by the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt in 1739, though the ancient Egyptians had already used traces of cobalt to make blue glass thousands of years before.

The name cobalt was derived in the 18th century
from the German word “kobald” that refers to an evil gnome

on the evil “kobald” or cobalt.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000386.claim_text: Wallach relays that the selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer considered selenomethionine — the form of methionine in which a selenium atom replaces the sulfur — to be the '13th essential amino acid.' WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000386.verbatim:
Selenium researcher, Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer, considers selenomethionine,
the selenium analog of methionine the 13th essential amino acid.

in India where sorghum
or millet is a common food, high levels of leucine in the

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000388.claim_text: Gallium's name traces to Gallia, the Latin word for France. WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000388.verbatim:
The history of gallium is unique as it is one of the
elements that was predicted to exist by Mendeleyev (creator of
the periodic chart) in 1871. Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran
identified gallium in 1875 and named it for Gallia, the Latin
word for France.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000389.claim_text: Wallach reports British research showing that when pregnant women's diets are supplemented with gallium, the rate of brain cancer in their children drops significantly. He connects this to gallium's specific metalloenzyme activity in the human brain and to laboratory findings that gallium reduces brain cancer in animals. For Wallach it is one more reason gallium belongs among the essential nutrients rather than being written off as a non-essential trace metal.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000389.verbatim:
British
research has shown that diets, of pregnant women that are
supplemented with gallium, significantly reduces the rate of
brain cancer in children.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000390.claim_text: Wallach explains that hydrogen is named for what happens when it burns: in air it reacts violently with oxygen, giving off large amounts of heat and forming water. That water-making reaction is the origin of its name, taken from the Greek words hydro, meaning water, and genes, meaning creator. So the word 'hydrogen' literally means 'water-creator.'
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000390.verbatim:
When hydrogen burns in air, it reacts violently with
oxygen to form large amounts of heat and water. It is this
reaction with oxygen that gave hydrogen its name, which
is translated from the Greek words hydro (water) and genes
(creator).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000391.claim_text: Wallach describes hydrogen gas as normally existing as a diatomic molecule, meaning each molecule is two hydrogen atoms bonded together (H2). The gas itself is colorless, odorless and tasteless, so it cannot be seen or smelled. Its defining hazard is that it is extremely flammable: when it burns in air it reacts violently with oxygen, releasing large amounts of heat and forming water.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000391.verbatim:
Hydrogen gas is typically a diatomic molecule, meaning
that a hydrogen molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms
(H2). Hydrogen gas is colorless, odorless and tasteless;
however, hydrogen is extremely flammable.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000392.claim_text: Wallach reports hydrogen's abundance across the natural world: roughly 1,000 ppm in igneous rocks, 5,600 ppm in shale, 1,800 ppm in sandstone and 860 ppm in limestone, but far more in water, at about 111,000 ppm in fresh water and 108,000 ppm in seawater. It is also plentiful in living things, reaching around 70,000 ppm in land animals. This pattern reflects his point that most of the hydrogen on earth is bound up in the water of oceans and lakes rather than existing as free gas.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000392.verbatim:
H-Hydrogen is found in igneous rocks at 1,000 ppm,
shale at 5,600 ppm, sandstone at 1,800 ppm, limestone at 860
ppm, fresh water at 111,000 ppm, sea water at 108,000 ppm,

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000393.claim_text: Wallach explains that nitrates and nitrites are added to canned foods and preserved meats to prevent bacterial growth and keep meat red. In the acid environment of the stomach they are converted to nitrosamines, and those compounds can in turn become cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens). He adds that they can also suppress thyroid function.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000393.verbatim:
Nitrates and nitrites are converted to nitrosamines in
the acid environment of the stomach; these compounds can
be converted to cancer causing chemicals (carcinogens) and
can suppress thyroid function.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000394.claim_text: In Wallach's framework minerals are the master key: you cannot physiologically use any nutrient, phytonutrient, or raw material without mineral cofactors. He pushes this to its limit, arguing that even oxygen and water — the most basic inputs of life — are unavailable to you at the cellular level without those mineral cofactors. He makes the point while criticizing an anti-aging position paper that dismissed all interventions, noting it left out both calorie-restricted diets and plant minerals. The takeaway: breathing and drinking are not enough if the minerals that let cells actually use oxygen and water are missing.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000394.verbatim:
You cannot effectively use any nutrients,
phytonutrients or raw materials physiologically without
mineral cofactors - even oxygen and water are unavailable to
you at the cellular level without mineral cofactors!

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000395.claim_text: Wallach approvingly quotes Dr. Roy Walford, who he says described oxygen-based free radicals 'very well.' Walford's point is that the oxygen of our atmosphere is a highly poisonous gas: alien entities arriving from a methane planet would choke and die on the stuff we breathe so casually. The same oxygen rusts iron, drives the decay and crumbling of granite boulders, and participates in every fire in town — yet we live in it, require it, and love it. Wallach uses the paradox to frame oxygen's double edge: essential for respiration, yet also the source of oxidative free-radical damage to cells and membranes.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000395.verbatim:
Not everybody realizes that the oxygen of our
atmosphere is a highly poisonous gas. Alien entities arriving
from a methane planet would choke and die on the stuff we
breathe so casually. It rusts iron, is involved in the decay and
crumbling of granite boulders, and participates in every fire
in town...

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000396.claim_text: Wallach points to Dr. Otto Warburg of the Max Planck Institute, a two-time unshared Nobel laureate, one of whose prizes was for discovering that the cancer cell's metabolism is fermentative and anaerobic while the normal, noncancerous cell's metabolism is aerobic. During the 1950s Warburg demonstrated clearly that cancer cells ferment sugar under anaerobic conditions and die in the presence of oxygen. This is the mechanistic backbone of Wallach's recurring theme that cancer cells do not like high levels of oxygen. It is why he favors oxygen-raising measures such as germanium (which increases oxygen flow into cells) and hydrogen peroxide in his cancer programs.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000396.verbatim:
the second for discovering that the metabolism of the cancer
cell is fermentative and anaerobic while the metabolism of
the normal noncancerous cell is aerobic. During the 1950s,
Warburg was able to demonstrate clearly that cancer cells
ferment sugar under anaerobic conditions and die in the

presence of oxygen.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000397.claim_text: Wallach describes hyperbaric oxygen therapy as putting a patient into a chamber pressurized to several atmospheres of oxygen. He says the same approach treats athletic injuries: an injured athlete placed in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber heals so much faster that they can return to play in weeks instead of months. It is one of several ways Wallach uses concentrated oxygen therapeutically.

that can be reactivated or jump started when they are exposed
to several atmospheres of oxygen in hyperbaric chambers.
Athletic injuries can also be treated by putting the injured
athlete into a hyperbaric oxygen chamber. The healing time
is shortened significantly so the athlete can return to play in
weeks instead of months.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000398.claim_text: According to Wallach, oxygen delivered as hydrogen peroxide has a long medical history: it has been used topically, intravenously, and orally since the Civil War. In Europe it has been used for more than 50 years for alternative cancer therapies, circulatory disease, arteriosclerosis, emphysema, asthma, and gangrene, and more recently as a therapy for stroke patients. He frames hydrogen peroxide as essentially a carrier of oxygen, since the body's catalase enzyme rapidly breaks it down into water and a singlet oxygen atom. That is why he counts hydrogen peroxide among his oxygen-based treatments.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000398.verbatim:
Oxygen in the form of hydrogen peroxide has been used
topically, intravenously and orally since the Civil War. It has been
used widely in Europe for over 50 years for alternative cancer
therapies, circulatory disease, arteriosclerosis, emphysema,
asthma, gangrene and more recently as a therapy for stroke
patients.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000399.claim_text: In Wallach's framework, silica is silicon dioxide (SiO2), the most important compound of the element silicon. Silicon is the second most abundant element in the earth's crust, exceeded only by oxygen, and its oxygen-bonded compounds make up most of the world's sand, rock and soil. Silica occurs in two familiar natural forms — a crystalline form called quartz, the tiny chips of which are the grains in sand, and a noncrystalline form called flint — while gems such as amethyst, opal, agate and jasper are simply quartz crystals carrying colored impurities. Wallach treats silica as an essential mineral, one needed for the optimal health of the bones, skin, hair and nails.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000399.verbatim:
The most important silicon compound is silica, or
silicon dioxide (SiO2). It exists in two familiar forms in nature:
a crystalline form called quartz, small chips of which are
found in sand, a a noncrystalline form called flint. Small gems
and semiprecious stones such as amethyst, opal, agate and
jasper are crystals of quartz with colored impurities.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000400.claim_text: Wallach explains that silica and everyday sand are the same material: silica as sand can be mixed with soda ash (sodium carbonate) and limestone (calcium carbonate) and then melted to become glass — of which he notes there are more than a thousand forms. Silica's crystalline form is quartz, the chips of which make up ordinary sand, and its noncrystalline form is flint. So the same mineral the body needs for bones, skin, hair and nails is also the raw material of sand and glass.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000400.verbatim:
Silica as sand can be mixed with soda ash (sodium
carbonate) and limestone (calcium carbonate) and when the
mixture is melted it becomes glass - there are more than 1,000
forms of glass.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000401.claim_text: Aluminum turns up even in baby food. Wallach cites a European survey - which was rerunning an earlier WHO report - that measured the aluminum in infant formula at an average of 0.9 mg per kg of body weight per week for milk-based formulas and 1.1 mg for soy-based ones. Some soy-based formulas ran about four times the average level found in that survey.

The amount of aluminum in infant
formulas averages 0.9 mg/kg of body weight per week for
milk based formulas and 1.1 mg/kg of body weight per
week for soy-based infant formulas.

It has been highly prized since ancient times, and was used in conjunction with silver and mercury by ancient Chinese alchemists as far back as 8,000 B.C. in their pursuit of 'immortality.'

Gold is considered the most precious of all metals and
was used in conjunction with silver and mercury by the ancient
Chinese alchemist 8,000 B.C. to provide “immortality”. In its
pure state, gold is one of the most beautiful of elements. With
its bright yellow color and its resistance to corrosion, it has
been highly prized since ancient times.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000403.claim_text: Wallach traces gold's naming to its chemical symbol Au, which comes from the Latin word aurum, meaning 'shining dawn.' The name has even older roots, descending from the Sanskrit word jval and the Anglo-Saxon word gold, both of which simply mean 'gold.' That sense of a 'shining dawn' suits a metal he calls the most precious and beautiful of all, prized for its bright yellow color since ancient times.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000403.verbatim:
Its chemical symbol,
Au, comes from the Latin word aurum, which translates to
“shining dawn.” It has even older origins, coming from the
Sanskrit word jval and the Anglo-Saxon word gold, both

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000404.claim_text: Wallach explains that gold dissolves in mercury to form an amalgam -- an alloy of mercury and gold -- and that this gold-mercury amalgam is used by dentists to fill teeth. It is one of the practical, non-nutritional uses he lists for the metal, separate from any role it might play inside the body.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000404.verbatim:
Gold dissolves in mercury to form an amalgam, or
alloy of mercury and gold - this gold-mercury amalgam is
used by dentist to fill teeth.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000405.claim_text: Strontium takes its name from Strontian, a village in Scotland where the English scientist Dr. Adair Crawford first identified the element; both the metal and the mineral strontianite were named in 1789. Wallach describes its natural sources as the mineral ores celestite, a form of strontium sulfate, and strontianite, a strontium carbonate.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000405.verbatim:
Natural sources of strontium are the mineral ores
celestite, which is a form of strontium sulfate, and strontianite,
a strontium carbonate. Both strontium and the mineral
strontianite were named in 1789 by the English scientist
Dr. Adair Crawford, who first identified the element in the
Scottish village of Strontian.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000406.claim_text: In its pure form bromine is a reddish liquid built from diatomic molecules — pairs of bromine atoms bonded together. Wallach highlights an unusual fact: bromine and mercury are the only two chemical elements that stay liquid at ordinary room temperature. In the body, though, it does not remain in that raw elemental form — it works in its active form as brominated amino acids.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000406.verbatim:
In its pure form, bromine is a diatomic molecule
(two bromine atoms) that is a reddish liquid. Bromine and
mercury are the only two elements that are liquids at room
temperature.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000407.claim_text: Wallach recounts that when the young French student Antoine-Jerome Balard added chlorinated water to the brackish salt-marsh water near Montpellier, it turned brownish — and that color change turned out to be caused by a new element. The French Academy named the element bromine, taken from the Greek word 'bromos,' which translates to 'stench.' In other words, the element's very name comes from a Greek word for a bad smell.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000407.verbatim:
The addition of the chlorine turned the water brownish. The
cause of the color change was found to be a new element that
the French Academy named bromine, taken from the Greek
word bromos, which translates to “stench.”

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000408.claim_text: Terbium is a rare-earth metal -- by Wallach's account one of the least abundant of all the rare earth elements. In its pure metallic form it is silvery-white and soft enough to be cut with a knife. Wallach catalogs terbium among the plant-derived rare earths and trace minerals he counts as part of the body's full essential-mineral complement, not as a mere geological oddity.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000408.verbatim:
In its pure metallic form, terbium is silvery-white and
is soft enough to be cut with a knife.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000409.claim_text: Wallach records that terbium was discovered in 1843 by Carl Gustaf Mosander, who isolated its oxide from the mineral yttria. Terbium is one of the least abundant of all the rare earth elements. It is also recovered commercially from monazite, but its original identification traced to Mosander's work separating its oxide out of yttria.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000409.verbatim:
Terbium is one of the least abundant of the rare earth
elements. Carl Gustaf Mosander discovered the element in
1843 by isolating its oxide from the mineral yttria.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000410.claim_text: Wallach reports that terbium is recovered commercially from monazite -- described as a mixture of rare earth elements combined with thorium and calcium. That mineral turns up in river sands from India and Brazil and in beach sand from Florida. Because monazite is itself a blend of the rare earths, terbium is extracted alongside the rest of the family rather than from an ore that is uniquely its own.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000410.verbatim:
Terbium is recovered commercially from the mineral
monazite, a mixture of rare earth elements combined with
thorium and calcium. It is found in river sands from India
and Brazil and in beach sand from Florida.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000411.claim_text: Wallach recounts that rubidium was discovered in 1861 by the German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, who found it as an impurity mixed in with the alkali metals they were investigating. They identified it as a brand-new element from the spectral lines it emitted — one of which was a distinctive deep-red color. It was the same pair of chemists who, a year earlier in 1860, had isolated cesium using the then-new technique of flame spectroscopy.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000411.verbatim:
In 1861, the German chemists Robert Bunsen and
Gustav Kirchhoff discovered rubidium. They identified
it as an impurity mixed with the alkali metals they were
investigating; they identified rubidium as a new element from
the spectral lines it emitted, one of which is a deep red color.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000412.claim_text: Wallach explains that the name rubidium comes from the Latin word rubidus, meaning 'deep red.' The element earned that name from the deep-red spectral line that Bunsen and Kirchhoff saw when they identified it in 1861 — the color that gave the new element away. The name is therefore a direct nod to how rubidium was first recognized: by the distinctive red light it emits.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000412.verbatim:
The name rubidium is taken from the Latin word rubidus,
which translates to “deep red.”

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000458.claim_text: Zirconium is a mineral Wallach counts among the essential trace elements and rare earths, and its best-known and most familiar form is the mineral zircon -- a crystalline compound of zirconium silicate. Because the colorless crystals of zircon have a high brilliance
they are oftentimes used as a diamond substitute in faux

jewelry.

Zirconium was discovered in 1787 by the German

Rare Earths added to laboratory animal's diets as a

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000463.claim_text: Nitrates are salt compounds formed when nitric acid is neutralized by bases such as sodium or potassium hydroxide. For that reason he classes both dietary nitrates (deli slices, sandwich meats) and water-borne nitrates among the "goitrogens" — substances that interfere with normal thyroid metabolism and can produce thyroid disease.

When nitric acid is neutralized with bases including

preserved meats to help prevent the growth of bacteria and to
color meat red.

Nitrates and nitrites are converted to nitrosamines in
the acid environment of the stomach; these compounds can
be converted to cancer causing chemicals (carcinogens) and
can suppress thyroid function.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000464.claim_text: Nitrites are preservative compounds added, alongside nitrates, to canned foods and cured or preserved meats — bacon, ham, sausage, bologna, salami, pepperoni, jerky and deli meats — to stop bacteria from growing and to keep the meat looking red. Nitrates and nitrites are added to canned foods and

WAL-CLM-LETS-000307.claim_text: Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is, in Wallach's view, almost always caused by food allergies that produce celiac-type intestinal changes and malabsorption of chromium and vanadium, and/or a high intake of purified sugar and refined flour that increases urinary chromium loss by up to 300%; untreated, it frequently develops into diabetes. Its symptoms are highly variable and include emotional ones (hyperactivity, paranoia, schizophrenia, memory loss, irritability, hallucinations, depression, manic-depression, dyslexia), sleepiness, fatigue, heart palpitations, sweating, inability to think through simple problems, explosive anger, and catatonia. Diagnosis requires a six-hour glucose tolerance test — a fasting blood sugar alone misses it in 98% of cases. Treatment: a high-protein (preferably animal) diet; chromium and vanadium — the 'magic bullets' — at 50-200 micrograms three times daily with meals (those on insulin should start at 25 micrograms three times daily to prevent a sudden blood-sugar dip); B-complex at 50 milligrams each three times daily; avoid alcohol; zinc at 25 milligrams three times daily; betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times daily before meals; resolve food allergies by avoidance, rotation diets, and autoimmune urine therapy; and adrenal cortical extract with adrenal support.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000314.claim_text: Impetigo (ecthyma) is a form of dermatitis in children — blisters filled with straw-colored fluid or pus, or skin ulcers, mainly on the face, arms, and legs. Wallach holds it is more than a simple Streptococcus infection: it is an early sign of immune depression (often from food allergies to milk, wheat, or soy) that lets normal skin organisms flourish unchecked; untreated it can cause deep tissue and lymph-node infection. If clumps of bacteria are involved (as in rheumatic fever), antibiotics (penicillin or tetracycline) are required.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000325.claim_text: Jaundice (icterus, yellow eyes) can be caused by blockage of the bile-duct system in the liver (gallstones, tumor, hepatitis) and/or destruction of red blood cells (Rh factor, blood parasites, malaria); diagnosis is critical. Examining the whites of the eyes (sclera) reveals true jaundice by a yellow coloration — which is absent when the skin is yellow from high beta-carotene intake; blood tests differentiate obstruction (bilirubin above 2.0-2.5 milligrams percent) from red-blood-cell destruction. Treatment: exposure to ultraviolet light to speed elimination; a liver flush (three days of apple juice, then a cup of olive oil and a cup of lemon juice); vitamin C to bowel tolerance; vitamin A at 300,000 international units per day as beta carotene; selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day; vitamin E at 800-1,200 international units per day; and herbs licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra), agrimony (Agrimonia eupatoria), celandine (Chelidonium majus), and chionanthus (Chionanthus virginica).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000328.claim_text: Keratomalacia (xerophthalmia) is a hazy, dry cornea (the clear domed bulge at the front of the eye) that becomes ulcerated — a sign of vitamin A deficiency. WAL-CLM-LETS-000340.claim_text: Lead poisoning (plumbism) can cause a wide variety of symptoms — learning disabilities, kidney disease, stunted bone growth, headaches, and gastrointestinal disease; often the lead is eaten because of 'pica', a compulsive eating of unusual things driven by mineral deficiencies. Wallach's treatment includes Laetrile, hydrogen peroxide, intravenous dimethyl sulfoxide (said to mature the immature cells), Onco-Tox, shark liver extract, hydrazine sulfate, cesium chloride, polyerga, germanium, carbamide, and as needed micro-dose chemotherapy, intravenous amino acids, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day, and vitamin A at 300,000 international units as beta carotene.

He also notes that 40% of hospital patients are there because of iatrogenic (doctor-caused) disease. (Captured for the search corpus as Wallach's general longevity guidance.)

WAL-CLM-LETS-000351.claim_text: For Lyme disease (Lyme arthritis) — a spirochete bacterial infection transmitted by ticks, first described in 1975 in Lyme, Connecticut — Wallach notes that 3 to 32 days after an infected tick bite a skin lesion called erythema chronicum migrans appears on the thigh, buttock or axilla and expands up to 50 cm, with recurring attacks of arthritis, fatigue, chills, fever, stiff neck, sore muscles, nausea and vomiting, and heart involvement (an enlarged heart and atrioventricular [AV] block) in 8% of patients. It occurs most in children who play in grass or deep woods or who have a dog that brings home the Ixodes dammini tick, clusters along the U.S. northeastern coast and in Wisconsin, California and Oregon, and is often misdiagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis. His treatment is tetracycline at 250-500 milligrams four times a day for 20 days; in children, whose teeth tetracyclines discolor, penicillin at 20 million units per day intravenously in divided doses.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000352.claim_text: Wallach defines malnutrition as occurring either as an overt nutritional deficiency, secondary to extended use of medications that interfere with nutrient absorption, or as malabsorption from celiac disease or low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria). He argues conventional doctors think of malnutrition only as protein/calorie deprivation and miss macro- and micro-nutrient deficiencies (singly or in combination, especially early), and miss that celiac changes in the small-intestine lining arise from subclinical allergies to wheat, cow's-milk albumen and soy (and rye, barley, beef, eggs). In his framework many degenerative diseases are really malabsorption: diabetes and hypoglycemia as chromium/vanadium deficiencies, cystic fibrosis as a selenium and essential-fatty-acid deficiency, arthritis as a calcium deficiency worsened by excess dietary phosphorus, and cancer as a depleted immune system run out of repair nutrients. He concludes malnutrition from malabsorption is the common denominator of almost all degenerative disease, and that liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals are the most efficient way to get minerals into malnourished people.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000354.claim_text: German measles (rubella, three-day measles) is a contagious viral disease that causes mild symptoms in children, including swollen lymph nodes of the head and neck; its incubation is 14-21 days and overt symptoms may be absent in teenagers and adults. The typical rash appears first on the face and spreads quickly to the body and limbs with a general flush like scarlet fever; adults may have enlarged head and neck lymph nodes and adult males may have brief testicular pain. Wallach's treatment is the same symptomatic therapy used for ordinary (nine-day) measles. He states emphatically (in capitals) that rubella is a dangerous disease in pregnant women that can induce spontaneous abortions and birth defects, and gives his editorial opinion that rubella vaccines will cause similar birth defects and so should be avoided during pregnancy.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000357.claim_text: Wallach describes menarche/menstruation: the regular monthly cycle alternating ovulation (mid-cycle, about day 14) with the 3-7 day 'period' (discharge of blood and uterine lining). Painful periods (which he usually attributes to essential-fatty-acid deficiency) can be severe enough to force bed rest. His treatment for painful or excessive ('heavy flow') menses: over-the-counter products (for example Midol) and/or herbs — snapdragon (Linaria vulgaris), bethroot (Trillium erectum), black cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa), blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides), tamarac (Larix americana), ragwort (Senecio fuchsii), lady's mantle (Alchemilla vulgaris), St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum), shepherd's purse (Capsella bursa-pastoris), white deadnettle (Lamium album) and yarrow (Achillea millefolium); plus essential fatty acids (salmon oil and flaxseed oil) at 5 grams three times a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 international units per day, selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day, and iron at 25-50 milligrams per day (especially for vegetarian women who don't eat red meat or liver regularly).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000358.claim_text: Meningitis (infection of the covering of the brain and spinal cord) can be caused by many organisms — bacteria (Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus/Diplococcus pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes), fungi, and hundreds of viruses. Wallach stresses it is especially dangerous because infants often show only fever and lethargy, and the blood-brain barrier keeps most medications out of the meninges and brain. Symptoms vary but usually include sore throat, fever, headache, stiff neck and vomiting, and children and adults can become critically ill within 6-24 hours of the first symptoms. He warns emphatically that this is NOT a self-help disease: if you suspect meningitis, get the patient to an emergency room immediately and demand help, because patients often die after waiting hours in a waiting room. Treatment requires rapid diagnosis (spinal tap) and injection of antibiotics into the subdural space (under the meninges), total intravenous fluid and electrolyte support, and frequently mechanical respirators.

Wallach attributes it to a deficiency of folic acid, vitamin B-12, or zinc and vitamin A during early pregnancy — deficiencies that may stem from a poor diet and/or malabsorption in the mother. Severe cases may be debilitating or fatal. Treatment is limited to surgery, so he emphasizes that prevention — correcting these deficiencies before and during early pregnancy — is the goal.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000360.claim_text: Menkes kinky hair syndrome is considered a genetic disease by conventional pediatricians, but Wallach argues it is a copper-deficiency malabsorption problem of early infancy (for example from celiac disease); he cites the veterinary parallel that copper deficiency causes 'kinky wool' disease. Features include retarded growth, anemia, progressive brain degeneration, sparse brittle hair, loss of hair color, arterial aneurysms and scurvy-like bone disease; hair analysis shows very low copper, and blood shows low copper and low ceruloplasmin. His treatment addresses the malabsorption (avoid wheat, cow's milk and soy) and gives copper intravenously at 200 micrograms per kilogram per day, then copper orally at 1-2 milligrams per day after symptoms improve.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000361.claim_text: Mercury poisoning can result from ingesting or inhaling any mercurial compound and from off-gassing of mercury vapor from mercury-amalgam dental fillings. Symptoms include gastroenteritis, salivation, burning mouth pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, colitis, kidney disease, gingivitis, mental and emotional disturbances and nerve deficits; Wallach notes many dentists and alternative practitioners think multiple sclerosis may result from mercury poisoning, and that the mental/emotional effects in Victorian 'hatters' gave rise to 'as mad as a hatter.' Diagnosis is easy via hair analysis plus a history of a mercury source. His treatment: remove the mercury source (including mercury-amalgam fillings), chelation with calcium-EDTA (with complete intravenous nutrition), and sweating (sauna), since mercury is excreted in sweat; he adds that selenium-containing colloidal minerals are very effective at removing mercury from the tissues.

The definition reflects his central premise: that chronic disease is best addressed by fixing whole-body nutrition and metabolism, not by isolating a single organ or complaint.

He recommends doubling the baseline nutrition program for 30 days to help the patient through withdrawal, then dropping to the baseline supplement program and staying on it; do the pulse test for food sensitivities/allergies and a six-hour glucose tolerance test, since people addicted to drugs and/or alcohol frequently have 'addictive allergies' to food and sugar.

Wallach's treatment is selenium at 500 to 1,000 micrograms a day, magnesium at 1,000 milligrams three times a day, salmon oil (a source of omega-3 essential fatty acids) at 1 to 5 grams three times a day and the herb hawthorne (Crataegus oxyacantha), in addition to the baseline nutritional supplement program. WAL-CLM-LETS-000371.claim_text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive disease of the central nervous system marked by scattered zones of demyelination (loss of the fatty insulating layer on nerves). Symptoms start between ages 20 and 40 — usually tingling or numbness in the arms or legs (a 'stocking and glove' pattern) — and progress to weakness, clumsiness, visual and balance problems, dizziness and bladder-control trouble; intention tremor, nystagmus and 'scanning' speech form Charcot's triad. Wallach links MS to mercury (he cross-references mercury poisoning) and to the loss of cholesterol-rich myelin. He criticizes the orthodox cortisone/prednisone approach and instead recommends: avoid animal fats; a high intake of fish oil (cod liver or salmon oil) at 5 grams three times a day and flaxseed oil at one tablespoon twice a day (said to raise survival by 50 percent); removal of mercury (amalgam) fillings; calcium 2-aminoethylphosphate (CaEAP) one dose four times a day; octacosanol two capsules three times a day; daily snake-venom injections; D-phenylalanine at 500 milligrams three times a day; betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day; avoidance of known food allergens with rotation diets; and avoiding vitamin C supplements (using green vegetables and juices as a natural source instead). Wallach says the same regimen has also worked for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, or Lou Gehrig's disease).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000372.claim_text: Mumps is a contagious viral disease that causes painful enlargement of the salivary glands, especially the parotids; the virus is highly aggressive and is present in saliva up to six days before illness is felt. Symptoms include fever (up to 104°F), chills, and tender, shiny, swollen skin over the salivary glands in front of and below the ear. In about 20 percent of adult males it causes a painful testicular infection, and testicular atrophy may follow (though hormone production and fertility are rarely affected). Wallach's treatment is symptomatic: pain relief (codeine, acetaminophen/Tylenol, aspirin), bed rest, a liquid diet (chicken rice soup, sugarless Jello, Gatorade, juices) and the herb mullein (Verbascum thapsus) for symptom relief.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000373.claim_text: Muscular dystrophy (MD) is, in Wallach's view, a preventable selenium-deficiency disease — he points out it has been eliminated in livestock ('white muscle disease') by giving selenium to pregnant females and fast-growing young animals. WAL-CLM-LETS-000380.claim_text: Night blindness (xerophthalmia) is caused by vitamin A deficiency — whether from an outright dietary lack, fat malabsorption (vitamin A is fat-soluble), or zinc deficiency, which impairs the liver's conversion of carotene to vitamin A. Cystic fibrosis, celiac disease and food allergies cause intestinal changes that block absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, E, D and K) and essential fatty acids. The symptom is delayed or complete failure of adaptation to darkness. Wallach's treatment is specific: 25,000-300,000 IU of vitamin A per day as beta carotene and zinc at 15-50 milligrams three times a day.

with 25,000-300,000 IU of vitamin A per day as
beta carotene and zinc at 15-50 mg t.i.d.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000381.claim_text: Night terrors (nightmares) are almost always caused by food allergies and hypoglycemia. Wallach uses the pulse test and a six-hour glucose tolerance test to find the cause, noting blood sugar bottoms out about 4 to 4.5 hours after eating (especially sugary foods), so night terrors tend to strike roughly four hours after a bedtime snack such as cookies and milk. Bedwetting in children often accompanies night terrors and likewise stems from food allergies (usually milk) and hypoglycemia. Treatment: avoid offending food allergens and sugar, chromium at 25-200 micrograms three times a day, a high-animal-protein diet, the baseline nutritional supplement program, and avoid caffeine.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000383.claim_text: Numbness and tingling in both hands (carpal tunnel syndrome) can be caused by neuralgia (diabetes, vitamin B-12 deficiency), circulation problems and the carpal tunnel itself; food allergies can also cause it, and multiple sclerosis should be considered. Tinel's sign (tapping the wrist to elicit pain) is a clue, and orthodox neurologists favor carpal tunnel surgery. Wallach's treatment is aggressive diagnosis and treatment of any underlying condition plus vitamin B-12 at 1,000 micrograms a day, vitamin B-6 at 200-300 milligrams three times a day, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 milligrams a day, zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day, and colloidal minerals.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000384.claim_text: Obesity (overweight) is, at its simplest, consuming and storing more calories than you use — but Wallach stresses it is not simple. Starvation backfires (the body conserves energy), so eat at least 1,000 calories a day for gradual, permanent loss, with moderate exercise (walking, tennis, golf, swimming, low-impact aerobics). He says 90 percent of obese people overeat and binge because empty-calorie diets trigger 'pica' — a nibbling driven by the body's search for trace minerals — so use colloidal minerals. Test for food allergies (pulse test) and do a six-hour glucose tolerance test for hypoglycemia or diabetes. His program: avoid food allergens, sugar (solid and liquid), caffeine and carbonated drinks (phosphates promote osteoporosis); drink filtered spring water, 8-10 glasses a day; use potassium salt with kelp; don't skip meals (large breakfast, moderate lunch with animal protein, light soup-and-salad dinner); salmon oil at 5 grams three times a day, flaxseed oil one tablespoon twice a day, two tablespoons of nutritional fiber before bed, glucomannan at 1 gram before meals, betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day before meals, and thyroid starting at 1-3 grains (adjust to avoid jitteriness; needing over six grains suggests celiac-type malabsorption). Herbal laxatives or diuretic teas and subliminal weight-loss tapes can also help.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000385.claim_text: Obstruction of the airways (choking) is heralded by the 'universal choking sign' — both hands clutched at the throat and loss of speech; it happens often in restaurants (a 'restaurant coronary' mistaken for a heart attack). Prevention: don't talk while chewing and swallowing, especially meat and firm raw vegetables. Treatment: (1) put a finger into the back of the throat and manually remove the obstruction; (2) perform a Heimlich maneuver (stand behind the patient, lock your arms around them with hands just below the xiphoid cartilage and thrust sharply; for babies use hands only). If the obstruction cannot be cleared, Wallach describes an emergency tracheotomy as a last-resort lifesaving measure — a dead-center incision midway between the base of the larynx and the notch where the collarbones meet the breastbone, large enough for the empty barrel of a ballpoint pen to maintain airflow — followed by CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) if the heart has also stopped.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000387.claim_text: Omphalocele (umbilical hernia) is a birth defect — a grape- to basketball-sized, peritoneum-lined skin sac at the navel that may contain fat and/or loops of intestine that can be pushed back into the abdomen. Wallach says it is a common birth defect caused by maternal (and therefore fetal) deficiencies of vitamin A and/or zinc. Treatment: surgery is needed if the hernial ring (the defect in the belly wall) is larger than a fingertip; if it is about a fingertip's diameter it can be healed at home without surgery by taping a golf-ball-sized ball of virgin wool firmly over the hernia and, three times a day, removing it, pushing the fat back in with the fingertip and rubbing the ring in a rotary motion for several minutes to irritate it — over weeks to months the defect fills in and heals.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000389.claim_text: Ornithosis (parrot fever) is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Chlamydia psittaci. It is caught by inhaling contaminated dust from the feathers, cage bedding, or droppings of infected birds — parrots, parakeets, lovebirds, canaries, and pigeons — and produces an 'atypical pneumonia.' Symptoms include fever, chills, weakness, loss of appetite, and a dry cough that becomes productive; early on it can be mistaken for flu, Legionnaires' disease, or Q fever, so exposure to birds (especially sick ones) is the key diagnostic clue, confirmed by a blood test. Treatment is the antibiotic tetracycline by mouth at 250-500 milligrams four times a day for 10-14 days, with the cough controlled by codeine and strict, enforced bed rest — untreated, parrot fever can be fatal.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000390.claim_text: Osteitis fibrosa (nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism), also known as Paget's disease of bone, is a bone disease — more common in men — in which hard bone is lost and replaced by fibrous connective tissue. It often shows up first in the jaw (separating and loosening the teeth), then in the weight-bearing bones of the pelvis, femur, and tibia, with loss of height and a 'dowager's hump' (kyphosis). Mainstream medicine calls the cause unknown, but in animals it comes from a reversed dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio together with relatively large amounts of vitamin D. It is diagnosed by x-ray and by elevated blood alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone. Treatment should include a vigorous effort to correct the dietary calcium/phosphorus ratio: reduce or eliminate red meat, avoid phosphate-containing soft drinks and supplements, reduce vitamin D intake and sun exposure (hats, long sleeves), raise calcium and magnesium intake to 2,000 milligrams and 1,000 milligrams per day, take betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day fifteen minutes before meals, and follow the baseline nutritional supplement program.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000391.claim_text: Osteoporosis is a loss of bone that usually develops in older people, more often in women. Wallach is critical of the standard push for estrogen and fluoride — he says those two alone do not solve the problem, and that estrogen may be contraindicated because of its potential to cause breast and uterine cancer. In his experience osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure with proper supplementation of stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) and calcium. He recommends a pulse test to find any food allergens that could be causing celiac-type changes and malabsorption. Symptoms include bone pain, joint pain, a 'dowager's hump,' and 'spontaneous' fractures; he calls osteoporosis the 12th most frequent cause of death in adults. Treatment should include betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams three times a day fifteen minutes before meals, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 milligrams and 1,000 milligrams per day (or more for the first 30 days), and plant-derived colloidal minerals that include calcium, magnesium, and boron.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000392.claim_text: Otitis (earache) is inflammation of the ear — externa affecting the outer eardrum and ear canal, interna affecting the inner eardrum and the eustachian tube. The standard ear-nose-and-throat approach is antibiotic eardrops and oral antibiotics for acute cases and surgically inserted 'tubes' through the eardrum for chronic ones. Wallach says that in reality 95 percent of all earaches are the result of a milk allergy, which can cause severe fever, painful earaches, and even burst eardrums if not corrected — so do a pulse test before the eardrums are pierced and weakened unnecessarily. Treatment should include hydrogen peroxide or mullein eardrops to relieve local inflammation, strict avoidance of cow's milk in all forms, and the baseline nutritional supplement program; aspirin or acetaminophen (Tylenol) may be needed for pain. Antibiotics are justified only when a streptococcal sore throat or an internal ear infection is cultured.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000395.claim_text: Parasites (worms) include roundworms (ascaris, hookworms, pinworms, whipworms), tapeworms, and microscopic single-celled organisms (amoeba, flagellates). WAL-CLM-LETS-000405.claim_text: Post-partum hemorrhage (bleeding after childbirth) results from an atonic uterus that fails to contract hard enough or long enough, letting the open blood vessels leak (occasionally a retained piece of afterbirth in the uterine lining is the source). Treatment should include firm digital pressure on the fundus of the uterus to stimulate contraction; the use of ergot (Claviceps purpurea) orally at 10-20 minims, or by injection, will add sufficient contraction power.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000405.verbatim:
Treatment of post paitum hemorrhage should
include firm digital pressure on the fundus of
the uterus to stimulate contraction; the use of
ergot (Claviceps purpurea) orally at 10-20
minims or by injection will add sufficient contraction power

WAL-CLM-LETS-000406.claim_text: In his home-medicine guide, Wallach lists two traditional herbs for strengthening labor during childbirth: red raspberry (Rubus idaeus) and blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides), both long used in folk midwifery to encourage effective uterine contractions. He discusses them alongside the tools for controlling postpartum bleeding, such as ergot, in his practical chapter on remedies.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000406.verbatim:
PREGNANCY LABOR (labor): can be enhanced by the use of herbs including raspberry (Rubus idaeus) and blue cohosh

WAL-CLM-LETS-000407.claim_text: Pregnancy toxemia (eclampsia) is, in Wallach's view, the result of the low-protein, low-salt diets women were put on to limit weight gain in pregnancy. Pre-eclampsia symptoms include sudden weight gain (fluid accumulation from low blood protein), high blood pressure, and albuminuria (protein in the urine); eclampsia adds convulsions and/or coma, and both characteristically occur after the 20th week of pregnancy. Against the orthodox approach (hospitalize, watch for convulsions, then give barbiturates), treatment of pre-eclampsia should include a high-animal-protein meal plan (150 grams or more, versus the RDA — Recommended Dietary Allowance — of 40 grams), not restricting salt, vitamin B-6 at 100 milligrams per day (dropping to 50 milligrams at birth if you plan to breast-feed, since high B-6 levels reduce breast-milk production), the baseline nutritional supplement program, and 10-12 glasses of water and/or juice per day, especially in the warm summer months.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000407.verbatim:
Treatment of preeclampsia should include a
high animal protein meal plan (150 gm or
more whereas the RDA is 40 gm), do not
restrict salt, B-6 at 100 mg per day (drop to 50
mg per at parturition (birth) if you plan to
breast freed as high levels of B-6 will reduce
production of breast milk), base line nutritional supplement program and 10-12 glasses
of water and/or juice per day, especially in
the warm summer months

WAL-CLM-LETS-000408.claim_text: Q fever is an acute rickettsial disease caused by Coxiella burnetii, marked by sudden onset, fever, headache, weakness, and pneumonitis (lung inflammation). It has a worldwide distribution and is kept endemic in domestic animals — sheep, goats, and cattle are the primary reservoirs for human infection, which spreads through bites from the infected tick (Dermacentor andersoni) and from drinking infected raw milk; diagnosis is by a positive blood test. Treatment should include tetracycline by mouth at 250 milligrams every 4 hours (chloramphenicol may be used in small children to avoid the tooth discoloration tetracycline can cause).
WAL-CLM-LETS-000408.verbatim:
Treatment of Q fever should include tetracycline orally at 250 mg q 4 h (Chloramphenicol
may be used in small children to prevent
discoloration of permanent teeth by tetracycline

WAL-CLM-LETS-000409.claim_text: Psoriasis is a cosmetically disfiguring dermatitis ('the heartbreak of psoriasis'), marked by dry, sharply demarcated, silvery scaling plaques that appear mainly behind the joints (elbows and knees), on the scalp, and behind the ears. Wallach attributes it to celiac-type changes in the intestines that cause malabsorption of essential nutrients, and advises a pulse test to identify specific food allergens. Treatment should include avoiding offending food allergens, rotation diets, folic acid at 15-25 milligrams per day, vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, lecithin at 2,500 milligrams three times a day with meals, flaxseed oil at one tablespoon twice a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day, copper at 2 milligrams per day, selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day, and betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 milligrams per day. Topical herbal washes and topical vitamin A & D creams are of palliative value.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000409.verbatim:
Treatment of psoriasis should include avoidance of offending food allergens, rotation
diets, folic acid at 15-25 mg per day, vitamin A
at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, lecithin
at 2,500 mg t.i.d. with meals, flaxseed oil at one
tbsp. b.i.d., vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day,
zinc at 50 mg t.i.d., copper at 2 mg per day,

mg per day

WAL-CLM-LETS-000410.claim_text: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is an infection of the tonsil, between the tonsil and the pharyngeal constrictor muscle. It is rare in children but common in young adults. The 'orthodox' ear-nose-and-throat doctor will want to do a tonsillectomy — Wallach urges patients to save their tonsils and refuse it. Treatment should include vitamin A at 300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 milligrams three times a day, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, gargles with herbal washes, and penicillin G or V at 250 milligrams every 6 hours for 12-14 days.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000410.verbatim:
Treatment should include vitamin A at 300,000
IU per day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 mg t.i.d.,
vitamin C to bowel tolerance, gargles with
herbal washes, penicillin G or V at 250 mg q 6
h for 12-14 days.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000411.claim_text: Rabbit fever (tularemia) is caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis, contracted by skinning and dressing infected rabbits or ground squirrels (87 percent of cases). It first appears as a local ulceration at the infection site, then goes systemic into a typhoid-like illness with diarrhea and pneumonia, with high fever and recurring chills and drenching sweats; sputum cultures are highly infectious, so labs should be warned. Treatment of tularemia is with streptomycin intramuscularly at 500 milligrams every 12 hours until the temperature drops into the normal range, then tetracycline by mouth at 250 milligrams four times a day for 10-12 days.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000411.verbatim:
Treatment of tularemia is with streptomycin
IM at 500 mg q 12 h until temperature drops
into the normal range; then give tetracycline
orally at 250 mg q.i.d. for 10-12 days.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000412.claim_text: Rabies (hydrophobia) is a highly dangerous viral disease transmitted through the blood, tissue (including transplanted corneas, livers, kidneys, or hearts), urine, or saliva of infected animals or people. Besides bites from rabid bats, foxes, skunks, and unvaccinated dogs, Wallach notes many fatal cases follow tissue transplants, because rabies in humans is a progressive paralytic disease often misdiagnosed as stroke. He also points out the incubation period is fourteen days, so if you have had the biting pet for three weeks or more, rabies is an impossible diagnosis. Treatment should be started quickly if it is to succeed, and includes the well-known 'rabies shots' every day for ten days plus respiratory support in a hospital setting; high-risk research personnel can get preventive vaccination.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000412.verbatim:
Treatment of rabies should be instituted quickly if success can be anticipated;
treatment includes the well known "rabies
shots" every day for ten days and respiratory
support in a hospital setting

WAL-CLM-LETS-000413.claim_text: Rachitic rosary is the beading at the junction of the ribs and rib cartilage, seen exclusively in small children kept indoors without an oral source of vitamin D; it is easily felt on examination. Wallach treats it as a sign of rickets (vitamin D deficiency). Treatment should include oral vitamin D at 400-1,000 IU per day plus the baseline nutritional supplement program including calcium and magnesium; once the abnormal bony changes normalize, drop the vitamin D dose to 250-400 IU per day, and afford daily sun exposure for at least 30 minutes.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000413.verbatim:

ing" of the junction between the ribs and the

WAL-CLM-LETS-000414.claim_text: Radial nerve palsy ('Saturday night palsy') results from compressing the radial nerve against the humerus — classically by draping the arm over the back of a hard-backed chair for an extended period during a drunken stupor or deep sleep — producing a wrist 'drop,' weakness extending the wrist and fingers, and sometimes a loss of sensory function between the first and second fingers. Treatment should include a B-complex 50 three times a day, topical dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), acupuncture, and hydrotherapy.

nerve palsy is charac-terized by a wrist "drop"

WAL-CLM-LETS-000415.claim_text: Raynaud's disease is marked by tingling and numbness in the fingers (and sometimes the nose and tongue) caused by spasms of the small arteries; the orthodox approach is to cut sympathetic nerves and give anesthetics and tranquilizers. Wallach notes food allergies can be the precipitating factor when arteries are the target tissue (do a pulse test), and to rule out thoracic inlet syndrome. Treatment should include calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, avoiding offending food allergens and caffeine (coffee, tea, soft drinks, chocolate), vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day, L-tryptophan at 500 mg three times a day, acupuncture, chiropractic, and circulation-boosting herbs such as cayenne pepper (Capsicum minimum).

Treatment of Raynaud's disease should include calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg per
day and 1,000 mg per day, avoid offending
food allergens, avoid caffeine (i.e. , coffee, tea,

1,200 IU per day, essential fatty acids at 5 gm

WAL-CLM-LETS-000416.claim_text: Rectal itching can be caused by candidiasis, food allergies, hemorrhoids, crabs, fleas, or pinworms; Wallach advises a pulse test for food allergies, a self/blood/skin test for candidiasis, the Scotch-tape test to identify pinworm eggs, and a mirror to self-examine the anal folds for fleas or hemorrhoids. Treatment can be palliated with a variety of herbal washes (see hemorrhoids), Preparation H, sitz baths with herbal washes and/or hydrogen peroxide, and specific treatments for the underlying parasites.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000416.verbatim:

with a variety of herbal washes (see hemorrhoids), Preparation H, sitz baths with herbal
washes and/or hydrogen peroxide, specific
treatments for parasites

WAL-CLM-LETS-000417.claim_text: Reye's syndrome occurs most often in young teens, usually in fall and winter, and is thought to be caused by consuming aflatoxin (a toxin of the grain mold Aspergillus flavus); it is marked by pneumonitis, nausea and vomiting, a sudden change in mental status to deep depression, amnesia, agitation progressing to coma and convulsions, fixed dilated pupils, and death in 42-80% of cases. Treatment includes barbiturate anesthesia to lower intracranial pressure, intravenous fluids and electrolytes, pulmonary support, exchange transfusions, and dialysis, plus vitamin C intravenously at 5-10 grams per day, B-complex and B-12 intravenously or intramuscularly, and selenium intramuscularly or intravenously at 250-500 mcg per day.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000417.verbatim:
Vitamin C IV at 5-10 gms per day, B-complex
and B-12 IV or IM, selenium IM or IV at 250-
500 mcg per day.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000418.claim_text: Rheumatic fever is caused by a Streptococcus Group A infection (usually starting as a 'strep throat') and is marked by arthritis, skin rash, fever, heart-valve inflammation, and brain signs (chorea); the residual heart-valve damage is the most dangerous consequence of untreated disease, and diagnosis rests on the typical symptoms plus positive Group A Streptococcus cultures. Treatment early in the course prevents the heart damage and should include aspirin for joint pain and sulfadiazine orally at 500-1,000 mg per day for 1-2 years, or penicillin G or V orally at 250,000 units twice a day for two years.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000418.verbatim:
Treatment of rheumatic fever early in the
course of the disease will prevent the heart
damage. Treatment should include aspirin for
joint pain and sulfadiazine orally at 500-1,000
mg/day for 1 -2 years or penicillin G or V orally
at 250,000 u. b.i.d. for two years.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000419.claim_text: Wallach holds that rheumatoid arthritis is not primarily an immune-system disease but is initially caused by infection with a Mycoplasma (PPLO, a pleuropneumonia-like organism) that causes an upper-respiratory infection and then attacks the joint membranes of the fingers and toes, and later the larger joints — a cause he says has been recognized and eliminated in veterinary medicine. Orthodox treatment (aspirin, gold shots, steroids) only relieves symptoms, though he notes 75% of patients improve in the first year with no treatment at all. Treatment should include specific treatment for Mycoplasma/PPLO (Tylosin, tetracyclines, etc.) for six months to one year, intravenous and/or oral hydrogen peroxide, chelation, acupuncture, enterically coated bromelain at 40 mg four times a day, autoimmune urine therapy, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), L-histidine at 1,000 mg three times a day, essential fatty acids at 5 grams three times a day, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, selenium at 500-1,000 mcg per day, copper at 2-4 mg per day, B-6 at 100 mg three times a day, cartilage at 5 grams three times a day, hydrotherapy, and herbs (topical camphor, black mustard, dandelion, devil's claw, juniper, stinging nettle, sweet vernal grass), plus plant-derived colloidal minerals.

(PPLO) (i.e., Tylosin, tetracyclines, etc.), for

benifit here.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000420.claim_text: Rickets is caused by a deficiency of vitamin D and is marked by stunted growth, joint pain, and deformed long bones (bow legs, dropped wrists, 'sickle shins,' barrel chest, rachitic rosary). Treatment includes supplementation with vitamin D at 400 IU orally, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, and exposure to sunshine for 30 minutes per day; advanced cases will require orthotic correction and, in some cases, orthopedic surgery.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000420.verbatim:
Treatment of rickets includes supple-mentation
with vitamin D at 400 IU orally, calcium and
magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1 ,000 mg per day,
and exposure to sunshine for 30 minutes per
day.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000421.claim_text: Ringworm is caused by fungi (most often Microsporum/Tinea capitis or Trichophyton/Tinea cruris, 'jock itch') that invade the skin, nails, and hair, producing the characteristic circular lesions; cats, rabbits, and children are the most common sources, and diagnosis is by the typical lesions, fungal culture, and a positive Wood's lamp test (Microsporum lesions fluoresce a bright pastel green). Treatment should include Griseofulvin orally at 250 mg four times a day for four months, vitamin A at 25,000-300,000 IU per day as beta carotene, zinc at 50 mg three times a day, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, ultraviolet light directly to the lesion for up to six minutes per day, and topical herbs including plantain (Plantago major) and castor oil (Ricinus communis).
WAL-CLM-LETS-000421.verbatim:
Treatment of ringworm should include
Griseofulvin orally at 250 mg q.i.d. for four
months, vitamin A at 25,000-300,000 IU/day as
beta carotene, zinc at 50 mg t.i.d., vitamin E at
800-1,200 IU/day, ultra violet light directly to
lesion for up to six minutes per day, and herbs
topically including plantain (Plantgo major)
and castor oil (Ricinus communis).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000422.claim_text: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (tick fever) is caused by a rickettsia (Rickettsia rickettsii) transmitted by the bite of an infected tick (wood, dog, or lone-star tick); it occurs May through October during tick season, mostly along the Eastern seaboard, and affects small children with access to wooded areas (often via the family dog). Symptoms follow 7-12 days after a bite — headaches, chills, weakness, muscle pain, fever, dry cough, and a skin rash starting on the wrists, ankles, palms, soles, and forearms then spreading. Wallach warns: do NOT wait for a positive blood test before starting treatment, as death may occur as quickly as 4-10 days after symptoms appear. Treatment should include tetracycline at 500 mg four times a day orally, or intravenously if the patient cannot swallow capsules, plus supportive intravenous fluids and electrolytes.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000422.verbatim:
Treatment of RMSF should include tetracycline at 500 mg q.i.d. orally or IV if the patient
can't swallow capsules. Supportive treatment
with rv fluids and electrolytes is essential to
rapid and full recovery

WAL-CLM-LETS-000423.claim_text: Roseola is an acute viral disease of infants and toddlers marked by high fever (up to 105 F) and a rash that predominates on the belly and chest and lightly on the face and limbs; convulsions may occur during the high-fever periods, and after 3-4 days the child feels completely well even though the rash persists. Treatment is directed to reducing the fever sufficiently to prevent convulsions, plus topical poultices on the rash (see measles).
WAL-CLM-LETS-000423.verbatim:
Treatment of roseola is directed to reducing
the fever sufficiently to prevent convulsions
and topical poultices on the rash (see measles).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000424.claim_text: Scabies ('itch') is caused by an almost microscopic mite (Sarcoptes scabiei) that burrows into the skin; it is very contagious person-to-person, and the original infestation usually comes from an infected animal or contaminated animal bedding. Treatment includes total-body application of 1% gamma benzene hexachloride (lindane) or 25% benzyl benzoate cream in adults, and 5-10% sulfur ointment in infants to avoid potential neurotoxicity; poke (Phytolacca decandra) may be used topically as a natural alternative.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000424.verbatim:
Treatment of scabies includes total body application of 1% gamma benzene hexachloride, 25% benzyl benzoate cream in adults and
5-10% sulfur ointment in infants to avoid potential neurotoxicity; poke (Phytolacca

alternative

WAL-CLM-LETS-000425.claim_text: Scarlatina (scarlet fever) is caused by a Streptococcus Group A throat infection; the organism releases a toxin that produces a rash most common on the belly, sides, and skin folds, plus a red pulpy 'strawberry' tongue, with fever common in the early stages. Aggressive treatment is recommended to prevent death or rheumatic fever, and diagnosis rests on the characteristic lesions plus positive Group A Streptococcus throat cultures. Treatment of scarlatina is oral penicillin V at 250 mg four times a day for 10-14 days.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000425.verbatim:
Treatment of scarlatina is oral peni-cillin V at
250 mg q.i.d. for 10-14 days.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000426.claim_text: Sciatica (low back pain radiating down the buttocks and legs) can be caused by subluxations of the lumbar vertebrae, thinning of a lumbar intervertebral disc, or even a thick wallet in one back pocket; in its most severe form it may result from a ruptured intervertebral disc. Treatment should include hydrotherapy, chiropractic, acupuncture, inversion-gravity therapy, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, and the baseline nutritional supplement program including plant-derived colloidal minerals.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000426.verbatim:
Treatment of sciatica should include hydrotherapy, chiropractic, acupuncture, inversion-gravity therapy, calcium and magnesium at
2,000 mg per day and 1, 000 mg per day and the
baseline nutritional supplement program to
include plant derived colloidal minerals

WAL-CLM-LETS-000427.claim_text: Scoliosis (curvature of the spine) occurs in preteens and teens (80% in girls) during rapid growth; it may be benign or herald early muscular dystrophy, and Wallach attributes it to one set of spinal muscles being stronger than the other from muscle degeneration, with celiac-type intestinal damage and malabsorption as a possible cause. Treatment in the early stages will result in a complete cure, while failure to aggressively supplement leads to persistent damage requiring back braces and surgery. Treatment should include avoidance of offending food allergens, vitamin E at 800-1,200 IU per day, selenium at 500-1,000 mcg per day, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day, and the baseline supplement program including plant-derived colloidal minerals; chiropractic can be very useful for the associated back-muscle spasms.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000427.verbatim:
Treatment of scoliosis in the early stages will
result in a complete cure; failure to aggressively take supplements will result in persistent damage requiring back braces and surgery. Treatment should include avoidance of
offending food allergens, vitamin E at 800-
1,200 IU per day, selenium at 500-1,000 mcg
per day, calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg
and 1,000 mg per day

WAL-CLM-LETS-000428.claim_text: Scurvy (bleeding gums) is caused by a vitamin C deficiency and may occur concurrently with gingivitis. Treatment should include vitamin C to bowel tolerance, increased intake of green leafy vegetables and fruit, and herbs including dog rose (Rosa canina).

dog rose (Rosa canina

WAL-CLM-LETS-000429.claim_text: A sebaceous cyst (wen, steatoma) is a slow-growing benign cystic skin 'tumor' containing sebaceous material, frequently found on the scalp (wen), ears, back, or scrotum; it ranges from pea- to golf-ball-sized, is firm (like a soft-shell egg), and painless. Treatment includes a 'stab' incision at the lowest edge of the cyst, evacuating the contents, and flushing with hydrogen peroxide; large cysts require removal of the cyst wall to prevent refilling, placing a sterile gauze drain in the empty cyst and gradually removing it over 7-10 days.

In the same passage he reports that it also inhibits cholesterol synthesis (lowering both blood and aortic cholesterol) and shows anticarcinogenic properties in animal studies, where it blocked induced mammary tumors in mice. Vanadium is best known in his framework as chromium's partner against adult-onset diabetes.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000255.verbatim: Vanadium initiates an increase in the contractile force of heart muscle known as the “inotropic effect.”

WAL-CLM-RARE-000256.claim_text: Beyond its better-known role against diabetes, vanadium acts on cholesterol, Wallach reports: it inhibits the body's synthesis of cholesterol in both animals and humans, and the result is lower cholesterol in the blood plasma and less cholesterol built up in the aorta, the body's main artery. He presents this alongside vanadium's insulin-sensitizing and anticarcinogenic effects as part of the case for treating it as an essential trace mineral for heart and metabolic health.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000256.verbatim: Vanadium inhibits cholesterol synthesis in animals and humans; this is followed by decreased plasma levels of cholesterol and reduced aortic cholesterol.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000258.claim_text: Xenon is a rare, chemically inert noble gas that Wallach includes in his catalog of trace elements, noting it occurs in nature only in vanishingly small amounts. Its one notable biological action, he says, is that it binds to hemoglobin and myoglobin — the iron-based proteins that carry and store oxygen in the blood and muscles — producing an anesthetic effect, a loss of sensation or consciousness. That property is the basis for xenon's real-world use as an anesthetic gas.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000258.verbatim: Xenon binds to mammalian hemoglobin and myoglobin producing an anesthetic effect.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000259.verbatim: Yttrium enhances normal cell growth and doubles the life span of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000260.claim_text: Wallach reports that yttrium readily crosses the placenta — exposure of pregnant mice to yttrium leads to rapid placental transfer, with 14 percent of ingested yttrium detectable in the newborn mice.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000308.claim_text: Wallach attributes aneurysms to copper deficiency. Copper is the cofactor for lysyl oxidase, the enzyme that cross-links pro-elastin into elastin, the protein that gives artery walls their tensile (elastic) strength. When copper is deficient, lysyl oxidase activity falls, elastin isn't properly formed, and the weakened arterial walls balloon and rupture as aneurysms. He points to famous "ruptured aneurysm" deaths (Albert Einstein and Conway Twitty among them) as copper-deficiency cases, and notes that four to six of every 100 Americans autopsied have died of a ruptured aneurysm, with another 40 percent carrying aneurysms that had not yet ruptured.
