than silver and they used eight platinum
lightning rods to protect it).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000392.claim_text: Wallach holds that gold, silver and copper were probably the first metals humans discovered, encountered in their native nugget form. He reasons gold was likely first of all, being the most widely distributed metal found as nuggets in nature; because gold resists corrosion, the bright color of a nugget would catch a primitive person's eye, and its refusal to chip or break like ordinary tool-making rocks would spark curiosity. Its beauty made gold a prized ornament long before it had any practical use.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000392.verbatim:
Gold, silver and copper were probably
the first metals (minerals) discovered in
their native nugget form.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000393.claim_text: Cerium has a documented history as a medicine. Wallach recounts that in 1854 James Young Simpson, a professor of obstetrics at the University of Edinburgh, supported using oxalate of cerium to treat the morning sickness of early pregnancy. In 1860 Charles Lee, a house physician at Blockley Hospital in Philadelphia, reported successfully using cerium to control the vomiting associated with phthisis (pulmonary tuberculosis), pyrosis (severe heartburn), hysterical vomiting, and atonic dyspepsia — a lack of muscular tone in the gastrointestinal tract.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000393.verbatim:
In 1854 James Young Simpson (1811-
1870) a professor of obstetrics at the University of Edinburgh supported the use of
oxalate of cerium to treat the morning sickness associated with early pregnancy. In
1860 Charles Lee, house physician to
Blockley Hospital, Philadelphia reported
the successful use of cerium for the control
of vomiting associated with phthisis (pulmonary tuberculosis), pyrosis (severe heart
burn), hysterical vomiting and atonic
dyspepsia ( lack of muscular tone of the
gastrointestinal tract).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000394.claim_text: Wallach recounts that a Dr. Costa reported using bromide of nickel as a therapy for epilepsy and similar diseases. He notes that in an 1884 'controlled' study at the Jefferson Medical College Hospital in Philadelphia, nickel was reported to work best in cases where the attacks came regularly and at long intervals, and where the case had a hysterical or hypochondriacal feature.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000394.verbatim:
Dr. Costa reported the use of bromide
of nickel as a therapy for epilepsy and similar diseases. In 1884 a “controlled” study
was made at the Jefferson Medical college
Hospital, Philadelphia; it was reported that
“nickel worked best in cases where attacks
occurred regularly and at long intervals and
when there was a hysterical or hypochondriacal feature to the case.”

WAL-CLM-RARE-000395.claim_text: Wallach recounts the historical medicinal use of barium: the 18th-century physician Adair Crawford, at St. Thomas Hospital, investigated 'barytes' (chlorinated barium) and found it useful in certain cases of scrophulous — tuberculosis of the cervical lymph nodes — and believed it usually improved the appetite and general health. Barium was also reported to act as an evacuant and a deobstruent, though it carried toxic side effects including nausea and vertigo. Today, he notes, barium's medical role is different: barium sulfate serves as the opaque contrast medium for X-rays of the digestive tract.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000395.verbatim:
Adair Crawford (1748-1795), physician
at St. Thomas Hospital investigated the
therapeutic value of barytes (chlorinated
barium) and determined that it was useful
in certain cases of scrophulous (tuberculosis of the cervical lymph nodes), he also
thought that it usually improved the appetite and general health. Barium was also
reported to act as an evacuant, a
deobstruent, and a toxic side effect noted
included nausea and vertigo.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000396.claim_text: Wallach pushes back on the idea that arsenic is nothing but a poison. He recounts that arsenic stayed an active medicine well into the 20th century — research into its medical uses remained vigorous until 1945, when penicillin took over as the preferred treatment for syphilis — and that it is still used today for sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis) and amoebic diseases. His conclusion: it is now generally accepted that, in trace levels, arsenic is in fact an essential element for optimal health and longevity.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000396.verbatim:
Research in the medical uses of arsenic
remained very active until 1945 when penicillin came into general medical use and was
thought to be a superior treatment for syphilis with fewer side effects. Arsenic is still used
today for the systemic treatment of sleeping
sickness (Trypanosomiasis) and amoebic
diseases. It is now generally accepted that
arsenic is in fact in trace levels an essential
element for optimal health and longevity.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000397.claim_text: Wallach traces tin's long medicinal history. In the Middle Ages, Paracelsus first recommended tin to expel intestinal worms, and it was also used as a sweat-inducer and as a purgative for fevers, hysterical complaints (which Wallach glosses as PMS), and venereal diseases. He notes alchemists even alloyed tin with mercury and distilled it with sulfur and ammonium chloride to make a gold-colored pigment they called mosaic gold.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000397.verbatim:
expel worms in the Middle Ages. Alchemists
produced mosaic gold (aurum musivum) by
alloying tin with mercury and then distilling this mixture with sulfur and ammonium
chloride. The resultant gold-like color gave
it its name. Tin was also used as a sweat
inducer and a purgative for fevers, hysterical complaints (PMS) and venereal diseases.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000398.claim_text: In his chapter on toxic metals, Wallach lists canned foods as a hidden dietary source of lead: the sealant used to close the seams of steel and tin cans leaches lead into the food sitting inside. He points to tuna as the clearest example, citing a study in which canned tuna carried nearly double the level of lead found in the same fish sold fresh. He frames this as just one of several everyday routes — alongside leaded-gasoline residue settled on crops, chipping old lead paint, and lead-glazed imported pottery mistakenly used for food — by which lead, which he calls one of the most universally dangerous toxic metals, quietly enters the body.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000398.verbatim:
Another source of lead in our food chain
is the sealant materials used to close the
seams in steel or tin canned foods. One
study showed that canned tuna has nearly
double the level of lead as fresh tuna.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000399.claim_text: Silver nitrate — historically called 'lunar caustic,' a name rooted in silver's ancient association with the moon (the same link behind words like 'moonstruck' and 'lunacy') — has a long medicinal history. In 1637 Angelus Sala used it as a purgative and for brain and uterine illness, and Robert Boyle rolled silver nitrate and nitre into bread-crust pills the size of small peas as a laxative. Beginning in 1826, John Higginbottom of Nottingham, England used lunar caustic to treat wounds and ulcers (from needles, hooks, bayonets, saws, leech and rabid-animal bites, and insect stings), to remove tumors, and to cauterize surgical wounds, and later described its use against erysipelas, varicose ulcers, diabetic (senile) gangrene, and burns. Its most enduring application came in 1884, when the German obstetrician Carl Sigmund Crede began placing a single drop of 2% silver nitrate in each newborn's eyes at birth to prevent gonorrheal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum); a diluted 1/2% solution became a standard burn treatment only after Carl A. Moyer's work in 1965.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000399.verbatim:
Angelus Sala (1637) employed silver nitrate (lunar caustic) as a
purgative and in brain and uterine illnesses.
Robert Boyle concocted pilulae lunara by
creating a mixture of silver nitrate and nitre,
dried and formed with bread crusts into pills
the size of small peas as a laxative.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000400.claim_text: Wallach ties adolescent violence partly to hormones interacting with nutrition. He points to the surge of the 'male hormone testosterone' during puberty, roughly ages 14 to 18, and argues that when it lands on top of specific mineral deficiencies — he names copper, chromium, vanadium and lithium — and a high-sugar diet (fruit juices, sodas, candy, ice cream, sugary cereals), the result fills jails and death rows with teenage killers. He calls testosterone surges, high sugar intake and mineral deficiencies 'as explosive a mixture as matches, nitroglycerine and gun powder combined.' It is a characteristic Wallach stance: behavior conventionally blamed on psychology or environment, reframed as a fixable hormonal-and-nutritional problem.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000400.verbatim:
Putting together the appearence of the
male hormone testosterone during puberty
between 14 and 18, mineral deficiencies
(especially copper, chromium, vanadium
and lithium ) and high sugar intakes (i.e.-
apple juice, grape juice, sugar drinks, colas, ice cream, candy, boxed cereals, pastries of all kinds, etc.), it is not surprising
that our jails are full and death row is populated by hundreds of teens waiting to be
executed for murder!!! Testosterone surges,
high sugar intake and mineral deficiencies
are as explosive a mixture as matches, nitroglycerine and gun powder combined!!!

WAL-CLM-RARE-000401.claim_text: Wallach counts honey as a sugar to eliminate, not a health food. He argues that sugar loads - natural and processed alike - raise the body's normal rate of mineral loss in sweat and urine by 300% for 12 hours, so honey on your English muffin at breakfast, ice cream at lunch, and a pastry at dinner will flush minerals out faster than any amount of supplementation or dieting can replace. He places honey squarely on his 'no' list alongside molasses, table sugar, and sweet juices, and notes that giving up sugar also sheds weight, clears thinking, reduces irritability, and moves anyone with hypoglycemia halfway toward fixing their problem.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000401.verbatim:
The next step in the See-Food Diet
program is to eliminate sugar, natural and
processed (sugar loads increase the
normal rate of mineral loss in sweat and
urine by 300 % for 12 hours - so if you
have honey on your English muffin for
breakfast, ice cream for dessert at lunch
and a pastry for dinner dessert, no
amount of mineral supplementation or no
diet will ever allow you to keep up with
or make up for your mineral losses).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000402.claim_text: Wallach holds that no named diet makes the real difference to health, because "we are what's in (or isn't in) the food we eat." He lists the Mediterranean Diet alongside the Beverly Hills, Atkins, Fit for Life, Immune Power, Pritikin, Macrobiotic, Life Extension and 120 Year diets, veganism, an Eskimo blubber diet, and eating dozens of burgers a day, and says it does not matter which you follow: unless you supplement daily with optimal amounts of each of the 90 essential nutrients, you throw away 50 to 75% of your life as surely as if you had jumped in front of a speeding train.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000402.verbatim:
therefore it matters not whether
one follows the concepts of the Beverly
Hills Diet, Dr. Atkin’s Diet, the Fit for Life
Diet,the Mediterranean Diet, Dr. Berger’s
Immune Power Diet, The Pritikin Diet,
the Macrobiotic Diet, Pearson's and
Shaw’s Life Extension Diet, The 120 Year
Diet, become a vegan or a carnivore and
eat blubber like an Eskimo or eat dozens
of burgers each day like Wimpy (the
original “junk food junky” from Popeye
cartoons) - if you don’t supplement daily
with optimal amounts of each of the 90
essential nutrients your throwing from 50
to 75% of your life away as sure as if you
had jumped in front of a speeding
commuter train.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000403.claim_text: Wallach lists sciatica among calcium-deficiency low-back problems whose complicating factors include deficiencies of magnesium, boron, copper, sulfur, selenium and strontium, plus an excess of phosphorus and dietary fat.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000403.verbatim:
Low back (sciatica, muscle spasm, disc problems)
Bell's Palsy (drooping facial muscle because of strangulated facial nerve)
NSH (nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism)
Osteofibrosis (enlargement of bones with fibrous scar tissue)
Tetany (convulsions, usually in infants fed undiluted cows milk which contains more phosphorus than calcium)
Panic attacks (hyperirritability)
Complicating factors: deficiencies of Mg, B, Cu, S, Se, St, Ac, Fl and excess of Fl, P, Cd, fat, Vit. D.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000404.claim_text: Wallach cites the NIH confirmation that peptic ulcers come from a bacterium and that drug therapy - a combination of bismuth, tetracycline, and metronidazole - can cure the ulcer and prevent a recurrence in 90% of cases.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000404.verbatim:
ULCER CAUSE: The National Institutes of Health
has confirmed that peptic ulcers can be caused by a
bacterium and drug therapy can prevent a recurrence in
90% of cases. An NIH panel stated Wednesday that
Helicobacter pylori plays a significant role in causing peptic
ulcer, which can be cured with a combination of bismuth,
tetracycline and metronidazole.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000405.claim_text: Wallach notes that certain food allergies, especially to dairy, can set off explosive, sociopathic behavior -- so a child's aggression can trace back to what they eat.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000405.verbatim:
mineral deficiencies aggravated by high
sugar diets (it is also known that certain
food allergies, especially dairy can initiate
explosive sociopathic behavior).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000406.claim_text: In the Maybrick case Wallach reads leg cramps so severe "they were like iron bars" as a calcium deficiency, and the accompanying leg numbness as a B-vitamin deficiency — a vivid picture of mineral-starved legs.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000406.verbatim:
Maybrick became seriously ill in April
26, 1889 and his doctor was summoned
because of headaches (hypoglycemia or
diabetes resulting from chromium and vanadium deficiencies), numbness ( B12 deficiency) of his legs and leg cramps (calcium
deficiency) so bad “they were like iron
bars.”

WAL-CLM-RARE-000407.claim_text: Wallach lists muscle aches, pains, and cramps among the symptoms of hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's disease), so a sluggish thyroid can be part of why the legs cramp and ache.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000407.verbatim:
SYMPTOMS of HYPOTHYROIDISM
(Hashimoto's Disease)
Fatigue
Cold intolerance
Muscle aches & pains
Heavy or more frequent periods
Low sex drive
Brittle nails
Weight gain
Hair loss
Muscle cramps
Depression
Constipation

WAL-CLM-RARE-000408.claim_text: Wallach attributes osteoporosis and ankylosing spondylitis, an inflammatory low-back arthritis, to deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, boron, copper and sulfur.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000408.verbatim:
Table 7-8. Common Degenerative Diseases of Humans and Their Cause.
Osteoporosis: Ca, Mg, B, Cu, S
Arthritis (Ankylosing spondylitis): Ca, Mg, B, Cu, S
Hypertension: Ca, Mg, B
Bone spurs, heel spurs, Ca deposits: Ca, Mg, B

WAL-CLM-RARE-000409.claim_text: Wallach lists infertility and a decreased sperm count among the diseases of chromium deficiency, tying the blood-sugar mineral to male reproductive health.

Table 11-12. Diseases and Symptoms

Low blood sugar
Prediabetes

Learning disabilities

WAL-CLM-RARE-000410.claim_text: Rare Earths reprints Schuessler's cell-salt table, which lists Calcarea Fluor (calcium fluoride) — a component of the elastic fibers of skin and blood vessels — for the relaxed elastic fibers behind dilated vessels, hemorrhoids, and enlarged varicose veins.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000410.verbatim:
Calcarea Fluor (Fluoride of lime) - is found in the surface of the bones, in the enamel of the teeth and in the elastic fibers of the skin,
muscular tissue and blood vessels. A deficiency results in a relaxed condition of the tissues and is a predisposing cause in a number
of diseases. It is indicated in ailments which can be traced to a relaxed condition of elastic fibers, including dilation of the blood vessels,
haemorrhoids, enlarged varicose veins, hardened glands, cracks in the skin, etc.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000411.claim_text: In Wallach's rundown of Schuessler's cell salts, Calcarea Sulph (sulphate of lime) is named as the remedy for slow-healing skin eruptions, including pimples and pustules of the face.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000411.verbatim:
Calcarea Sulph (Sulphate of Lime) - is found in the epithelial cells in the blood. It acts as a preventitive of cell disintegration and
suppuration. A deficiency allows suppuration to continue too long; therefore, wounds that are too slow to heal (i.e.- catarrhs, boils,
carbuncles, ulcers, abscesses, pimples and pustules of the face) need this remedy.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000412.claim_text: Wallach says a hair analysis showing all minerals uniformly low points to malabsorption -- often from a hidden wheat gluten or cow's milk allergy damaging the gut.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000412.verbatim: If all of the mineral levels in the hair analysis are universally low it indicates maldigestion ( hypochlorhydria - low stomach acid) and/or malabsorption ( celiac disease - wheat gluten or cows milk albumen allergy).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000413.claim_text: Wallach warns that vegetarians and vegans who don't supplement always develop mineral deficiencies -- including bone-building calcium and copper -- because of their high phytic-acid intake.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000413.verbatim: Vegetarians and vegans who do not supplement with minerals rarely have P deficiency, however, because of their high phytic acid intake they always have other mineral deficiencies including Ca, Cu, Cr, V. Li and Zn.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000414.claim_text: Wallach points out that traditional Eskimos eat a diet that is roughly 90% meat, blubber and fish yet have no cholesterol problems, because the essential fatty acids in cold-water fish let the liver process cholesterol properly.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000414.verbatim:
Although the Eskimo diet
is comprised 90% of meat (i.e.- whale
meat, whale blubber, walrus meat, walrus
blubber, reindeer meat, fish, etc.) and
bone, they do not have heart disease,
cholesterol problems or strokes. The
salmon and other cold water fish in their
diet provide rich sources of the essential
fatty acids required by the liver to
properly process cholesterol and prevent
platelet clumping.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000415.claim_text: Wallach shows the effect of sugar on behavior with a child's own drawings — a six-year-old's giraffe drawn before a high-sugar breakfast versus the same child's degraded drawing an hour and a half after — as a simple at-home way to spot sugar-driven ADD/ADHD tied to low chromium, vanadium and lithium.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000415.verbatim:
A. Six year olds drawing of a giraffe before high sugar breakfast.

B. Same six year olds drawing of a giraffe one and a half hours after a high sugar breakfast.

Simple method for diagnosing ADD and ADHD associated with high sugar low Cr, V and Li diets.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000416.claim_text: Wallach recounts that magnesium-rich Epsom water was taken as a medicine for constipation and prized as a very effective purgative.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000416.verbatim:
Before long this magnesium rich
spring was found to produce water that was
beneficial for external and internal medical use. For the next 10 years only the local
people used this healing spring; about that
time Lord Dudley North “under a melancholy disposition (constipation, depression), drank the mineral waters as a medicine and noted it to be a very effective purgative.” “Epsom Water” was rapidly accepted as an internal remedy and purifier
of the blood.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000417.claim_text: Wallach relays that taking bismuth, the active ingredient still sold today as Pepto-Bismol, reliably produces constipation.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000417.verbatim:
The French physician Armand Trousseau (1801-1867) stated,” when an individual in good health takes sub-nitrate of
bismuth, the only phenomenon to be noticed is constipation, but the nervous functions, the animal heat, the movements of
the heart, the urinary and cutaneous secretions are not influenced in an appreciable
manner.”

In 1868 Adolf Kussmaul used bismuth
to treat gastric ulcers. Bismuth is still in
general use today as an OTC (over the
counter “drug”) to soothe the irritated gastrointestinal tract, diarrhea and dyspepsia
as the tasty pink Pepto Bismol!!

WAL-CLM-RARE-000418.claim_text: Wallach flags common muscle relaxants - cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril), orphenadrine (Norflex), and methocarbamol (Robaxin) - as causing dizziness, drowsiness and falls, and offers calcium, magnesium, boron and lithium as the mineral replacement.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000418.verbatim:
Muscle Relaxants, Spasm Relievers — Mineral Replacement: Ca, Mg, B, Li:
Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril) - Causes dizziness, drowsiness, fainting, falls.
Orphenadrine (Norflex, Norgesic) - Causes dizziness, drowsiness, fainting, falls.
Methocarbamol (Robaxin) - Causes dizziness, drowsiness, falls.
